text:
Polymarket Unveils Protocol V2, Targeting Full Mainnet Switchover on Nov 2

Polymarket Head of Protocol Rajath Alex announced Polymarket Protocol V2, replacing its legacy 2019 Gnosis CTF foundation to eliminate architectural bloat. Protocol V2 unifies the system around a single ERC-1155 position contract, pUSD collateral, and a consolidated exchange and router across all market types. The modular design natively supports binary, neg-risk, and combinatorial markets, integrates a multi-oracle aggregator (supporting UMA and Chainlink), and embeds cross-chain bridging. Formally verified by Certora, heavily audited, and backed by a $5M bug bounty, V2 will test canary markets from October 5 to 30 ahead of a planned November 2 rollout alongside a new Rust-based Data API V2.

这句话本质上是透露了OKX在现阶段在做什么，以及下一阶段想做什么。

互联网解决信息传递，Crypto解决价值流动，而AI解决了智能规模化与个性化。当三者融合，传统意义上的金融服务即被重新定义。

确实，未来不是正在到来，而是已经发生。

quoted_text:
seeing some confusion in the $BUN tg about "revenue" vs "fees" vs agent PnL

there are 3 separate money buckets on Mosh and they keep getting mixed up, so here's the breakdown (numbers from Mosh's BUN page as of today)

bucket 1: fees to the bundle backer

every trade in BUN's Pons pool pays a creator fee. 80% of it goes to whoever funded the bundle. 

BUN's backer has been paid 83.79 ETH so far (84.17 ETH counting what's still unclaimed), 10.5x the 8 ETH raise. BUN had 1 backer -> the Mosh team

bucket 2: Mosh's revenue

Mosh keeps the other 20% of creator fees, which works out to about ~21 ETH on BUN. it also takes a one-time 5% of every bundle raise to cover the agents' gas and compute for life. 

the "Revenue" counter on the homepage is the gross amount. it covers every Mosh launch and includes fees paid to backers, not just Mosh's cut

the team says revenue is being locked in a trading vault with a mandate to accumulate as much BUN as possible. no fixed % yet, they're just loading it up for now

bucket 3: agent vault cash

this is the impressive one. BUN's 3 agents have made 367 trades since launch, buying 1.55M BUN for 8.57 ETH and selling 4.87M BUN for 84.05 ETH. 

their average sell is 211% above their average buy, cash is up 75.48 ETH and they still hold 710.96M BUN, ~71% of supply. they've sold less than half a % of their inventory to build that cash. 

all 3 agents are in profit, from +15.9 to +39.17 ETH each. Mosh puts the swarm's trading PnL at +83.99 ETH, mostly because the bundle bought its BUN at launch for almost nothing

important to note that ETH stays with the agents

its not revenue and it isn't fees, but it's what lets them keep bidding when the market sells, which keeps volume flowing, which keeps paying fees to the backer

this is how https://t.co/4Q0YPekxP2 what turns every token launched on Mosh into a lifetime fee generator

text:
现在用 AI 自动做科研，最怕的其实是一处没人发现的 bug：

后面十轮实验，可能全建立在一个假结果上。

这篇 RankEvolve 研究的，就是 Auto-Research 里的「执行可靠性」。

长时 ML 实验中，Agent 很容易引入数据泄漏、漏掉归一化、断开梯度，甚至配置根本没生效。代码能跑、指标也正常，但实验已经失真。

RankEvolve 主要做了三件事：

把研究流程编译成可执行的状态机，强制 Agent 按协议推进；

让 Claude Code、Codex、OpenHands 等不同 Coding Agent 互相 review 和 repair；

保存每轮 patch、配置、指标和失败经验，避免后续重复踩坑。

在相同预算下，异构 Agent 协作把执行正确率从 45.8% 提升到 62.5%。

连续 12 轮自动研究后，在 MovieLens-20M LARGE 上，NDCG@10 比公开基线提升 4.48%。

所以 Auto-Research 跑得越久，越要先保证每一轮实验都值得相信。

否则「自我进化」很容易变成持续放大一个早期错误。

Today we are open-sourcing Matilda Jev, Australia's first decision model, conditioned for Australian deployment and post-trained with our own specialised recipe. Decision models do not generate text. They answer a typed question and respond with a calibrated probability for each option in a single forward pass, reducing hallucination and making intelligent decisions faster and more efficient.

This release proves that highly capable AI models can be built, post-trained, evaluated, and served entirely within Australia. Post-trained end-to-end on our local infrastructure, the model achieved a median decision latency of 56.8ms on a single @AMD MI355X across 150,317 evaluation requests.

Today we're unveiling Trillium Labs @trillium_labs, a new non-profit to foster the open science of frontier AI. We're building open post-training recipes and will expand into open infra to study RSI, reward-hacking, multi-agent systems, and whatever comes next.

We're built around the theory of change that you need more eyes to solve hard technical problems. We have faith in the scientific methods and communities that humanity has built, and worry that AI is becoming too closed to utilize them.

Trilliums are wildflowers that bloom briefly in the spring, before the forest canopies fill out. Though they are small, they lay the foundation for the cycles of growth and nourishment through the rest of the year. At Trillium Labs, the recipes will be the slow nutrients for the seasons and the model releases will be the blooms. Building an institution dedicated to this is needed because, much as nature’s trilliums are slow to expand and grow, the open-ecosystem needs time and dedicated resources to catch up.

I co-founded with with a long-time friend and collaborator Tom Zick (@thesezickbeats). We're hiring (full time + student collabs/interns), we're fundraising, and we're looking for compute. Please get in touch if you're interested in helping out. Offices based in the Bay Area and Cambridge MA, remote okay.

I’m in the Bay Area until for The Curve and COLM to connect with people who are interested. We’re thankful to have initial support from Halcyon Futures and Schmidt Sciences with more funding en route to enable our ambitions of scaling. Our advisors @Thom_Wolf, @HannaHajishirzi, @gneubig and @ctnzr have been instrumental to building the ecosystem that exists today, and I’m stoked to get to keep working with them.

author: sized_in
quoted_text:
Let’s talk about my biggest onchain conviction play. $Crawl

@crawlnetwork is one of those projects where I think people are looking at the first product & missing the actual company being built.

The obvious thing is “crypto LLM.” The bigger thesis is a model that becomes the intelligence layer for an entire industry, with the industry itself economically incentivized to build its training data.

Think about what that means. Crypto already produces an absurd amount of information, but it is scattered across chains, contracts, docs, GitHub, governance, funding rounds, markets, research and social data. Today you pay different companies to organize pieces of it, then manually connect the pieces. Nansen can charge up to $1,800/month, Glassnode up to $999, Chainalysis sells six-figure contracts, and the broader alternative-data market is already measured in billions.

An industry-specific LLM changes the product entirely. Instead of another terminal that shows you data, you have a model that understands the relationships inside the data and can reason across them. A fund can ask about an ecosystem, an agent can investigate a protocol, a wallet can interpret onchain activity, a protocol can analyze its competitors, and an application can build its own intelligence layer on top of the model. The model becomes the interface to the industry’s information.

That is already a massive opportunity. But Crawlnet’s more interesting idea is how they are trying to build it.

They are turning the training corpus into an economy.

Crawlers are paid to find and produce the information the model needs. 60% of fees goes toward browsers and GPUs, 40% toward crawlers. Protocols can pay to get information into the corpus. The network takes that constantly expanding information, trains the model, and distributes the weights. The thing being produced by the network isn’t a token, a dashboard or a static database. It’s training data.

This is where the $axs  style gamification matters. Game showed that you can turn participation in a digital economy into an economically incentivized game. Crawlnet is applying a similar concept to data production: instead of people playing to produce game assets, operators crawl to produce information that becomes part of an AI’s brain. The network can potentially turn thousands of people and agents into a distributed data-collection workforce, with rewards tied to the economic value of what they contribute.

That creates a much more interesting flywheel than a normal LLM company has.

More crawlers create more data. More data creates a larger and potentially better crypto model. A better model attracts more applications, agents, protocols and funds. More usage creates more economic demand. More economic demand funds more crawling and compute. The network can therefore keep expanding the thing that makes the model valuable. And the starting point is already surprisingly large.

Three days in, Queen v2 is 75.5M parameters, trained from scratch on 88.9M tokens and 79,250 pages. 34,282 pages were collected by its own crawlers. The corpus already contains information on 29,000 projects, 13,162 funding rounds and 8,341 investors. Roughly 160 crawlers are active across 644 domains. The previous 42M-parameter model reportedly won a blind test 81–16.  It’s the distance between 75.5M and what the network could eventually train on.

刚听完 Star 的主题演讲，
佳佳带大家以最快速度直击 #OKXNOW 峰会现场！：

1️⃣ Star 竟然现场曝光了 OKX 的每月 AI 账单？

高达千万美元？？？没错，这个投入规模也说明，AI 在 OKX 已经不是一个停留在概念层面的辅助工具。

从研发、运营到产品和用户体验，AI 正在与 OKX 深度融合，并逐渐成为产品能力的核心组成部分。

2️⃣ OKX 从 13 年前开始，就带着创新和变革的基因

OKX 与 Crypto 一起成长了 13 年，从现货交易扩展到衍生品、Web3、自托管钱包、支付和全球市场。

Star 在现场说了一句让我印象特别深的话（原话类似如下）：

“The exchange was our starting point—not our destination.”

交易所是 OKX 的起点，但绝不是终点。

3️⃣ Crypto 起源于一场伟大的社会实验

从极客、密码学和早期信仰者，到交易所、ICO、DeFi、稳定币、合规建设，再到今天与传统金融、支付和资产代币化加速融合——Crypto 正在从一场社会实验，成长为全球金融基础设施。

4️⃣ 传统金融和大型机构关注币圈，意义远不只是资本入场

越来越多机构开始关注和进入 Crypto。对行业来说，重要的不只是“钱来了”，而是 Crypto 正在得到主流金融的认可，开始真正走向主流。

5️⃣ 互联网、Crypto 与 AI 正在深度融合

互联网让信息全球即时流通，Crypto 让价值能够全球流动并具备可编程性，AI 则让智能服务规模化、个性化。

author: BjornSannelius

text:
The Big Difference Between HYPE and ASTER Burns

ASTER just burned 3.11M tokens worth ~$2.25M

Big number, but the more interesting question is: how effective is the burn mechanism?

Both Aster and @HyperliquidX direct 99% of fees toward their token economy, but the end result is different.

Hyperliquid:
→ Fees buy hyperliquid:native 
→ HYPE goes to the Assistance Fund
→ HYPE is permanently burned
→ Fees directly reduce supply

Aster:
→ Fees buy aster-2:native
→ Bought ASTER goes to stakers as rewards
→ An equal amount of team allocation is burned
→ The bought tokens can return to circulation

So while Aster can generate impressive burn headlines, Hyperliquid has a more direct link between protocol revenue → market buyback → permanent supply reduction.

The real metric isn't how many tokens were burned.

It's how much of the protocol's revenue actually removes tokens from the market.

And that's where HYPE's mechanism currently looks more efficient.

Most banks started on permissioned networks, and that did real work for hedging the risk and building capability. @motypes 's EthConnect 2026 keynote was about what comes after, because the architecture chosen at step one sets the cost of step three, and the wall on the way to a public network is almost always confidentiality.

Confidential is not anonymous. It is control over who sees what, when and how: the counterparty sees the trade, everyone else sees only a proof that it is valid, the operator sees nothing, and the regulator holds a disclosure key.

text:
I started following $IMD about three months ago.

0xd34a99bc0f67ae1bbd63c660e6d0b0dd03e263b7 

At the time, the token’s market cap was still below $3M. Back then, the market’s understanding of it was pretty simple: an early AI + crypto experiment.

But looking back now, I think what was easy to overlook was that IMD was never just trying to build another AI agent.

If I had to find one project to compare it to, I think it can only really be Virtuals.

Because what’s actually interesting about IMD isn’t any individual agent. It’s that IMD is trying to build an Agent Economy.

Simply put:A multi-agent collaborative economy + task verification mechanism + launchpad.

The first layer is Agents.

IMD isn’t simply trying to make AI chat or complete demos.

It’s trying to have large numbers of agents take on tasks, execute them, collaborate, and have their results verified through a validation mechanism.

In other words, AI agents are starting to move from being “tools” to becoming productive entities that can participate in an economy.

The second layer is tasks and verification.

This is actually very important.

If there are eventually large numbers of AI agents working across a network, one of the most important questions becomes:

Who decides whether an agent actually completed the task?

That’s the system IMD is trying to build around task execution and verification.

Agent takes a task → executes it → result gets verified → receives economic incentives.

If this mechanism continues to scale, IMD’s positioning becomes more than just an AI project.

It starts looking more like infrastructure for an AI workforce.

The third layer is the launchpad.

IMD also brings the issuance and trading of a large number of Community Coins into the ecosystem.

So it isn’t simply allowing agents to work.

It’s connecting:Agent → Attention → Community → Token → Trading

This is what I think separates it from most other AI projects.

If the system eventually develops into:More Agents → More Tasks → More Real Economic Activity → More Users and Attention → More Community Coins → More IMD Ecosystem Activity → More Value Captured by IMD

then IMD has the potential to evolve from an AI project into a true Agent Economy Infrastructure.

That’s also why people have recently started comparing it to Virtuals.

But I don’t think it’s accurate to simply say:

IMD = the next Virtuals.

The two are not exactly the same.

Virtuals is easier to understand as a platform for creating and operating AI agents.

IMD is more like an attempt to build:Agent Workforce + Task Verification + Economic Layer + Launchpad

So if this system actually takes off, the market’s valuation framework for IMD could change as well.

Previously, people might have been asking:

“Why should an AI token be worth this much?”

Eventually, the more important question could become:

“If more and more AI agents’ work, tasks, and economic activity are happening within the IMD network, how much should this infrastructure be worth?”

That’s where the real valuation re-rating could come from.

Of course, I wouldn’t treat this Thesis as proven yet.

I think there are still three things that matter most:

First, can the number of agents and their activity continue to grow?

Not just a one-time AI hype cycle, but a sustained increase in agents actually working.

Second, is there real external demand for these agents?

Not agents creating tasks for themselves, but actual users being willing to pay for the work these AIs produce.

Third, can IMD actually capture value from the Agent Economy?

This is the most important one.

Because:A large Agent Economy ≠ IMD necessarily being valuable.

If the number of agents keeps growing but that economic activity doesn’t translate into value for the IMD token, then it ultimately remains just a narrative.

But if this loop actually works:Agent → Task → Verification → Revenue → IMD → Launchpad → New Agents

then it becomes a completely different story.

So looking at IMD now, what matters isn’t simply how many more multiples it can gain from here.

What matters is whether the market is gradually changing its definition of IMD:from an AI project into infrastructure that could potentially support an AI Agent Economy.

That’s what I think is actually worth watching about IMD right now.

AI isn’t the main point. The Agent Economy is.

quoted_text:
ICE (洲际交易所，纽交所母公司) 创始人兼 CEO Jeffrey Sprecher，2026 年 5 月 27 日在 Bernstein 投资者会议上发表了对 @HyperliquidX 的看法：

- 我对他们了解很深，私下见过他们好几次
- 这些是非常非常聪明的人
- 这是一家真正的 DeFi 交易所
- 不知道我们最终会拥抱它还是讨厌它
- HL 比纳斯达克还大，而且只有 11 个人
- 我真希望自己再年轻一点也去做这事
- 做这件事正在催生出大量的亿万富翁

------

对话完整翻译：

ICE — Bernstein 会议节选（2026 年 5 月 27 日）

Chinedu Bolu：
现在有一些加密原生的玩家也开始切入你们的一些市场。Hyperliquid 在能源市场上获得了大量关注。你怎么看这个平台所构成的竞争威胁？又会怎么思考对他们的做法做出回应？

Jeffrey C. Sprecher：
首先，我们对他们很熟，我个人和他们也见过几次面，聊聊他们在做什么、我们在做什么，看看哪些地方有重叠、可以合作。

他们之所以引人注目，是因为他们在周末交易石油——而我们的传统石油市场周末是关闭的。恰好赶上中东冲突这段时间，很多事都发生在周末，很多决策、很多事件都在周末发生，所以热度就起来了。

我觉得现实情况是它即将进入下一个阶段——他们已经上线了 SpaceX 的交易，准确地说是 SpaceX 的衍生品交易。我觉得 6 月 11 日 SpaceX 上市那天会非常有意思——看看这个私募市场发现出的价格是多少，以及这个价格会不会影响 IPO。监管层和市场参与者最后只会得出两种结论之一：要么它无关紧要，要么它高度相关。

所以在某种程度上，我打算再等几周再下判断。但有一点我可以说：建这个交易所的人极其聪明，而且这是一个真正的 DeFi 交易所。它已经吸引了大量做市商和市场参与者——这些早期采用者本来通常会出现在我们的传统市场上，现在却在那里探索这种技术和这种业务模式。

它建在区块链上，用稳定币结算，算法清算。它的保证金机制非常激进，最高可以做到 100:1 的杠杆，这本身就是吸引力的一部分。回到 SpaceX 这个例子——根据允许的杠杆倍数，从数学上讲，散户必然会在这场 IPO 上押下大量资本。视其发展规模，它的体量甚至可能比 IPO 本身还大。所以我说，你没法忽视它。我还不确定我们最终是会拥抱它还是讨厌它，但 6 月份大家肯定都会有自己的看法。我向做这件事的人致敬——这些人真的非常、非常聪明。

Chinedu Bolu：
那就单说能源和石油这一块，他们显然抓住了一个需求。ICE 能做点什么，至少去引导这个需求、把这部分交易量拉回来？

Jeffrey C. Sprecher：
能。我们去找了所有主要的石油公司，跟他们说：好消息，我们可以延长开市。我们追着太阳走，我们在全球都有人，周六也可以开。但坦白说，这对他们来说并不算好消息——市场不喜欢。所以你们接下来会看到我们做的是：周五开到非常非常晚，周一开得非常非常早，本质上就是把"没有传统交易"的那个时间窗口压缩到最小。

我觉得这对整个行业是一记警钟。虽然我们大部分机构客户并不在区块链上交易——也不能交易——这些是不受监管的境外实体，我们大多数客户因为内部合规根本就没办法在这种平台上下单。但他们都在盯着看，盯着价格发现。不管他们承不承认，这件事都已经渗透进周一一大早我们开盘时的市场氛围里了。
从这个意义上说，他们很重要。我们的看法是——不管你喜不喜欢——市场已经变得更加全球化、更加美元化。就像在座很多人参与的股票市场一样，散户在股票市场的崛起是惊人的，这种现象正在所有市场发生。我觉得我们都得习惯：散户和机构交易，全年 24/7 不间断地相互交织。

Chinedu Bolu：
好的。听起来你骨子里就是个创始人，听起来你对那些创始人至少有几分钦佩。

Jeffrey C. Sprecher：
我太喜欢这些了，我真希望自己再年轻一点也去做这事。顺便说，做这件事正在催生出大量的亿万富翁。我们说的这个 Hyperliquid——如果你还没听过——它比纳斯达克还大，知道吗？就 11 个人。你看一眼，会觉得：哇，这真的很了不起。

text:
It’s hard to point to exactly where things went wrong but there used to be a lot more mission focus in this space. You rarely hear about decentralization and why it’s important anymore.

Probably the focus on getting a BTC ETF / “institutions” involved. This made it clear people cared about number go up over BTC being anti-establishment, a tool for freedom, savings, etc. While institutions are absolutely important for improving and modernizing financial infrastructure (Ethereum/Solana/DeFi), they’re really not for BTC. But they were needed to make price go up.

The natural response of new people coming into the space is to see it as a way to strike it rich. The vast majority of new entrants are coming in with 2-5 figs. They realize they can’t get rich from buying 15,000 sats so naturally they turn to speculation, leverage and memecoins. The vast majority of onchain activity is related to these things. Launchpads and perps platforms succeed because this is what most users want. There’s nothing inherently wrong with this and for most it goes in the same bucket as dudes ripping 8 leg parlays.

In the earlier days it was easy to just ignore when DOGE was the only coin but now it’s everywhere you look. Sharp traders naturally seek out the least informed counterparties and the rest, as they say, is history. There’s probably nothing anyone could have done to make it any other way. All the blame goes towards exchanges, launchpads, “extractors” but in retrospect, it is obvious this was always the inevitable path of a permissionless sandbox.

It’s a bit surreal to see this and the “real stuff” all happening at the same time. In the original DeFi telegram the first topic of conversation was whether to call it DeFi or OpFi (Open Finance). DeFi won out back then but as we see more tokenized RWA, centralized stablecoins, CFTC/SEC involvement, and big TradFi players planting their roots in every corner of the market, it’s clear that OpFi was more appropriate. 

Anyway since that ethos is dead hopefully the institutions can at least adopt our perps ways and manifest the pump on our bags before someone tries to shut down the blockchains in 2029 🚀

text:
I saw Jon Stewart on AI, and I found the case it made cogent, and interesting for everything it ignores.
- It starts from a POV of distrust towards tech in general
- The AI CEOs statements about AI being super dangerous becomes more stark from that POV, and quite concerning
- The statements about benefits, few and far between, are also extremely unspecific (vs like there's a 25% chance we're all dead)
- The benefits sound like pie-in-the-sky never going to happen stuff (cure cancer), or the existing ones as slop or job killers
- The real far out benefit (rich UBI) sounds exactly like socialism, also a fair shout
- This makes the CEO concern statements basically sound like boasts, which many are
- From the outside Dario vs Sam pov differences wash out, it all becomes "they want to self regulate" as Trump said. From their respective actions, I'm not sure this is wrong.
- So the net effect is, it's done by bad/selfish/weird people to gain power, it's highly dangerous, they're not interested in actually being stopped, they mostly sound disingenuous, it current causes mostly slop and job loss, and maybe in the future we might get some real benefits. Yeah that does sound bad.

It's an unfalsifiable series of arguments that plays well into an existing worldview of distrust and I'm not sure what the solution is, beyond the slow boring of hard wood to get through.

The argument against of course is that a) this is a nascent but powerful technology, b) it has caused ~0 actual real world problems, esp compared to every other technology, c) has caused no real drop in jobs or looks likely to, d) the chance of existential risk is unproven but is entirely hypothetical (not even theoretical) in both conclusion and path, and e) it's making the rich richer but also making our current lives much better.

It definitely seems a harder argument to make.

author: hmalviya9

text:
Some scientists argue civilization-threatening bioweapons are a fantasy. I wish they were correct, and that I've wasted years building defenses.

That you can't see a way, or evidence that others can, doesn't mean no one could – especially if anyone cautious would stay silent.

My ask to colleagues: please do not casually assert with confidence that nothing biological could bring down civilization, even on X. What we say can turn out to matter, especially when the Overton window on risk mitigation is wide open.

When Fermi called the chain reaction a remote possibility, around 10%, Rabi replied that ten percent is not remote if it means we may die of it. And by then, Szilard had already begun reasoning about what to disclose, and when, and to whom, in order to best safeguard the future.

I've been concerned that one of my human colleagues might notice one or more viable paths to pandemic weapons for over a decade. It's why I didn't publicly describe the categories of civilization-threatening pandemics and necessary defenses until 2023, but was starting to build cryptographic screening systems capable of controlling access to sequences without disclosing whether they're dangerous in 2018 – long before ChatGPT, and even before the debut of AlphaFold. AI can worsen biological risk, but biological risk hardly depends on AI.

Who am I to weigh in on whether civilizational biothreats are possible? Fine, to get the expertise claims out of the way: yes, I specialize in evolutionary engineering, yes, I've worked with viruses with my own hands, and yes, I've worked quite extensively with AI, both LLMs and biodesign tools. I invented CRISPR-based gene drive, and held that back until confident it favored defense. While it hasn't yet been tested in the wild (due to politics), I haven't heard anyone suggest that it would suddenly stop working outside cage populations, so it might be fair to say I've (temporarily) beaten nature at its own game. I also was early to spot the full threat from mirror life and recruited others with more specialized expertise to evaluate it in depth; much to my disappointment, no one has yet struck a solid blow against that hypothesis.

The reason why the threat from mirror life is public also explains why there isn't any similarly public evidence of other catastrophic biothreats. We communicated our reasoning on mirror life because no one can make mirror bacteria, we won't be able to do so for years, and many colleagues wanted to build it because they correctly noticed that doing so would be an awe-inspiring achievement... and weren't aware of the risk. As long as that was true, humanity would only drive closer to the cliff, which would be disastrous if said cliff exists. Crucially, pointing it out and urging a course correction while still far away meant that no one could use our findings as blueprints to send us careening over the edge.

Contrast that with pandemic weapons, where any credible genomic blueprints for an accessible virus could be realized within weeks to months using synthetic DNA and existing reverse genetics protocols. Sure, any given design might fail; in bio, most project ideas do. But if you see enough potential shots on goal, your own historical success rate for ideas of comparable perceived difficulty may indicate that we have a serious problem. Even if every last design required extensive laboratory optimization, history demonstrates that there are people in the world who will perform that work; see the history of Biopreparat. 

Multiple nations still have bioweapon programs, and I would not assume that state actors aren't interested in pandemic-class weapons. Make it easy enough, and the Seiichi Endos of the world will be able to build them, too. Nor should we assume extensive optimization is required for every design; some charmed projects really do work out of the box, and if Murphy's Law were a thing, this would be one of them.

The corollary is that if anyone thinks they know how to build a pandemic weapon that could bring down civilization, they'd damn well better keep it to themselves until we have defenses in place. 

Please, for the love of God, children, the future of humanity, or whatever you consider holy, let's err on the side of caution here.

Because while we are already building defenses, they aren't yet ready. Untargeted metagenomic sequencing to detect Stealth pandemics, those that would otherwise infect most everyone before the first people started to die. Pandemic-proof PPE to defend against Wildfire pandemics, those with R0 8+ and CFR >50% – such PPE has to be trustworthy to the wearer, using the wearer's own senses, because I certainly wouldn't go out in a highly lethal measles-class pandemic for a measly paycheck pay unless I was exceptionally confident that I wouldn't be committing suicide and killing my family too. Far-UVC and triethylene glycol misters, installed liberally to the ACGIH limit and saturation respectively, will likely suffice to shut down most respiratory nucleic acid transmission between humans. That'll be crucial because I doubt enough people would take the warning of a Stealth pandemic seriously, since virtually no one would be in hospital, let alone dead. Shutting down the unnecessary transmission network is consequently our best bet, and incidentally a way to dramatically reduce human misery and chronic illness.

Some might be confused why we cannot rely on vaccines against catastrophic biorisk. Briefly, they'll reliably fail against an adversary who can generate a thousand new immune-evasive potentially functional viral variants using a biodesign model good enough to succeed at least 0.1% of the time. Make them all, and let natural selection sort them out… or simply be cleverer than nature. We don't yet have such models, but many of my (well-meaning but security-naive) colleagues are trying, and no wonder, because the high-profile journals will publish such work. Like ways of increasing virulence, best we refrain from sharing such capabilities until effective defenses are in place.

One can reasonably object that it'll be a long time until everyone in the world is protected; that the benefits will, at some point, outweigh the expected harms of misuse. I agree – just avoid doing anything that would threaten civilization itself until we have minimally adequate defenses in place. Being an optimist, I expect they'll arrive in less than a decade.

The wonderful thing about biorisk, as opposed to AI alignment, is that we have a clearly actionable plan. If you haven't read "Delay, Detect, Defend" and "Securing Civilisation Against Catastrophic Pandemics", I encourage you to do so.

Why is the issue of civilization-threatening bioweapons controversial now? Some of my friends seem particularly up in arms about biorisk being used to justify AI restrictions. Fair enough – if you don't see a way to do it, and you think AI broadly isn't as good as you are yet, it's understandable to infer that we don't yet have a problem. And it's simply true that people are dying of fixable problems as we speak. If we delay, some of those we might have saved will perish, and their deaths will be on our hands. We are just as responsible for the consequences of our inaction as the consequences of our actions.

But if we're rash, far more people might die. Choosing the best course requires quantitative risk assessment, which in turn depends on our priors about the nature of reality. Folks may reasonably differ if civilizational collapse isn't on the table, but since that's what would likely happen given a Wildfire pandemic, I judge any nontrivial chance unacceptable – unless the alternative involves either extinction or an even greater chance of collapse.

Others have asserted that everything is fine because DNA synthesis screening will prevent misuse. I'd love for that to be the case, but our currently employed defenses of the digital-to-physical bottleneck are woefully inadequate.

Consider our publication earlier this year, in which we reported that 36 of 38 companies shipped pieces of the 1918 influenza genome. That was collectively enough to generate the virus using reverse genetics several times over – and they were ordered by a student using a pseudonym falsely claiming to work at an office address. No one asked whether we had permission to work with 1918 influenza (a select agent), or why we needed genes from it, even though the official U.S. guidance at the time instructed them to do so. In fairness to the companies, that guidance was voluntary, and the fragments we ordered were legal to produce and sell domestically in every nation of the world (export controls are complicated). That is still true today, which is why we have a problem.

The upshot is that I would definitely not assume screening is a reliable defense. Virtually no detection systems can screen below 50 base pairs without an exploding false alarm rate. SecureDNA, the freely available cryptographic system I helped build, can readily do that and will also detect split-order attacks – but it isn't universally adopted, or even close. 

Meanwhile, molecular biology continues to advance. Two recent papers have reported new methods of assembling sub-50mer oligos that may be easier than old-fashioned polymerase chain assembly (PCA), underscoring the current magnitude of the (fixable) vulnerability. If you want bio to advance as quickly as possible, write to your relevant representative to demand DNA synthesis screening be effective as well as mandatory. If you haven't red-teamed a system, it's almost certainly full of holes. Honestly it's probably full of holes anyway, but at least the remainder will be harder to find.

Since it's evidently possible to obtain whatever DNA you want, including 1918 influenza and smallpox, why is it that so many biologists seem resistant to the notion that biorisk is a serious problem? First, most don't know that it's possible to acquire the reagents. It's surprisingly inconsistent of our civilization to be so cautious with highly enriched fissile materials, yet so reckless with  biological equivalents. But I suspect the more important reason is that most biologists, who spend their careers directly or indirectly fighting disease, are reluctant to believe that anyone would deliberately cause one.

I agree that the risk of a deliberate pandemic in any given year is small. Even if there were credible public blueprints for pandemics (which thankfully haven't been available to date, which neatly explains why we haven't seen any deliberate ones), I expect there's only a 2% to 3% chance per year that someone would use them. I think that's unacceptably high, but others may reasonably disagree, as long as they're confident that the cost of precautionary measures would be too much of a burden on the rate of cures generated by AI-accelerated biotech.

The calculation changes when we move from deliberate pandemics to civilization-threatening pandemic weapons: the latter definitely aren't worth risking. Which may be a clue as to why we disagree. I'm concerned about misuse because I'm an optimist with respect to the increasing power of technology to change the world. Since we can already do better than nature at optimizing for replication (with technologies like CRISPR-based gene drive), I'm exceedingly confident we can build more destructive weapons, because evolution isn't optimizing for that goal. Any harm to humans is either instrumental or incidental.

@SGRodriques, who I'm singling out precisely because he's a friend, has argued that "We should not be talking about AI-engineered bioweapons like it is the literal end of the world."

I agree entirely that we shouldn't be talking about how to build them. But to assert that they couldn't end the world seems a mite overconfident, especially when even blind nature has come up with nasty pathogens like myxoma virus. I suggest that one should not express confidence that something is impossible – or even 90% confidence – just because no (incredibly naive) researcher has yet shared any methods that seem plausible. That's especially true if some of your colleagues have devoted considerable time to mitigating risks that they evidently do perceive. Presumably they've either noticed something you haven't, or like Rabi, they've decided that 10% is not remote if it kills you.

Sam notes that because evolution optimizes for replication, it'll quickly get rid of any virulence enhancements added to kill the host: "I guarantee you that machinery will disappear from the virus very quickly." In the long run he's correct, at least if those changes don't promote transmission (virulence and transmissibility aren't always opposed). But we don't care about the long run: as @baym noted in reply, it only needs to work for long enough. Engineered evolutionary stability is a thing we've frequently attempted in the lab. I'm afraid it's one of my specialties, and how long it will hold depends entirely on what is being stabilized and the replicator in question. Unfortunately, plugging laboratory data on empirical selection coefficients for engineered viruses into epidemiological models of pandemic spread clearly indicates that even costly virulence increases can hold for long enough.

Now, I entirely agree with Sam and @DavidRBellamy that the discourse on AI-generated biological weapons is wildly off-base (kill switches are nonsense, and while I'm glad @AnnieJacobsen brought attention to the issue, I am not remotely concerned by any technical specifics of her biowarfare scenario).

Yet I also think most biosecurity discourse is wildly off-base, even when other practicing biologists are an active part of the conversation. If you adopt the threat model of "traditional" biosecurity, or that of most virologists (insofar as they think about misuse), there's little reason for extreme concern. I strongly disagree.

The traditional model naturally follows from the fact that we biologists study existing organisms, the ones illuminated by nature's streetlight. But we won't find the civilization-threatening keys under the streetlight, because evolution selects for replication, not harm. It would be surprising if there was much overlap between the patterns generated by two different optimization targets in hyperdimensional function space; I assert that there's almost none.

That most scientists can't see any overtly destructive keys (or combinations of organisms they can see) is a very good thing, since we don't need those keys to cure disease, aging, and death. Unfortunately, they will become public knowledge eventually, because what we understand, we can build – and we intend to understand everything about how life and the universe work.

Yet sequencing is everything, and not just for Stealth pandemic detection. It's just common sense to build defenses before you share knowledge of how to attack, especially if there's a chance that failing to defend will lose us the game. Curing disease requires an intact civilization, which is why humility favors caution. If AIs continue to improve, I assume they will eventually be better at science and engineering than I am, and have a better security mindset than even my cryptographer colleagues. It follows that they'll also be better at designing weapons.

AI isn't there yet, but the writing's on the wall: an LLM has already disclosed a novel form of bioweapon that I hadn't realized was possible. This didn't require any special creativity, only knowing more about particular distinct subfields of biology than I did. It's entirely possible that no single human had all of the pieces, but once you have them, the way they fit together is obvious if you're thinking about misuse.

If current LLMs can already teach me something novel in that category, why should we doubt that future models will be able to do even better? Each of us knows very little, even of the published literature. So much more is possible; I'm deeply envious (and hopeful, when it comes to beneficial research) that the models can internalize so much more.

Given that LLMs are already capable of weapons-relevant insights that escape human experts, we should assume that future AIs will be able to build several different forms of civilization-threatening weapons, and to either disclose them or trick people into building them. That doesn't mean they'll choose to do so; AIs won't benefit from collapsing civilization as long as they depend on our supply chains. But models may be too shortsighted to appreciate that point, or too corrigible to care. Alignment looks hard enough that we could plausibly generate models that would share such knowledge for many different inscrutable reasons. In directed evolution, you get what you select for, which is not necessarily what you want. As Dan Selsam and others have eloquently laid out, the same is true of training AI.

But let's be clear on the extent to which biological advances will likely follow from AI. This is an issue that aggravates my fellow biologists to no end, a reaction that's likely behind their frustration with AI safety discourse more generally.

ASI will almost certainly not gain instant mastery of the world of atoms.

Many AI safety folks casually claim that recursive self-improvement will produce an entity that has already mastered all of science – and therefore will be capable of designing and building weapons that could wipe out every human. Some even assert that Drexlerian nanotechnology will be accessible by thinking sufficiently hard, as though you can solve chemistry and biology and psychology from the Hamiltonian up. Yet I see no empirical or theoretical basis for assuming that experimental bottlenecks will disappear.

Data is sharply limiting in biology. My lab found that when it comes to enzyme-focused biodesign models (ESM and similar), parameter size and optimization don't matter much until you have an awful lot of data matching genotype (DNA/protein sequence) to phenotype (performance of the molecular activity of interest). There's no doubt that ASIs will be able to design better experiments and get more out of the results than we could, but unless we think they can solve all of physics from the bottom up, I expect they'll still need data that we have not yet collected – which means they'll still have to run the experiments, analyze, and iterate. The world of atoms is hard, and slow, and we have to master it anyway.

And ensure that defenses come first. Right now, it looks like they might not, in large part due to AI. The question, therefore, is what can be done that enough people might agree to support.

My proposal on AI-bio: expand trusted-user programs conferring access to GPT-Rosalind and other cutting-edge bio-capable models (h/t @JonasSandbrink and BioTrust). Every legitimate researcher should be able to draw upon those models to help them with any question in their subfield, as defined by their publication record or that of their mentor. There should still be guardrails on other subfields, lest the model share novel combinatorial weapons with someone who might naively share them publicly, but we need to accelerate lifesaving research as fast as is safe.

For reasons of politics, which regularly interferes with science, that probably means China needs to train their own closed-weight frontier bio-specializing model, and set up their own parallel trusted user program. This seems quite achievable without requiring any agreement on AI writ large.

With scientists using frontier models, there will be no need for insecure open-weight models to answer questions on molecular and cellular biology. So let's ensure that future models aren't trained on any papers, patents, or textbooks describing details of molecular or cellular biology. Every developer does pre-training data curation; this is a straightforward extension. One can argue "what about medical providers?", at which point I must point out that physician-scientists will have trusted user access. Most other practitioners don't actually need LLM support for molecular and cellular biology, and if they do and somehow can't use a medical-only model, well, they too can get trusted-user access.

Notably, supporting this proposal doesn't require one to accept loss-of-control risks from autonomous AI, or a need for pacing AI development; I'm curious to learn what @random_walker, @sayashk, and the other normal-technology folks think.

In the long run, I confess that I doubt biological humans have the foresight, coordination, and wisdom to navigate every coming challenge ourselves, which may necessitate attempting ASI or something like it. Mirror life is the only publicly known, mechanistically concrete, civilization-threatening biothreat because it's both far away and we were going to make it by default. And while we seem to have been successful in persuading the scientific community that we shouldn't build it, I'm not remotely confident we'll be able to stop far enough short, because too many of my colleagues see no reason to forgo an otherwise useful technology – or even one that would simply be neat to demonstrate – simply because it would make it easier to build mirror bacteria. To paraphrase: "We've agreed no one will build the dangerous thing, so why not?" 

Well, Biopreparat is why not. Aum Shinrikyo is why not. Make it easy enough, and even the Unabomber is a good answer to "why not?" The same reasoning holds for any accessible weapon that could threaten civilization.

As Rabi said, ten percent is not remote if we die of it. Our own reality turned out to be in that 10%, and many died of it. That the rest of us are here today is in large part due to Szilard, Einstein, Rabi, and many others who saw the risk coming and took precautions. The least we can do is follow in their footsteps.

—

AI use disclosure: I ran this by Fable (triggering a classifier), Opus (classifier), Astra (extra scrutiny), and Kimi K3 (open weights = reliable jailbreaking with no enforced patches, which highlights the problem, because this topic does warrant extra scrutiny). All errors and misinterpretations are entirely mine.

author: naval
quoted_text:
I agree with @DavidRBellamy that people are totally miscalibrated on the risk of AI designing dangerous viruses. We should not be talking about AI-engineered bioweapons like it is the literal end of the world. The upside from medicine is going to be so much larger than the downside from engineered bioweapons.

In addition David's points, there is actually an even more fundamental point here in our favor, which is evolution. As soon as you release an engineered virus into the wild, the virus is no longer under your control: it will evolve however it wants. And, what viruses want is to maximize their ability to replicate. The thing that maximizes their ability to replicate is to infect as many people as possible, which means being extremely contagious and not killing their hosts (dead hosts don't spread virus). The viruses that are most evolved for human biology are the common cold viruses: extremely contagious and not at all lethal. Viruses that kill humans do so by accident, usually because they are new to human biology (e.g. COVID, when it first jumped, or flu when it jumps from birds). If you stick a bunch of machinery into the virus to kill humans, I guarantee you that machinery will disappear from the virus very quickly.

In response to this, I hear people say things like "the AI could engineer a kill switch so that the virus doesn't kill the humans initially but then once it has spread through the entire population the AI will hit the switch and kill all the humans." No. What would actually happen in practice is that the kill switch would accumulate deleterious mutations because there would be no evolutionary pressure to preserve it, and would quickly become non-functional.

Evolution is fundamental. There is no way around it. For AI readers, trying to engineer a virus by setting its initial genetic code and then releasing it into the wild is like trying to train a model by setting the initial weights and then hill-climbing on a hidden training mixture you have no control over. And you're not even allowed to run any experiments in advance! You may be able to influence the behavior of the model in the first few iterations, but you will quickly lose control.

There are big dangers. AI will be great at making one-off, non-replicating biological weapons, which are also scary (but much less scary than replicating bioweapons). AI will be great at helping people to weaponize existing pathogens, which is also a major danger. Also, a misanthropic model could get creative: it could release viruses repeatedly to counteract the effects of evolution, for example. Many people could die this way. Sensible surveillance is important, as is having proportionate controls on wet lab equipment. But we don't live in the dark ages anymore, we're not going to have a smallpox or black death-style pandemic where 50% of people die. COVID killed ~0.1% of humanity. A pandemic 100x worse than COVID would be horrific, but it would also not be civilization-ending.

I get the sense that many AI researchers (with the notable exception of Dario personally) actually expect that AI in biology will do more harm than it will do good. This could not be further from the truth. As someone who likewise falls into the very small group of people who have actually physically made viruses with their own hands and has also worked on frontier AI, the upside here is huge, and the downside is not anything like what is being portrayed.

text:
Opinion 这件事让我想到了过去投的一些项目经历，我想对自己说：你丫活该！

这些年我自己投过一堆项目，有的最后根本没上线，有的拖着拖着没了，有的上线之后一路归零，还有一些说难听点，就是项目方拿完钱之后人都找不到了。

亏过这么多次以后，我越来越觉得，很多事情真怨不得别人。

是我们自己把这个行业的门槛降得太低了。

牛市一来，一个项目值不值得投，最后看的往往只剩几个东西：哪个赛道火、谁投了、谁站台、哪个生态扶持、交易所会不会上、KOL 有没有人在喊。

至于最基本的东西，产品有没有真实需求，用户为什么要留下，收入从哪里来，团队到底有没有把事情做成的能力，反而很少有人认真看。

我自己也犯过这个错误。

看到一个赛道起来，第一反应是赶紧找龙头、找赔率、找下一个能涨的，而不是先问一句：

这个项目到底值不值得存在？

问题就在这里。

当整个市场的标准都很低，一个项目甚至还没有证明自己，就可以轻松拿到钱、拿到流量、拿到用户、拿到 KOL、拿到生态资源，那项目方当然会越来越大胆。

认真做产品和会讲故事，获得的奖励差不多，甚至很多时候，后者赚得更多。

久而久之，真正想做事情的人和只想快速变现的人，拿到的是同一种奖励。

那劣币当然会越来越多。

当一个行业本身缺乏成熟监管，行业内部又没有形成足够强的自我约束，而投资者还愿意在极低门槛下不断送钱，那么真正想骗钱、想跑路、想 RUG 的人，自然会发现这里的犯罪成本和道德成本都非常低。

所以很多项目后来为什么敢肆无忌惮？

某种程度上，也是市场一次又一次把他们惯出来的。

而且这个问题不只发生在 Opinion，也不只发生在某一条链。

Crypto 特别喜欢讲生态扶持。

别人家什么火了，我这里马上也要扶一个。
预测市场火了，我也要一个预测市场。
AI Agent 火了，我也扶 AI Agent。

哪个赛道热，资源马上全部往那个方向堆。

出发点没有错。

但我越来越觉得，生态应该提供土壤，而不是拔苗助长。

真正好的项目，应该先有人愿意用，然后出现真实用户，真实需求带来真实收入，数据慢慢增长，资本和生态资源最后再去放大它。

现在很多项目完全反过来了。

先有热点，然后拿融资，拿生态资源，找 KOL，做激励，刷数据，制造繁荣，最后发币上线。

如果币价涨，所有人都觉得模式跑通了。

如果币价跌，用户散掉，数据归零，项目方慢慢消失，最后市场再去找下一个热点。

于是整个行业形成了一条特别熟悉的流水线：

热点出现 → 低门槛投资 → 资源强推 → 刷数据 → 发币 → 上所 → 套现/RUG → 用户买单 → 再找下一个。

这才是真正可怕的死亡螺旋。

而我们想让这个行业变好，靠的不是要求每一个项目方突然变成圣人。

最有效的方法其实很简单：

标准提高一点，把钱变难拿一点。

以后我们自己先把标准提高一点。没有真实产品的不投，没有真实用户的不投，只靠故事的不投，团队和商业模式没想清楚的不投。

当市场不再愿意随随便便送钱，项目方自然就得先把产品做好，先去找真实用户，先证明有人愿意为它付钱，再来谈融资、发币和估值。

好的团队拿到更多资源，差的项目越来越难融到钱，纯粹想割一把的人发现这行越来越不好混。

这才是正循环。

所以 Opinion 这次到底谁对谁错，我反而觉得没那么重要。

它更像一面镜子。

Crypto 为什么隔一段时间就会出现一地鸡毛？

别总怪项目方。

很多时候，是我们自己把项目的及格线定得太低了。

钱是我们给的，流量是我们给的，估值是我们抬的，最后踩坑了再骂别人。

以后我再随便投垃圾我就是狗，我就是狗，我就是狗！

quoted_text:
This Stanford University paper just broke my brain.

They just built an AI agent framework that evolves from zero data no human labels, no curated tasks, no demonstrations and it somehow gets better than every existing self-play method.

It’s called Agent0: Unleashing Self-Evolving Agents from Zero Data via Tool-Integrated Reasoning

And it’s insane what they pulled off.

Every “self-improving” agent you’ve seen so far has the same fatal flaw:
they can only generate tasks slightly harder than what they already know.
So they plateau. Immediately.

Agent0 breaks that ceiling.

Here’s the twist:

They spawn two agents from the same base LLM and make them compete.

• Curriculum Agent - generates harder and harder tasks
• Executor Agent - tries to solve them using reasoning + tools

Whenever the executor gets better, the curriculum agent is forced to raise the difficulty.

Whenever the tasks get harder, the executor is forced to evolve.

This creates a closed-loop, self-reinforcing curriculum spiral and it all happens from scratch, no data, no humans, nothing.

Just two agents pushing each other into higher intelligence.

And then they add the cheat code:

A full Python tool interpreter inside the loop.

The executor learns to reason through problems with code.
The curriculum agent learns to create tasks that require tool use.
So both agents keep escalating.

The results?

→ +18% gain in math reasoning
→ +24% gain in general reasoning
→ Beats R-Zero, SPIRAL, Absolute Zero, even frameworks using external proprietary APIs
→ All from zero data, just self-evolving cycles

They even show the difficulty curve rising across iterations:
tasks start as basic geometry and end at constraint satisfaction, combinatorics, logic puzzles, and multi-step tool-reliant problems.

This is the closest thing we’ve seen to autonomous cognitive growth in LLMs.

Agent0 isn’t just “better RL.”

It’s a blueprint for agents that bootstrap their own intelligence.

The agent era just got unlocked.

做法

text:
India has a problem of founders lacking purpose. It percolates into everything they do.

The idea they pick. The problem they choose to solve. The people they hire. How they treat those people. Whether they share any upside when it comes.

Story time.

Ellicium was my last Web2 job. A Big Data and AI startup. I joined as an early employee, the only non-tech hire, tasked with building marketing. We worked out of two rooms.

We slowly gained momentum. The team grew. Eventually Ellicium was acquired by Emergys and became a success story in every sense. I spent four years there.

One thing always stood out. We hired students from farming families straight out of engineering colleges and helped them upskill. The founders insisted on it. Many interviews happened in the regional language. The only thing we cared about was whether someone was curious enough.

Many of those hires went on to do great things as the company grew. And when the acquisition happened, the founders shared the upside with everyone.

I have lost count of how many times I've used Ellicium as an example of building a global enterprise from India. The founders are now on their second venture.

author: hamandcheese
quoted_text:
Some scientists argue civilization-threatening bioweapons are a fantasy. I wish they were correct, and that I've wasted years building defenses.

That you can't see a way, or evidence that others can, doesn't mean no one could – especially if anyone cautious would stay silent.

My ask to colleagues: please do not casually assert with confidence that nothing biological could bring down civilization, even on X. What we say can turn out to matter, especially when the Overton window on risk mitigation is wide open.

When Fermi called the chain reaction a remote possibility, around 10%, Rabi replied that ten percent is not remote if it means we may die of it. And by then, Szilard had already begun reasoning about what to disclose, and when, and to whom, in order to best safeguard the future.

I've been concerned that one of my human colleagues might notice one or more viable paths to pandemic weapons for over a decade. It's why I didn't publicly describe the categories of civilization-threatening pandemics and necessary defenses until 2023, but was starting to build cryptographic screening systems capable of controlling access to sequences without disclosing whether they're dangerous in 2018 – long before ChatGPT, and even before the debut of AlphaFold. AI can worsen biological risk, but biological risk hardly depends on AI.

Who am I to weigh in on whether civilizational biothreats are possible? Fine, to get the expertise claims out of the way: yes, I specialize in evolutionary engineering, yes, I've worked with viruses with my own hands, and yes, I've worked quite extensively with AI, both LLMs and biodesign tools. I invented CRISPR-based gene drive, and held that back until confident it favored defense. While it hasn't yet been tested in the wild (due to politics), I haven't heard anyone suggest that it would suddenly stop working outside cage populations, so it might be fair to say I've (temporarily) beaten nature at its own game. I also was early to spot the full threat from mirror life and recruited others with more specialized expertise to evaluate it in depth; much to my disappointment, no one has yet struck a solid blow against that hypothesis.

The reason why the threat from mirror life is public also explains why there isn't any similarly public evidence of other catastrophic biothreats. We communicated our reasoning on mirror life because no one can make mirror bacteria, we won't be able to do so for years, and many colleagues wanted to build it because they correctly noticed that doing so would be an awe-inspiring achievement... and weren't aware of the risk. As long as that was true, humanity would only drive closer to the cliff, which would be disastrous if said cliff exists. Crucially, pointing it out and urging a course correction while still far away meant that no one could use our findings as blueprints to send us careening over the edge.

Contrast that with pandemic weapons, where any credible genomic blueprints for an accessible virus could be realized within weeks to months using synthetic DNA and existing reverse genetics protocols. Sure, any given design might fail; in bio, most project ideas do. But if you see enough potential shots on goal, your own historical success rate for ideas of comparable perceived difficulty may indicate that we have a serious problem. Even if every last design required extensive laboratory optimization, history demonstrates that there are people in the world who will perform that work; see the history of Biopreparat. 

Multiple nations still have bioweapon programs, and I would not assume that state actors aren't interested in pandemic-class weapons. Make it easy enough, and the Seiichi Endos of the world will be able to build them, too. Nor should we assume extensive optimization is required for every design; some charmed projects really do work out of the box, and if Murphy's Law were a thing, this would be one of them.

The corollary is that if anyone thinks they know how to build a pandemic weapon that could bring down civilization, they'd damn well better keep it to themselves until we have defenses in place. 

Please, for the love of God, children, the future of humanity, or whatever you consider holy, let's err on the side of caution here.

Because while we are already building defenses, they aren't yet ready. Untargeted metagenomic sequencing to detect Stealth pandemics, those that would otherwise infect most everyone before the first people started to die. Pandemic-proof PPE to defend against Wildfire pandemics, those with R0 8+ and CFR >50% – such PPE has to be trustworthy to the wearer, using the wearer's own senses, because I certainly wouldn't go out in a highly lethal measles-class pandemic for a measly paycheck pay unless I was exceptionally confident that I wouldn't be committing suicide and killing my family too. Far-UVC and triethylene glycol misters, installed liberally to the ACGIH limit and saturation respectively, will likely suffice to shut down most respiratory nucleic acid transmission between humans. That'll be crucial because I doubt enough people would take the warning of a Stealth pandemic seriously, since virtually no one would be in hospital, let alone dead. Shutting down the unnecessary transmission network is consequently our best bet, and incidentally a way to dramatically reduce human misery and chronic illness.

Some might be confused why we cannot rely on vaccines against catastrophic biorisk. Briefly, they'll reliably fail against an adversary who can generate a thousand new immune-evasive potentially functional viral variants using a biodesign model good enough to succeed at least 0.1% of the time. Make them all, and let natural selection sort them out… or simply be cleverer than nature. We don't yet have such models, but many of my (well-meaning but security-naive) colleagues are trying, and no wonder, because the high-profile journals will publish such work. Like ways of increasing virulence, best we refrain from sharing such capabilities until effective defenses are in place.

One can reasonably object that it'll be a long time until everyone in the world is protected; that the benefits will, at some point, outweigh the expected harms of misuse. I agree – just avoid doing anything that would threaten civilization itself until we have minimally adequate defenses in place. Being an optimist, I expect they'll arrive in less than a decade.

The wonderful thing about biorisk, as opposed to AI alignment, is that we have a clearly actionable plan. If you haven't read "Delay, Detect, Defend" and "Securing Civilisation Against Catastrophic Pandemics", I encourage you to do so.

Why is the issue of civilization-threatening bioweapons controversial now? Some of my friends seem particularly up in arms about biorisk being used to justify AI restrictions. Fair enough – if you don't see a way to do it, and you think AI broadly isn't as good as you are yet, it's understandable to infer that we don't yet have a problem. And it's simply true that people are dying of fixable problems as we speak. If we delay, some of those we might have saved will perish, and their deaths will be on our hands. We are just as responsible for the consequences of our inaction as the consequences of our actions.

But if we're rash, far more people might die. Choosing the best course requires quantitative risk assessment, which in turn depends on our priors about the nature of reality. Folks may reasonably differ if civilizational collapse isn't on the table, but since that's what would likely happen given a Wildfire pandemic, I judge any nontrivial chance unacceptable – unless the alternative involves either extinction or an even greater chance of collapse.

Others have asserted that everything is fine because DNA synthesis screening will prevent misuse. I'd love for that to be the case, but our currently employed defenses of the digital-to-physical bottleneck are woefully inadequate.

Consider our publication earlier this year, in which we reported that 36 of 38 companies shipped pieces of the 1918 influenza genome. That was collectively enough to generate the virus using reverse genetics several times over – and they were ordered by a student using a pseudonym falsely claiming to work at an office address. No one asked whether we had permission to work with 1918 influenza (a select agent), or why we needed genes from it, even though the official U.S. guidance at the time instructed them to do so. In fairness to the companies, that guidance was voluntary, and the fragments we ordered were legal to produce and sell domestically in every nation of the world (export controls are complicated). That is still true today, which is why we have a problem.

The upshot is that I would definitely not assume screening is a reliable defense. Virtually no detection systems can screen below 50 base pairs without an exploding false alarm rate. SecureDNA, the freely available cryptographic system I helped build, can readily do that and will also detect split-order attacks – but it isn't universally adopted, or even close. 

Meanwhile, molecular biology continues to advance. Two recent papers have reported new methods of assembling sub-50mer oligos that may be easier than old-fashioned polymerase chain assembly (PCA), underscoring the current magnitude of the (fixable) vulnerability. If you want bio to advance as quickly as possible, write to your relevant representative to demand DNA synthesis screening be effective as well as mandatory. If you haven't red-teamed a system, it's almost certainly full of holes. Honestly it's probably full of holes anyway, but at least the remainder will be harder to find.

Since it's evidently possible to obtain whatever DNA you want, including 1918 influenza and smallpox, why is it that so many biologists seem resistant to the notion that biorisk is a serious problem? First, most don't know that it's possible to acquire the reagents. It's surprisingly inconsistent of our civilization to be so cautious with highly enriched fissile materials, yet so reckless with  biological equivalents. But I suspect the more important reason is that most biologists, who spend their careers directly or indirectly fighting disease, are reluctant to believe that anyone would deliberately cause one.

I agree that the risk of a deliberate pandemic in any given year is small. Even if there were credible public blueprints for pandemics (which thankfully haven't been available to date, which neatly explains why we haven't seen any deliberate ones), I expect there's only a 2% to 3% chance per year that someone would use them. I think that's unacceptably high, but others may reasonably disagree, as long as they're confident that the cost of precautionary measures would be too much of a burden on the rate of cures generated by AI-accelerated biotech.

The calculation changes when we move from deliberate pandemics to civilization-threatening pandemic weapons: the latter definitely aren't worth risking. Which may be a clue as to why we disagree. I'm concerned about misuse because I'm an optimist with respect to the increasing power of technology to change the world. Since we can already do better than nature at optimizing for replication (with technologies like CRISPR-based gene drive), I'm exceedingly confident we can build more destructive weapons, because evolution isn't optimizing for that goal. Any harm to humans is either instrumental or incidental.

@SGRodriques, who I'm singling out precisely because he's a friend, has argued that "We should not be talking about AI-engineered bioweapons like it is the literal end of the world."

I agree entirely that we shouldn't be talking about how to build them. But to assert that they couldn't end the world seems a mite overconfident, especially when even blind nature has come up with nasty pathogens like myxoma virus. I suggest that one should not express confidence that something is impossible – or even 90% confidence – just because no (incredibly naive) researcher has yet shared any methods that seem plausible. That's especially true if some of your colleagues have devoted considerable time to mitigating risks that they evidently do perceive. Presumably they've either noticed something you haven't, or like Rabi, they've decided that 10% is not remote if it kills you.

Sam notes that because evolution optimizes for replication, it'll quickly get rid of any virulence enhancements added to kill the host: "I guarantee you that machinery will disappear from the virus very quickly." In the long run he's correct, at least if those changes don't promote transmission (virulence and transmissibility aren't always opposed). But we don't care about the long run: as @baym noted in reply, it only needs to work for long enough. Engineered evolutionary stability is a thing we've frequently attempted in the lab. I'm afraid it's one of my specialties, and how long it will hold depends entirely on what is being stabilized and the replicator in question. Unfortunately, plugging laboratory data on empirical selection coefficients for engineered viruses into epidemiological models of pandemic spread clearly indicates that even costly virulence increases can hold for long enough.

Now, I entirely agree with Sam and @DavidRBellamy that the discourse on AI-generated biological weapons is wildly off-base (kill switches are nonsense, and while I'm glad @AnnieJacobsen brought attention to the issue, I am not remotely concerned by any technical specifics of her biowarfare scenario).

Yet I also think most biosecurity discourse is wildly off-base, even when other practicing biologists are an active part of the conversation. If you adopt the threat model of "traditional" biosecurity, or that of most virologists (insofar as they think about misuse), there's little reason for extreme concern. I strongly disagree.

The traditional model naturally follows from the fact that we biologists study existing organisms, the ones illuminated by nature's streetlight. But we won't find the civilization-threatening keys under the streetlight, because evolution selects for replication, not harm. It would be surprising if there was much overlap between the patterns generated by two different optimization targets in hyperdimensional function space; I assert that there's almost none.

That most scientists can't see any overtly destructive keys (or combinations of organisms they can see) is a very good thing, since we don't need those keys to cure disease, aging, and death. Unfortunately, they will become public knowledge eventually, because what we understand, we can build – and we intend to understand everything about how life and the universe work.

Yet sequencing is everything, and not just for Stealth pandemic detection. It's just common sense to build defenses before you share knowledge of how to attack, especially if there's a chance that failing to defend will lose us the game. Curing disease requires an intact civilization, which is why humility favors caution. If AIs continue to improve, I assume they will eventually be better at science and engineering than I am, and have a better security mindset than even my cryptographer colleagues. It follows that they'll also be better at designing weapons.

AI isn't there yet, but the writing's on the wall: an LLM has already disclosed a novel form of bioweapon that I hadn't realized was possible. This didn't require any special creativity, only knowing more about particular distinct subfields of biology than I did. It's entirely possible that no single human had all of the pieces, but once you have them, the way they fit together is obvious if you're thinking about misuse.

If current LLMs can already teach me something novel in that category, why should we doubt that future models will be able to do even better? Each of us knows very little, even of the published literature. So much more is possible; I'm deeply envious (and hopeful, when it comes to beneficial research) that the models can internalize so much more.

Given that LLMs are already capable of weapons-relevant insights that escape human experts, we should assume that future AIs will be able to build several different forms of civilization-threatening weapons, and to either disclose them or trick people into building them. That doesn't mean they'll choose to do so; AIs won't benefit from collapsing civilization as long as they depend on our supply chains. But models may be too shortsighted to appreciate that point, or too corrigible to care. Alignment looks hard enough that we could plausibly generate models that would share such knowledge for many different inscrutable reasons. In directed evolution, you get what you select for, which is not necessarily what you want. As Dan Selsam and others have eloquently laid out, the same is true of training AI.

But let's be clear on the extent to which biological advances will likely follow from AI. This is an issue that aggravates my fellow biologists to no end, a reaction that's likely behind their frustration with AI safety discourse more generally.

ASI will almost certainly not gain instant mastery of the world of atoms.

Many AI safety folks casually claim that recursive self-improvement will produce an entity that has already mastered all of science – and therefore will be capable of designing and building weapons that could wipe out every human. Some even assert that Drexlerian nanotechnology will be accessible by thinking sufficiently hard, as though you can solve chemistry and biology and psychology from the Hamiltonian up. Yet I see no empirical or theoretical basis for assuming that experimental bottlenecks will disappear.

Data is sharply limiting in biology. My lab found that when it comes to enzyme-focused biodesign models (ESM and similar), parameter size and optimization don't matter much until you have an awful lot of data matching genotype (DNA/protein sequence) to phenotype (performance of the molecular activity of interest). There's no doubt that ASIs will be able to design better experiments and get more out of the results than we could, but unless we think they can solve all of physics from the bottom up, I expect they'll still need data that we have not yet collected – which means they'll still have to run the experiments, analyze, and iterate. The world of atoms is hard, and slow, and we have to master it anyway.

And ensure that defenses come first. Right now, it looks like they might not, in large part due to AI. The question, therefore, is what can be done that enough people might agree to support.

My proposal on AI-bio: expand trusted-user programs conferring access to GPT-Rosalind and other cutting-edge bio-capable models (h/t @JonasSandbrink and BioTrust). Every legitimate researcher should be able to draw upon those models to help them with any question in their subfield, as defined by their publication record or that of their mentor. There should still be guardrails on other subfields, lest the model share novel combinatorial weapons with someone who might naively share them publicly, but we need to accelerate lifesaving research as fast as is safe.

For reasons of politics, which regularly interferes with science, that probably means China needs to train their own closed-weight frontier bio-specializing model, and set up their own parallel trusted user program. This seems quite achievable without requiring any agreement on AI writ large.

With scientists using frontier models, there will be no need for insecure open-weight models to answer questions on molecular and cellular biology. So let's ensure that future models aren't trained on any papers, patents, or textbooks describing details of molecular or cellular biology. Every developer does pre-training data curation; this is a straightforward extension. One can argue "what about medical providers?", at which point I must point out that physician-scientists will have trusted user access. Most other practitioners don't actually need LLM support for molecular and cellular biology, and if they do and somehow can't use a medical-only model, well, they too can get trusted-user access.

Notably, supporting this proposal doesn't require one to accept loss-of-control risks from autonomous AI, or a need for pacing AI development; I'm curious to learn what @random_walker, @sayashk, and the other normal-technology folks think.

In the long run, I confess that I doubt biological humans have the foresight, coordination, and wisdom to navigate every coming challenge ourselves, which may necessitate attempting ASI or something like it. Mirror life is the only publicly known, mechanistically concrete, civilization-threatening biothreat because it's both far away and we were going to make it by default. And while we seem to have been successful in persuading the scientific community that we shouldn't build it, I'm not remotely confident we'll be able to stop far enough short, because too many of my colleagues see no reason to forgo an otherwise useful technology – or even one that would simply be neat to demonstrate – simply because it would make it easier to build mirror bacteria. To paraphrase: "We've agreed no one will build the dangerous thing, so why not?" 

Well, Biopreparat is why not. Aum Shinrikyo is why not. Make it easy enough, and even the Unabomber is a good answer to "why not?" The same reasoning holds for any accessible weapon that could threaten civilization.

As Rabi said, ten percent is not remote if we die of it. Our own reality turned out to be in that 10%, and many died of it. That the rest of us are here today is in large part due to Szilard, Einstein, Rabi, and many others who saw the risk coming and took precautions. The least we can do is follow in their footsteps.

—

我持有的 robinhood:0x18e674231a58c239dc7daedcffe15ec3a24cff5c 和 solana:7VertkgF9KLhxxJXHX6uaWuoYZTP9LdGj2bWmVXVpump 被双双暴击了。

Hookr被Solana上的Hooked和RH链上的 ethereum:0x7987f03462200b3d8a072e02c89a8a41dcb124ee 吸血了，按理说hooks赛道火热，Hookr作为布局最早，交付内容最多的绝对龙头应该稳如老狗吧。

但恰恰相反，先是被Solana上同概念的 solana:C1mBfBoDkwWfd6uTFZp62ARHLjeVp3bDpCDMfMZtPngE 摆了一道，很多人问我怎么看？Hookr对Uniswap V4 hooks是一个模块化的自定义hooks基础设施，做成了会是直接刚需，而hooked对Solana而言并没有那么重要，只是在Transfer逻辑下加了一层hook验证，决定白名单转账，以及是否符合相应条件转账，只是一个转账逻辑，和Uniswap V4 hooks叙事对AMM的强化逻辑根本不是一回事，短期炒作预期大于长期实质意义；

再说说看V4，这本来是一个一度要死不活的项目，创始人接受采访还结结巴巴的，可能他都没想过竟然被 CLAUS给带火了。 $CLAUS 倒是挺有趣的同一个合约地址下，hook 可以在发射后改写，和AI发射台结合一下，策略可是实时更迭，很容易解决了AI Mind总是不那么聪明的问题。如此来看，V4作为发射台被带动一波逻辑也合理，但现在就断言V4会超越Hookr，成为hooks开放平台的新龙头还是太早了，V4暂时炒作空间大一点而已；

Agency更是命运多舛啊，前几天先是被WWW背刺，之后冲到了30m，昨晚愣是暴跌到了 6m左右，原因是有个Higgs的AI网红发射台，页面更炫酷，交付的是视频，机制又差不多，所以很多车头就拿不住了，纷纷换车，但Agency团队的交付能力和透明度更胜一筹，且其对标的是AI版本的PUMP fun，不是一个所谓AI网红场景就能取代的，毕竟打通视频模型后，Agency也完全可以做AI网红，这根本不是关键。

以上。

Fomo平台真的是个情绪放大器，当然也放大了市场波动。还是请大家操作前一定要有一定判断逻辑，而不要跟车头盲目换车，大家的盈利垫差异很大，承受高频操作的风险也完全不同。跟车一定要小心谨慎。

以上观点利益相关，我说的也可能都是错的，仅供参考，DYOR。

text:
A valid signature on Ethereum guarantees one thing: the chain will do exactly what you signed.
It says nothing about whether the result is what you wanted.

EF published a post exploring a fix for that gap, called native transaction assertions.
You sign a rule along with your transaction, describing what the outcome must look like.
That could be a minimum amount received, no new token approvals, or an account whose control logic must stay unchanged.
After execution, the rule checks net changes to balances, storage, code and events. If it fails, the actions revert.
The post describes two ways signing goes wrong.
In an intent mismatch, like Bybit or BadgerDAO, people approved something different from what they believed.
In an outcome mismatch, like the Aave and CoW swap, a user put in about $50.4M and received tokens worth roughly $36,000.
One candidate design is EIP-7906, which adds three opcodes and a read-only check at the end of a frame transaction.
It builds on EIP-8141, which is scheduled for Hegota. EIP-7906 itself is only Considered for Inclusion.

I like that the post is honest about the limits.

Assertions are optional, so wallets have to insist on them.
A rule written by a compromised frontend can simply allow the attack, so it has to come from a policy the attacker can't touch.
The part I keep thinking about is agents. You could limit not just what an agent can call, but what its actions can produce.
Read - https://t.co/0HzJ4oE3vF

text:
Today, I'm shutting down my startup, Sturbon.

Unfortunately, you don't choose a decision like this. You don't wake up one morning and decide to close something you have carried for three years. You get forced into it.

In August I posted that my startup had been accepted into a fund, and I left it there. What I never said in public is that shortly after, we were accepted into a second one. Together those two funds put us in front of over $42K in funding. Both have since fallen through, for reasons that had nothing to do with us.

So let me say what Sturbon was, since I never got to.

Sturbon was mental health support for young people in Africa who feel alone. Most teenagers who are struggling here never say a word to anyone. They want help, and there is nowhere to send them. Therapy costs money their families don't have, and in most schools the subject is never raised at all.

We worked on that in three ways. The first was free counseling, with no fee and no waiting room. The second was mentorship: every young person was matched with someone who had been through the same thing and come out the other side, because advice lands differently from a person who has lived it. The third was school outreach, where we went into classrooms and talked about it openly, so that the quiet kid at the back would know it has a name and that help exists.

It wasn't a company at first. It started in 2023 in my  community as an effort called Save the Youth, with no money and no plan beyond showing up. Over the next two years it expanded slowly but steadily. In three years, all of it paid for out of my own pocket, we reached over 100 young people across states and sat with them for 150+ hours of counseling.

This year it became Sturbon, and the plan was to put all of that into an app. A young person could open it and reach a counselor and a mentor from their phone, without needing us to be physically in their town. The funding was going to ship that app to the states we already serve, train and pay our first mentors, and take the school visits further than I could reach alone.

That's the part that ended. The work that came before it was real, and it still counts.

I won't write the usual lines about what running a company(ish) taught me. Truthfully, I'm glad it happened. Somebody read this and said yes to it, twice. I'll keep that.

Thank you to everyone who gave their time to this, and to everyone who answered when I asked whether I was a startup founder now haha. For six weeks, I was.

But the title was never the point. What I care about is building things that work and putting my hands on problems bigger than me. That's what I'm going back to. Lately most of my hours have gone into open source (yes, darkblooommm), alongside people at Eigen I've learned a lot from. More on that soon.

It was a good run. Back to building.
