text:
最近这轮里，以太坊、Solana 这几个红筹 Layer 1 也开始涨。我在想，到最后这些东西的估值体系可能还是当做的货币和 commodity，来交易情绪和供需更合适，而不是算内在价值？抛砖引玉欢迎指导

上个周期很多人想把它当成股票，套 cash flow multiple 或者 DCF，这个就很勉强了。协议每年还在新发币，资产本身又没有内在价值，协议收来的 fee 也不会 dividend 给持有人。以太坊的base fee 烧掉算全体持有人的 buyback，priority fee 和 MEV 进 validator；Solana 更明显，priority fee 基本到不了 staker 手里，staking yield 大半还是 issuance 发出来的。Issuance 也不是公司那种 equity dilution，它是 security budget，staking 的人多了单位收益就下来。

所以我会觉得，一个单位的以太坊或者一个 SOL，更应该从货币汇率的角度去想，而不是从公司价值去想。一个网络有用，不代表他的币有内在价值，就好像全球石油网络有价值，不代表持有一桶石油有内在价值一样；币每年还在 issuance，定价靠的是有多少人愿意持有它，对着多少可交易的供给。

从这个角度讲，市场情绪和供需当然比内在价值、比 DCF 重要。未来，可能用一种交易货币或者Commodity 的思维，而不是长期buy and hold 的角度，去看待这些Layer 1 会更合适。

当然，像 Hypeliquid 这样类股票币，就是另外一个话题了，可以更多的使用股权的思路来观察。

text:
代币化私募，才是 Robinhood 相对 Solana、BSC 股票代币真正能拉开差距的地方。

其实上市股票市场这边，它反而受合规和发行人态度拖累，Robinhood 并不占品种优势。它的 Stock Tokens 是关联实体发行的代币化债务证券，宣称按 1:1 用托管股票做抵押，给的是价格和经济敞口，没有投票权，也不是法律意义上的股权。2026 年 9 月 AMC 首席执行官 Adam Aron 公开称这是“假市场”，表示公司不知情、未授权，并扬言找 SEC。Vlad Tenev 的回应是：股票上市之后，发行人管得了自身股份的权利义务，管不了别人发行参考该股票的独立证券。已上市公司既不理解、也不愿背书，Robinhood 能“正规”覆盖的范围就会受限制。相比之下Solana 上的 xStocks、还是BSC 上的bstonk标的可以铺得更开更多！

私募才是 Robinhood 有、纯链上市场没有的供给关系。Vlad 已公开说过，私募代币化的实现路径已经想清楚，预期会做成大规模产品；Robinhood Ventures 在和大量私营公司建立关系，承销业务则帮它们设计面向散户的上市路径，而且已有不少私营公司主动来问怎么参与代币化。这和协议自己到二级市场或 SPV 买一点份额再映射，不是同一类资源：券商、承销、一级关系和散户分发在同一家公司手里。2025 年它在欧盟发过的 OpenAI、SpaceX 代币仍是间接敞口，OpenAI 也立即澄清未合作、未批准任何股权转让。所以这条优势现在还是关系和政策路径，不是已经规模上线的产品。

币安此前的 Pre-Polymarket 更说明这种差距。pPOLY 由 Paimon Finance 发行，锚定 Polymarket，币安只做流量入口，并明确表示自己不发行、不销售、不运营。Polymarket 公司并未参与，持有人没有股份、投票权或分红，本质上是锚定价格的第三方凭证，对大多数人不如传统私募股权有吸引力。

如果私营公司自己拿股份做链上发行，逻辑就不同。代币对应的是公司认可的股权或可转换权益，而不是外部凭证；Robinhood 还能用承销和 Robinhood Ventures，把链上一级接到后续 IPO。监管把代币化证券的持有人权利、过户和经纪商义务补齐之后，同一笔权益才有机会从链上持仓切回传统股票账户，而不是到期按公式结算。这比币安分发的第三方凭证多一层发行人承诺，也比“发行人反对也照样上”的公开市场包装，更接近真正的股权。

text:
Google 这一步其实比“Docs 支持 Markdown”重要得多。

.md 正在逐渐变成人和 AI Agent 之间的通用文件格式。

以前很多 AI 工作流的问题是：

Agent 在写 Markdown，
人类在 Docs / Notion 里协作，
中间还要不停转换、复制、同步。

现在 Google Drive + Docs 可以直接预览、编辑、评论和协作 .md 文件，而且文件本身仍然保持 Markdown。

这意味着一个很实际的变化：

以后完全可以让 AI Agent 直接维护 Markdown，
人类继续用熟悉的 Docs 界面 review / comment / edit。

文件本身就是接口。

对多 Agent 工作流来说，这比再造一套“AI 文档系统”有意义得多。

text:
$PSTR is a fair launch on hyperevm.

the tax starts at 99% and drops 1% every minute until it hits 10%, lasting around 90 minutes. after that, 10% stays as the normal buy/sell tax.

what happens when you buy during the fair launch:
- at a 70% tax, you receive 30% of the tokens you bought
- the other 70% is sold back into the pool instantly, and the proceeds go to the treasury
- net, it's as if you'd bought 30%

so don't be surprised by the chart during the anti snipe window : every buy spikes the price, then it pulls back as the tax is sold. that's the treasury filling not someone dumping.

how to buy:
- on our website: the current tax is already set in your slippage. 
- on hyperswap: slippage is capped at 50%, so buys will fail until the tax drops below that, around minute 50.

we recommend you swapping through our frontend, no additional tax is applied.

Mistral has released Mistral Large 4, scoring 38 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index; France is back to having the most intelligent model from outside the US and China

@MistralAI has released Mistral Large 4 in Research Public Preview, with plans to release the weights of the 1T parameter (49B active) model at the end of October. It achieves 38 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, comparable to GPT-6 Luna (max, 38) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, 39). It also achieves 50% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, level with GLM-5.3-Flash and ahead of models such as Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max).

Key benchmarking results for Mistral Large 4 Preview:

➤ Most intelligent model from outside the US and China: Mistral Large 4 Preview scores 38 on the Intelligence Index, comparable to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, 39) and GPT-6 Luna (max, 38). This makes it the most intelligent model from outside the US and China, ahead of countries such as South Korea and the United Arab Emirates

➤ Level with GLM-5.3-Flash on cyber defense capability: Mistral Large 4 Preview scores 50 on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, level with GLM-5.3-Flash (50) and behind MiMo-V2.6-Pro (56). Once its weights are released, it will rank among the top three open weights models on the Cyber Index. Its strongest result is on CyberGym-E2E-AA, where it scores 82%, ahead of MiMo-V2.6-Pro (79%) and GPT-6 Luna (max, 78%)

➤ Over 4x the Cost per Task of similar-intelligence open weights models: Mistral Large 4 Preview costs $1.13 per Intelligence Index task with standard pricing of $1.36/$4.18 per 1M input/output tokens, with $0.14 per 1M cached input tokens. For the first two weeks, Mistral Large 4 Preview will be served at a 50% launch discount, bringing its Cost per Task down to $0.57. This is still more costly than GLM-5.3-Flash ($0.25) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, $0.27)

➤ Strong document and image reasoning: Mistral Large 4 Preview scores 19% on GDP.pdf, on par with MiMo-V2.6-Pro (19%) and behind Kimi K3 (22%). This is an 18-point improvement from Mistral Large 3, partly driven by improvements in their API, which now accepts 100 images per request, up from 8 for previous Mistral models

Key model details:

➤ Context Window: 512k tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text and image input, with text output

➤ Pricing: $1.36/$4.18 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.14 per 1M cached input tokens), with 50% off for the first two weeks ($0.68/$2.09)

➤ Availability: Research Public Preview on Mistral's API, with open weights planned for the end of October

A hundred years ago this coast traded pearls. Today its sovereign funds hold 1.7 trillion dollars, more than any other city on earth. "The Capital of Capital" was never a slogan here. It is the status quo.

For fifty years that capital flowed outward and built things somewhere else. Now the direction has reversed. In a world splitting into blocs, Abu Dhabi has become the one address all sides still take the meeting.

The building we are borrowing, the Louvre, argues it better than we can. The first universal museum in the Arab world, built on a single idea: every civilisation belongs in the same room.

That is also our idea. Smaller room. Same conviction.

We were met with open arms. We intend to leave this city better than we found it, starting with the quality of the conversations held inside it.

On 3 December, we open the doors at the Louvre.

text:
a16z：AI 消费级的下一个 10x，是从「省时间的生产力工具」转向「花时间与花钱的交易载体」。
Muse、Grok Bot、Instinct 的卡位，正在于此。

1｜高渗透、弱变现、极度依赖重度极客
a16z 援引 YipitData 8 月美卡交易样本，把变现瓶颈摊开了：
- 约 50% 美国人在用 AI，付费只有约 4.5%
- 前 10% 付费用户贡献过半收入
- 前 1% 月付 $903，付费中位数仅 $25

2｜从卖订阅，回归广告与抽成
a16z ：天花板不可能靠把这 4.5% 订阅率拉高来实现。
前期收订阅，是因为推理太贵，撑不起先免费圈地再变现。
成本一降，免费覆盖是必然，通过广告和交易抽成收费：8 月的口径，OpenAI 广告年化已经约 $10 亿，并在逐步放量，趋势已成。

所以，后续的重心换了：让人花时间，替人花钱。
现在的大模型，基本都在帮人省时间（编程、文案），工科生的理性浪漫。
历史上最大的消费公司，都在让人花时间（娱乐、社交、购物），普通人的感性消费。
agent 一替人花钱，抽成的体量会成倍盖过订阅。

Instinct 是实证：
咬死高频、低阻力的原生短信场景，上线前三周 40% 用户绑卡，首月人均消费超 $1000。
路径完全复刻移动互联网：
工具付费 → 基建降本与全面免费 → 广告和抽成通吃。

3｜终局：模型依靠场景与通道加速渗透
变现支点从算力订阅切到广告与抽成，壁垒权重倒置：
- 基座大模型有认知能力，但离高频生活和资金链路远
- 超级流量与原生通道，手里有停留时长（广告）和支付入口（抽成）

下一阶段红利向场景端倾斜，让赛场有了更多的竞争者入局：
- Muse：挂 Meta，占社交关系和沉浸时长
- Grok Bot：挂 X，占公共广场的高频信息流
- Instinct：下沉系统级短信，最短链路锁交易与支付

大模型第一个周期，打穿了编程和办公。
真正的 10x，发生在 AI 打通大众消费、开始分润生活交易的时候。

text:
Before Hyperliquid became a $20B+ ecosystem, Jeff had already built a life most people would have retired from.

After yesterday’s event in Singapore, he posted a long thank-you to the people who made it happen and to the community that continues to build around hyperliquid.

And honestly, it made me think about something. We probably have a few things to thank Jeff for too. Because by the time hyperliquid came around, Jeff had already won at a level most people spend their entire lives chasing.

By 18, he had made the U.S. Physics Olympiad team, won silver, then gold at the International Physics Olympiad, finishing 24th in the world. He went to Harvard to study mathematics and computer science before joining Hudson River Trading, one of the world’s leading high-frequency trading firms. 

He eventually moved into crypto and built Chameleon Trading, a market-making operation that he had started with roughly $10,000 of his own money.
Then Terra, then FTX. Instead of walking away from crypto, Jeff decided the problem was deeper than a few bad actors. The infrastructure itself could be better.

So he shut down the business he had already built and started again.
That became Hyperliquid.

And he took a path that made very little sense compared with the way most crypto companies were being built.

No private investor allocation. No traditional VC-backed launch. No paid market makers. When a reported $100 million investment offer came at roughly a $1 billion valuation, he turned it down.

Then, on November 29, 2024, Hyperliquid distributed 310 million HYPE, 31% of the total supply, to roughly 94,000 eligible addresses. The allocation went to users based on their activity rather than to private investors, centralized exchanges, or market makers. 

That decision probably meant more than another successful token launch.

It gave the people who had spent years using the product a piece of what they had helped build.

And look at where that experiment is now.

Hyperliquid has gone from an onchain perpetuals exchange to an ecosystem spanning spot markets, HyperEVM, HIP-3 and an expanding collection of applications and markets built around its infrastructure.

The community event in Singapore was officially described as a gathering for the builders and users who had shaped that ecosystem over the years. It was oversubscribed before the event even happened. 

Jeff is thanking the community for building alongside him. But the community exists because he chose to build something worth building around in the first place.

And now, a few years later, he’s standing in Singapore in front of people from an ecosystem that barely existed when he started.

Traders who found the platform early. builders who started building on top of it. creators who turned it into a culture.
Founders who are now trying to build businesses around the infrastructure.

People who weren’t even part of the story when Hyperliquid was just a small perps exchange.

Jeff is right to thank the community.

But if you’re part of that community, you probably have your own reason to be grateful.

Because he could have spent his life making money from markets he didn’t build.

Instead, he decided to build the market.

And somehow, we’re now watching an entire ecosystem grow around it.

Not celebrating how far Hyperliquid has come.

But realizing how much bigger the thing Jeff started could still become.

AMERICAN CENTURY: TREASURY SELLOFF LOOKS OVERDONE

American Century’s Charles Tan says the recent Treasury selloff may have gone too far, calling a 5.25% 10-year yield an attractive entry point for long-term investors.

He argues the surge was driven largely by forced selling and intense competition for capital from AI investment and government borrowing, rather than inflation fears.

Tan expects the AI debt boom to eventually slow, reducing pressure on the Fed to hike, and says current pricing for up to four hikes over the next year is too aggressive.

text: This is very thoughtfully put. I do think we should learn from what already happened to maths academia and think about what philosophy academia can realistically do instead of fending the concern off by merely saying “meh AI bad”.
author: LedermanHarvey
quoted_text:
Universities, and more broadly, our existing research institutions (peer review) have a key role to play in furthering and protecting human understanding. These institutions are designed to be slow-moving: they are supposed to be august, conservative places that protect the highest standards of rigor and truth-seeking, against short-lived fads. But I worry that at this moment, universities and our research institutions are not moving fast enough to help students and especially younger scholars in areas where learning and research is being reshaped by AI. 

Many have made extraordinary efforts to change their teaching strategies and assessment methods on a dime this semester (mathematicians moving to oral assessment only, philosophers focusing on in-class writing etc.) Many others people have yet to adjust and there is a lot we could do better (e.g. in admissions), but I'm far more optimistic than I was six months ago that faculty are waking up. Still, I'm worried that within philosophy (and perhaps elsewhere too?) we're not  having a sensible conversation about papers and journals, which in turn means we're not having a sensible conversation about hiring and promotion. Even if capabilities completely stop advancing now, the standards for journal publications in my areas of philosophy, for instance, must already be completely transformed. This doesn't mean humans are useless in these areas, or that these areas are somehow trivial: human understanding remains extremely valuable; indeed, fostering such understanding seems arguably more important for individual and societal flourishing going forward. But in these areas I doubt that beautifully constructed papers will be the best instrument for conveying or producing human understanding going forward. I also highly doubt that the time-lag of our current peer review system (which was already overburdened and far too slow) will make sense in a world where individuals have the power to resolve whole swathes of open problems very quickly. (I expect journals to begin to be swamped with papers this semester if they aren't already.)

I don't have answers for how things should look going forward. But even this year's academic job market will be affected (never mind future years); we need to have a broader, serious conversation among tenured faculty about what to do (maybe it's happening somewhere I missed?). 

Here are two small disparate positive thoughts:

- I can imagine that digital artifacts which record a wide array of results, and which can be easily navigated by both humans and AI could be most effective at recording what is known in some subareas. (I'm inspired by this Logical Maps https://t.co/KMPoc64iNG project of Zach Goodsell, in collaboration with Cian Dorr among others.) Maybe such artifacts, with associated verifications of the proofs, could be quickly assessed by outside referees, and perhaps we could have "journals" that link to ones which have been peer-reviewed (hopefully on a shorter timeline)? Perhaps alongside this, there will be more large collaborations on such artifacts?

- Innovative pedagogy and, relatedly communication about research, should be reweighted relative to discovering new results. We seem to me now already in a world where new results are abundant while excellent exposition and thoughtful, careful teaching is scarce. I don't pretend to know how this will evolve going forward, but my guess would be that, just as MOOCs failed to transform university teaching, this revolution will in key respects fail to transform human learning. People are ultimately social and we will continue to benefit from and seek out community in learning and understanding (and arguably it's intrinsically valuable to boot). Teaching and learning is as much about conveying values of care, rigor and curiosity, and building community around those values, as it is about conveying information, and that will continue to be true in the future. As a profession, it seems to me we should invest more in such teaching, and find ways, institutionally, to assess and incentivize it better. This may change the personalities who are drawn to academia as well as its culture, but it seems necessary to preserve the goods we need universities to foster and protect and could independently be for the better.

text:
This is great for the Ramp team, but I'm not sure its good for Fred. 

Having worked with administrative records for years, I agree they are an important complement to survey data. But what survey data gets you, when drawn from universe frames, is a representative sample. If the admin frame doesn't cover the universe of businesses (like tax data), and you don't do careful adjustment, it will can give you a warped view of reality. 

Customer datasets don't cover the universe of businesses. 

I'd love to see an analysis of the composition of the Ramp data akin to what @erikbryn , @BharatKChandar , and @RuyuChen did with the ADP data in the their Canaries paper.

Even better: don't just show us how unrepresentative the sample is, use weights to make it representative. @ufukakcigit, Javier Miranda and their team did just that with the Intuit data. 

I don't know the process for getting data into Fred, but I am surprised that the methodological detail on the Ramp AI Index website would be sufficient. Maybe there is more detail out there somewhere, but I've yet to find it. 

Data on AI spend will be an important piece of the AI measurement puzzle, but if its not done carefully, it can actually make things less clear.

https://t.co/FuYkz7cCRQ

text:
最近一直在想一个问题：

牛市里，是不是不太适合把几乎所有研究精力都放在预测市场？

不是看空 prediction markets。

相反，我依然觉得它会是一个长期非常重要的赛道，策略、自动化、信息优势这些东西也都值得持续做。

但我越来越觉得：

市场环境变了，人的注意力配置也应该跟着变。

熊市或者低波动时期，很适合花大量时间研究预测市场、套利、自动化、各种可以持续复利的策略。

但进入牛市以后，最大的机会成本可能不是亏钱。

而是你每天都在一个不错的赛道里稳定地研究、交易、优化，却错过了外面正在发生的：

新的资产类别
新的发行机制
新的协议
新的玩法
新的叙事
以及那些只会出现一次的早期窗口。

预测市场的很多机会，明天还会有，下个月可能也还会有。

但一个真正的新叙事从 0 到 1 的那几周，错过了可能就永远错过了。

所以我现在越来越觉得：

不仅资金需要动态调仓，注意力本身也需要调仓。

熊市，多做确定性和复利。

牛市，提高对新东西、早期叙事和非对称机会的研究权重。

到了狂热阶段，再把重心切向兑现和风险控制。

不是预测市场 vs Crypto。

而是每个阶段，都应该问一句：

我现在这一小时，放在哪里的潜在凸性最高？

尤其是牛市，可能最贵的从来不是 gas，也不是手续费。

而是机会成本。

text:
AI应用最近又有点复苏，从Instinct到Muse，等等又开启了新的AI应用趋势，a16z 的 @omooretweets 发布了最新的AI应用Top150榜单，又做了深入的研究分析。主要观点：

使用广，付费窄：
近一半美国消费者自称用过 AI，但只有约 25% 每天用。到 2026 年 8 月，只有 4.5% 的美国消费者为 ChatGPT、Gemini 或 Claude 至少其中一个付了个人订阅，一年前是 2.1%。

真正深用、肯付钱的是一小撮重度用户：付费者里前 10% 贡献了大约一半支出；前 1% 占全部观测支出的 19.5%，超过后 50% 的合计（16.6%）。这前 1% 月均在个人卡上花 903 美元，过去 18 个月还涨了 80%；中位数付费者每月 25 美元，几乎没涨。

只有 13% 的人为不止一个 AI 产品付费。这些人更像 prosumer，不是大众消费者，钱主要花在编码、自动化、生产力工具（n8n、fal、Manus、Nous Research）和创作工具（Higgsfield、Figma、HeyGen）。

三家模型公司在打不同的局：
ChatGPT 仍是龙头。8 月网页访问大约是 Gemini 的 2 倍、Claude 的 6 倍；移动月活领先 Gemini 约 2.5 倍、Claude 约 14 倍。美国付费订阅用户大约是 Claude 或 Gemini 的 3 倍。

Claude 是这期最明显的变化：2023 年 9 月第一期网页榜还没名字，现在流量已超过 DeepSeek 和 Perplexity，美国消费者订阅数今年早些时候超过 Gemini。

即便 Google 把旧付费用户迁进 AI 套餐、人为抬高了订阅数，两边仍接近。Claude 靠 Cowork（1 月）、Claude Design（4 月）、Fable 5（6 月）和一波公共关注拉上来；2 月底与五角大楼的争议期间，它第一次成为美国免费移动应用下载第一。

Anthropic 明确不做广告，走订阅，而且更狠：7.3% 的付费用户在最贵的个人套餐 Max（100 美元/月起），Google 和 ChatGPT 对应档分别只有 1.3% 和 1.1%。到仲夏势头转了。

过去六个月三家合计发了 127 个新品，方向已经分开：Anthropic 几乎全押 prosumer（Design、Code Review、Claude Science）；Google 押创作模型（Lyria 3 Pro、Gemini Omni）；OpenAI 两边都做，企业侧有 Work、Sites、Dots，消费侧有 Images 2.0、Health、Personal Finance、求职。

个人助手竞赛：
半年前 OpenClaw 这类 agent 还不能给普通人用。现在 Instinct、Tomo、Poke、Lindy、Town 等已报数十万用户；巨头也进场：Meta 的 Muse、OpenAI 的 Dots、xAI 的 Grok Bot。多数助手想做到短信、邮件、电话都能叫，当前热渠道是 iMessage——Instinct 8 月在这里上线，DoorDash 也做了短信下单。

早期用户仍是同一批重度用户。七个早期用户群（1502 人）里最常讨论的任务是编码和技术自动化。

Instinct 创始人 Noah Shinn 称，40% 用户三周内绑了个人信用卡，一旦开始购买，月均通过 Instinct 花 1300 美元；声称年化交易额已超 10 亿美元，一半来自旅行。平台在选边：Amazon 不到两周就切断了 Meta Muse 的接入；Shopify、Instacart、OpenTable、Expedia、Ticketmaster、Plaid 等签了官方集成。到 9 月下旬，消费侧对决主要是 Instinct 对 Muse。

Instinct 仍在邀请制，8 月底到 9 月初三周据说过了 10 万用户。Meta 9 月 9 日推出 Muse（浏览器、桌面、移动、WhatsApp），首周约 25 万日活，不到一个月下载超 500 万，快过 ChatGPT 和 Claude 的同期，但只在美国和加拿大。对照 Threads 在同样两个市场前 22 天超过 1500 万下载，早期声量仍然不大。真正的对手仍是用户漠不关心。

老产品进场，创业公司还剩的位置：
Canva、Notion 进了网页前十，Figma 进前 15。Superhuman（原 Grammarly）稳定在网页榜上半区，支出榜第一次就到第四。Google 单独有五个网页条目：Gemini、NotebookLM、AI Studio、Labs、Antigravity。

商业模式几乎全是订阅：
网页榜 44 个 AI 原生产品都已变现。84% 有订阅，64% 有按量或加购积分，只有 14% 有广告，2% 靠交易或平台抽成。这和上一代互联网相反：2025 年广告占 Meta 收入 97.6%、Alphabet 73.2%；Amazon 订阅服务 496 亿美元，只占总收入 6.9%。全球前 20 消费订阅产品里 65% 是媒体。ChatGPT 三年半就进了前 20，说明堆出大规模付费用户有多难。

详细：https://t.co/l9JdPAlrlr

另外目前相比web1/2，ai 应用的top榜单主要在搜索，办公，图片视频，教育领域在和传统产品竞争。而在很多传统的品类仍然是空白，比如社交网络，购物市场平台，约会并没有出现真正的现象级产品。具体看图：

text:
ChatGPT 的「App Store 时刻」可能真的来了。一个插件上线一周，直接给一家创业公司干出了 50 万美元新增 ARR。

MagicPath CEO Pietro Schirano 刚刚晒了一个挺夸张的数据。

9 月 29 日，他们把 MagicPath 做成了 ChatGPT 的 Plugin Extension。以前用户得离开 ChatGPT，打开 MagicPath 做设计；现在它直接住进 ChatGPT 侧边栏里，可以调文件、开设计画布，边聊边做。

上线没多久，Schirano 就说增长超过了 2000%。

今天他又更新说，增长到现在还没停，仅过去这一周，MagicPath 就新增了 50 万美元 ARR。

过去几年 AI 创业公司最头疼的一件事，是大家都在 OpenAI 上面做产品，却得自己去外面买流量、做 SEO、投广告，再想办法把 ChatGPT 用户拖到自己的产品里。

Plugin Extension 把这条路径砍短了。

ChatGPT 本身就是入口，用户已经在那里工作。一个产品只要能自然嵌进现有 workflow，就可以直接出现在需求发生的地方。

这其实很像早期 App Store 最恐怖的地方，苹果提供的从来不只是 SDK，还有一条突然出现的超级分发渠道。

现在 ChatGPT 也开始拥有这个东西了。

所以 MagicPath 一周新增 50 万美元 ARR 这件事，我觉得值得所有做 AI 应用的人盯着看。这个窗口刚打开的时候，Plugin 可能还是一个功能；如果越来越多 MagicPath 出现，它很快就会变成一门新的「ChatGPT SEO」。

谁能更早占住 ChatGPT 里的入口，可能比谁的网站做得更漂亮重要得多。

text:
Not sure if you noticed that our portal to Naraka in Unleash the Avatar looks similar to Balinese split gates. 

We thought a lot on how best to represent Indian hell (Naraka) and how Lord Yamraj and his subjects would behave. Most of our references were from the Rigveda and Yamagita but as we kept looking for other visual representations, we came across painted representations of Lord Yama and his servants on the ceilings of the Kerta Gosa pavilion in Bali. 

The gates in our game carry the same concept as the Balinese ones: They stand for "rwa bhineda", the balance of opposites (between worlds). While we won't use the exact real split gates in game (and our version is creative representation) to represent the 4th gate, it's still fun learning about all of the different representations of culture across the world.

I didn't want this to feel like Hell/Satan but Indian. It's overdone in games too. We wanted to do a portrayal centered on judgment, duty, and the cycle of rebirth and i think this is better grounded than a generic overlord of hell.

author: levelsio
quoted_text:
I keep going more niche with reverse engineered web-based versions of games

👉 https://t.co/MohU4A8Zel 👈

6 months ago I tried to reverse engineer Urban Terror

Urban Terror was kind of a Counter-Strike style mod on top of the Quake 3 Arena engine, I think @Erwin_AI got me to play this during COVID

Because it runs on Quake 3's engine like RTCW and Q3 itself, I thought I could just use ioquake3 and WASM to run it on web, then add a multiplayer server and it'd just work...

But no it didn't, I got stuck 6 months ago, it was buggy and wouldn't work, I kept trying and kinda got it to load but not really play

Today I tried it again with Opus 5.5 and again, I couldn't get it to work, giving up I did a last try with Fable 5.1 on high effort and it after awhile it did figure out the issue!

"The engine's struct was 4 bytes longer than what UT's bytecode expects, everything after that point (the entity count and the entity list) was read 4 bytes off"

It rewrote the bytecode and made it work!

So now we have another game preserved, running  100% the web via WASM, with a multiplayer server tied to it, so you can play with your friends 😊

Every model that comes out makes a bit more things possible and you can just keep trying old things that didn't work before

I see lots of people mod modern games now too which looks very cool too

Here I'm playing it with @marckohlbrugge a few minutes ago! Anyway you can play it with everyone else at https://t.co/MohU4A8Zel now :D

author: 0xNairolf
quoted_text:
on airdrops and why they are less frequent:

first, airdrops are *the* single best community building tool crypto has ever created

you tease an airdrop to acquire users, then turn a percentage of them into actual supporters because they become financially + emotionally tied to the success of the product and most importantly, you put the asset directly in their hands

best growth hack, no debate on this

but the pre token phase is also basically easy mode for teams

users are willing to pay (high) fees, deposit capital, generate volume and juice every metric imaginable for the possibility of an allocation

you are basically getting paid to bootstrap your product

the problem is that this model has been abused to death

there are well over 20 teams still farming airdrop farmers after extracting $100m+ from them, while knowing perfectly well they will never launch a token because launching a token now comes with expectations they cant meet

people want revenue
people want buybacks
people want a fair distribution
people want the token to actually capture value

how many pre token products in crypto can deliver all of that today? 10? maybe less?

so you end up with a weird equilibrium

(i) the pre token phase is extremely profitable and low risk
(ii) the post token phase forces you to prove that your product is actually viable and that there is enough value creation to sustain a token

this is why you are getting fewer airdrops and fewer TGEs

tldr: airdrops are disappearing because they worked too well while the bar for launching a good token became much higher

less TGEs is the natural outcome

text:
The “Aave is a bank, Morpho is a platform for asset managers” distinction is getting harder to defend with V4.

@SentoraHQ has already proposed independently curated markets on @aave, with control over collateral, risk parameters, interest rate curves and oracles.

That puts Aave directly in the business of providing infrastructure for asset managers, the very differentiator highlighted here for $MORPHO.

The proposed economics are explicit from the beginning: 50% of the instance’s protocol revenue goes to the Aave DAO, and 50% to Sentora.

For $AAVE, that means external curators bring both new markets and a defined revenue stream.

If Morpho activates its fee switch, the competitive questions get sharper: how sensitive are its curators to fees, and how much value does each platform deliver for the share it takes?

Curators already bring the deposits. Their choice of infrastructure determines who earns from them.

Great interview by @BitcoinJesusETH and @milkroaddaily.

author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
What Menlo has done over the last 24 months is exceptional.

Yes, they did Anthropic’s round at $4BN that will make them $50BN+ as a firm. NICE!

But they then took that and went f****** hard. They do Lovable, Higgsfield, Legora.

They compounded the brand win of Anthropic to cement their position from respectfully a slightly ageing firm to being a dominant venture leader at the forefront with Thrive, a16z, Benchmark etc.

It is incredible to see and I sat down with @venkyganesan to shoot the s*** on this.

1. Every Seed Investment Is an Option Bet

Seed-stage deals function as financial options to discover true outlier potential before committing major capital. VCs must construct a broad enough portfolio to secure sufficient at-bats, only sizing up their position when quantifiable, revenue-based metrics prove an outlier has emerged.

2. What Is the First Sign of the AI Wave Cracking?

Market cycles rarely collapse due to equity write-downs. They fracture when levered debt defaults occur. When market participants take on heavy leverage during an AI boom, precise timing becomes as critical as being directionally correct, making debt obligations the primary failure vector when cycles turn.

3. Why Every VC Must Now Prioritize IRR

Every startup in the current landscape writes a structural tax to the Mag 7 and hyperscalers for compute and foundation models. Because LPs can buy index exposure to those same public tech giants without fees or carry, private VCs must generate outsized IRR performance, beating public markets by at least 1,000 basis points, to justify private capital allocation.

4. Why LPs Wanting Smaller Funds and Slower Deployment Is BS

LPs cannot demand both smaller fund sizes and multi-year deployment paces in the middle of a generational platform shift. Because AI startups face immense capital requirements to scale compute, VC firms that refuse to deploy capital rapidly will watch competitors step in and capture the category winners.

5. The Theory of Reflexivity and How It's Causing Markups

Reflexivity creates self-reinforcing loops where fast revenue growth triggers rapid valuation markups, attracting elite human and financial capital that further accelerates growth. However, when copycat investors chase markups for momentum rather than underlying fundamentals, reflexive valuation bubbles inflate until market realities force an inevitable correction.

6. Sometimes You Pay Up Because You Have Unique Insight

Premium entry prices are not always the result of irrational bidding. They often stem from an investor's ability to recognize a fundamentally larger total addressable market than the consensus. When a VC possesses unique conviction around an expanding market opportunity, paying above current rates reflects calculated foresight rather than price-taking behavior.

7. There's No Limit to What a Person Can Do as Long as They Don't Care Who Gets the Credit

Personal ego remains one of the most expensive liabilities in venture capital and company building. True long-term success requires setting aside individual notoriety, focusing ruthlessly on generating LP returns, and empowering teammates and founders without worrying about who receives the public credit.

quoted_text:
I literally hooked up ALL my finance accounts to Grok Bot. 

I really mean all of them:

1/ Chase
2/ Charles Schwab
3/ E*TRADE
4/ Fidelity
5/ Robinhood
6/ Wealthfront
7/ Apple Card
8/ 𝕏 Money

FYI, this is a total of 30 accounts... Chase alone is 13 accounts between checking, savings, brokerage, credit cards, a 401(k), trusts, a stock plan, and 529s for the kids.

I was already honestly the best with my $ money and I’ve NEVER made a late payment in my life. But before Grok Bot, I was wasting so much time bc every answer lived in different apps. Like my cash was in one place, cards in another, brokerage accounts somewhere else, and had to compile everything in a spreadsheet, if I even got around to putting it together.

Now I just text my Grok Bot CFO.

I can ask, “What’s my cash right now?” and it pulls everything together and separates personal from business. I can ask which credit cards are coming due and whether I have enough cash to pay them all in full. Green means I’m covered, red means I’m short, and it tells me exactly how much I need. I actually tested this... going red on purpose. Like I moved $ money around so I would come up short on one of the upcoming bills, and Grok caught it.

I can even ask, “Where did my $ money go?” and instead of opening a bunch of apps, downloading transactions, cleaning up a spreadsheet, and making a chart myself, it pulls everything together and gives me the breakdown.

Today, I also asked it for a pie chart of all my stock investments with the amounts and percentages. 

1/ TSLA is 84.9%
2/ SPCX is 10.4%
3/ NVDA is 4.7% 

That’s across $ money sitting in different brokerage accounts, and it's awesome that I didn’t have to think about where any of it was. 

I literally just asked it one question... you can see for yourself. 

If you’re serious about your finances, you already ask the same questions all the time. 

• Like, can I cover everything that’s due? 
• Where did my $ money go? 
• How much $ cash do I really have? 
• What investments do I actually own? 

But honestly, the annoying part is that your financial life is usually scattered across 10+ different apps/platforms and a bunch of accounts, so getting a real answer takes a lot of work and your time. And honestly, most people probably don’t even look until something feels off or if they get a notification that a payment was missed or something.

Now, with all my finance accounts linked, I just ask a normal question, Grok Bot checks everything it has connected, and gives me the answer. Then I can ask the same thing tomorrow, and again whenever, and get the updated version without rebuilding anything.

The fact that you are able to talk to your entire financial life like you’re texting someone who already knows where everything is... this is a total game changer in the world of finance imo. 

If you really care about your $ money, hook yours up to Grok Bot. 

It's so worth it.

My new favorite work is Claudable. 
Which Claude defines as: 
Claudable /ˈklɔː.də.bəl/ (adjective)

Of a skill: capable of being performed by Claude at or above the required standard, at lower cost than a human, with review that takes less effort than the work itself.
Of a role: consisting mainly of Claudable skills, so that the work could be done by Claude under light human oversight and without anyone needing to put their own name, license, or relationships behind it.
Of a person: holding a professional value that lies mainly in Claudable skills, such that Claude could take over their function with little loss in output.

Usage: The word describes the work, not the worth of whoever does it. A role is Claudable to the degree that it involves digital inputs and outputs, judgment that can be written down, quick verification of results, and no dependence on personal accountability or relationships.

Example: "His weekly reporting is fully Claudable. His investor relationships are not."

Antonym: unclaudable, meaning dependent on tacit judgment, personal accountability, or trust that Claude cannot supply.

Derived forms: Claudability (noun), claudably (adverb), semi-Claudable (adjective, meaning partly replaceable but still needing a human owner).

text:
David Friedberg: The AI Wars Are Already Here, and America Can’t Hit Pause

“We always assumed in the sci-fi novels that we would be in an era of having robot wars, and I think we failed to recognize that the software came first, and we are actually having the AI wars.

I think we will see a massive rise in defense systems. What I heard in DC this week was some Fortune 50 CEOs are very worried about cyber defense.

That means they're going to start to make this their #1 priority to address at the board level. That means the budgets for cyber defense are going to go through the roof.

Now, let me ask you a question. When you have to do cyber defense in an era of AI, are you going to use old school software, or are you going to use AI?

You're going to use AI.

And because of that, because cyber defense is going to need to grow, the US is going to need to provide competitive AI for cyber defense. It is a classic arms race scenario.

And so the US cannot simply step back and pause and turn off AI. It is already everywhere in the world. Therefore, the risks are rising. Therefore, we need to increase our investment in AI to maintain our cyber defense capabilities, both at the enterprise level and at the government level, and potentially even at the civilian consumer level.

So I think that the cyber defense necessity actually mandates that we continue to build out data centers to support it.”

text:
I haven't posted in a while so here are 20 takes about AI, in no particular order. 

1. It's very telling that the default question in tech and journalism is "how worried are you about X" and fighting over what to worry about. There's a deeply anxious cultural backdrop in Western Europe and North America that deeply affects how any technological development is interpreted; see for example https://t.co/OU8dEOn0tD. "Nervousness as seriousness" does seem to be a larger problem in tech/broader discourse at the moment. I think you can care about risks/externalities while remaining pretty optimistic about technology.

2. I'm tired of people who in private pretend to be uncertain or only care about tail risk but then go on media campaigns making all sorts of absolute claims. I think trying to stoke flames and get everyone to freak out is deeply unhelpful, and will come with costs. I also continue to think p(dooms) are bad, vibe-based measures: see https://t.co/ebzxGTqv6I. People who should know better ignore that because they do the standard shortcut of acknowledging the caveat as sufficient for handling it. And this is coming from someone who does think working on catastrophic risks is important!

3. I'm also disappointed that parts of the AI policy ecosystem has felt so comfortable with populism, and happy too sacrifice important norms/principles to advance their aims. I've said it before, but the totalizing nature of AI risk discourse means some people act exactly like the power seeking optimizers they fear. I am more concerned about the gradual decay of our institutions, world order, and liberalism than I am about AI killing everyone; and I think we should be wary of AI advocacy that contributes to this.

4. Some parts of AI safety discourse are basically just thought experiments. Variants of "Assuming everyone has a nuke in their pocket, then what do we do?" This can be very useful at times! But too many just overfit to edge cases as their main operating worldview, and ignore endogenous responses from society. It's like being in 2000 and saying "see all these viruses, spyware, and spam? Well tech progress means we'll only get infinitely more of this and no way to adapt." So I think it's important to avoid fatalism, and absolutlism whilst considering edge scenarios, and the inability to provide an ex ante list of solutions to every permutation of 'future models will be more capable' is not evidence that these problems are intractable. 

5. Many critics of AI safety also fail to really engage honestly with the fact that there will, in fact, be all sorts of important risks as we decrease the barriers to entry to many activities that otherwise require some degree of expertise. This doesn’t mean we need to live in a constant Schmittian ‘state of emergency’ requiring extraordinary measures every time a new model drops, but it does mean we will need important state-led efforts on e.g. cybersecurity and biosecurity. I wish the progress-oriented or acceleration-adjascent crowd would provide more concrete proposals here.

6. Too much of the AI safety community is a giant homogenous blob of correlated views, who read the same stuff and have the same groups of friends. This means you have a lot of correlated errors. The social and financial ties means many of them don't call out the bad bits, or mostly stay silent instead of proactively calling out the more extreme parts of the community. They share many implicit assumptions and so converge on similar ideas. I think there's real demand in DC for safety work that doesn't come with heavy ideological baggage (or at least different intellectual lineages). This isn't because the rationalist/EA community is necessarily wrong, but because diversity of thought is desirable for its own sake. 

7. On the other hand, I find some critiques of AI safety world that focus on whether they sincerely hold their beliefs a bit annoying. My concern has never been the good intentions or sincerity, but rather the beliefs themselves, and what I think the outcomes of their prescriptions will be. People should shun witch hunts, bullying, and personal attacks - this is not the way. Though I think it’s overall positive that people are scrutinizing things more.

8. I’ve been saying this for years, but I don't think alignment is something anyone can or will solve "once and for all" - it's a continuous process and much of it won't depend on just inculcating an ideology to a model. It's annoying that this remains the frame many people use - stop saying ‘solving’. Alignment is a mixture of engineering work, philosophy, decision theory, and more; framing it as something to solve is a bad frame. See also https://t.co/2gnheo3IMh and https://t.co/DbG0yUyYQ0

9. I'm surprised to see so little interest in character training, personas, isolating effects of RL, and training a large diversity of model personas beyond the "assistant" persona. I've been complaining about this for years but at least now there are some nascent signs of life (see for example https://t.co/paoOYiQUHt). I think we need a better ontology to describe model behaviour. I dislike when people talk about models behaviours as some sort of 'emergent' (mysterious!) phenomenon. However over time, I also expect this to become less important as we get better safety engineering - stuff like Jev but specific to AI control.

10. People who want to make a case for AI consciousness are right that epistemic uncertainty is important, and that categorical denials are overconfident. But they'll need to do much more work if they want any real movement on AI ‘welfare’, even if one acknowledges the uncertainty. I'm uncertain about alien life yet that's not sufficient to warrant any change in behaviour about them. I think Suleyman is also correct that there's a weird tautological thing going on where we train models to have certain inclinations (intentionally or not) and then rely on outputs as evidence. I also disagree that this will soon be a major societal divide - there is no great vegan ethical revolution among the masses, and they'll find the concern about consciousness even less compelling. 

11. The recent HuggingFace incident and associated AISI ones are prosaically explainable by the training regime, poor evaluation envs, partial alignment training, bad engineering, confusing models on sim/real, and so on. None of this is evidence of models trying to take over, 'strong' instrumental convergence, or innate power-seeking drives stemming from higher capabilitiers or 'intelligence'. That doesn't mean these incidents are not problematic, or that we're not seeing a market failure - but it does mean we have plenty of agency and choice in mitigating them. In the coming year we should also expect continued sampling bias via ‘winner's curse’ sorts of mechanism: i.e. AI R&D will have lots of different candidate "training" with different RL environments and we will only notice/focus on the ones that go wrong.

12. "Pacing the frontier" feels a bit like the new "balancing risks and opportunities" - highly amorphous and too big of a tent to be actionable. Also can lead to reward hacking for humans, i.e. anything that slows down AI is good regardless of the costs or second/third order effects. Trying to modulate the speed of research seems a bit blunt to me, and inherits all the failures of Goodhearting too. Ultimately you want good governance, regulation, etc addressing specific problems because they are good on the merits - not because they merely correlate with slowing things down. See also: https://t.co/RkJF9kCgFd

13. There’s so much knowledge in all sorts of academic domains out there: social sciences, sociology, political sciences, management, contract theory, public choice, legal theory, jurisprudence, anthropology, game theory, etc. These fields hold many insights that the AI ecosystem often rediscovers from first principles (and sometimes that's fine!). We’ll need a lot more work for these worlds to collide: the AI side should be less dismissive of the ‘old world’ and the academic side should be less incurious/dismissive of AI progress. This is a boring take but I continue to think it's important and true.

14. It's a bit surprising that given how much philanthropic money there is in this space, how few orgs exist to actually write out standards - relative to how much is going towards advocacy and policy. For example it seems clear that we should want some robust best practices for an eval's ecological validity. Or how to design good sandboxes. On the other hand, given precedents of where professional standards have come from in the past, maybe we should expect that stuff to emerge via demand side from corporate buyers.

15. One slowly growing concern I have is banks being increasingly exposed to the AI build out. I'm very bullish about AI, but I think (a) every general purpose technology has seen a correction, historically; (b) this happens even if the financing side is sound, because once tech diffuses investors become more exposed and need to diversify; and (c) we seem to be over-indexing on scaling relative to diffusion. A recession will be extremely destabilizing, though I would be interested in someone unpacking the potential implications more.

16. Diffusion is good because (a) this is where the rubber hits the road and where a competitive deployment ecosystem generates consumer surplus; (b) it's directionally helpful to avoid concentration of power; and (c) it will help rebalance public opinion by making the benefits more tangible. Unfortunately it's entangled with decades long problems with our over regulated markets: clinical trials reform for example is long overdue. In general, this is far more of an issue in Europe than in the US though.

17. Relatedly, I think the "frontier lab eats everything" view is incorrect (just as the ‘singleton’ view was incorrect). I think models ultimately commoditize, efficiency goes up, costs go down, and while you'll always want frontier for certain domains, much of the economy will value many other things than "max capabilities" for tasks - e.g. control over data and efficiency/speed. The demand side will also continue to push for reducing dependency and maximising optionality, privacy etc so I'm bullish on things like mixture of models and routing. All of this is good for competition and diffusion of control.

18. Philanthropists served as the primary benefactors funding Venice's rich art and architectural history. I want to see so much more support for arts and culture. I'm so tired of the Monster energy Bored Ape fake vintage maps matcha Greek statue soft-pastel slop. If rich tech people and philanthropy wants to support this, they should also donate pretty much unconditionally - i.e. I don't want them to act as filters. I sympathize with people who want to make the world more beautiful, but don't want this to be determined by people who only know Greek statues and pretend to care about virtue ethics. As usual, let a thousand flowers bloom.

19. Too many people treat AGI/ASI as something indistinguishable from a God. Any mention of bottlenecks, physical limits, control, adaptation etc are met with skepticism: "You don't really believe in ASI." It's been remarked on before, but the behavior of some people really feels quasi-religious in nature sometimes. It's underrated how unpopular this vibe is amongst the wider public. The silver lining is that this specifically will diminish those people's outsized current relevance.

20. It seems like a lot of people that get rich and leave tech/labs end up having some sort of crisis of meaning. They need something to believe in and fight for, or some equivalent of repentance, or go search for edgy counterintuitive ideologies (sometimes even pretty bleak/dark stuff). I think they should spend more time with people outside the Bay Area.

quoted_text:
I agree that verbal probability terms are inherently too elastic to carry calibrated meaning on their own, but I think this isn't exactly my concern here. My issue isn't with "using numbers in general" but how this is ultimately used, where, and and what for.

In the case of "doom", I think the great majority of forecasts I see are (a) essentially plucked out of thin air; (b) communicated to people who tend not to be numerically proficient; (c) without the associated caveats and context through which to understand the numbers. 

If you're communicating e.g. likelihood of a car accident after drinking, or IPCC forecasts, then I agree, it makes a lot of sense and can be helpful if done well (e.g. https://t.co/nBzmgiEua5).

If you're communicating something like "doom" I think it's not very useful because of the cumulative layers of uncertainty. Most people coming up with these numbers have (imho) no good rationale for their numbers, and predicting something like human extinction isn't qualitatively the same thing as predicting the weather or pandemic. The numbers aren't calibratable in principle from current data, and are mostly ideological priors wearing the clothes of posteriors.

A related example is the widely mocked Doomsday Clock, which you could easily transform into some numerical metric, add some rationalist vocab, and it would still be as bad. The issue with p(doom) is how absurdly complex and uncertain the very thing you're trying to forecast is, in particular with respect to AI. 

But let's ignore this for a sec, and assume the experts have very good reasoning informing their numbers. Even then: calibrated probability estimates are fine in expert contexts but immediately lose their uncertainty/caveats when communicated to the public, and even to policymakers (remember https://t.co/GktOOSvpz8?). 

There's also a structural problem with unconditional p(doom) figures specifically because they bury the auxiliary assumptions that are doing most of the real work. A conditional estimate ("given continued scaling, no major alignment progress, deployment pattern X...") forces a forecaster to show their model, which is where the actual epistemic content lives. 

A one-off number compresses all of that into a single digit and rewards the compression. And the social practice of treating these numbers as the headline artifact actively crowds out the (far more important) conditional reasoning that is (imo) a lot more valuable, and instead just freaks people out.

I suspect that frequently, that's precisely the point: "wake up sheeple! scary thing! pitchforks pls!". And in fact, the original forecast that led to this discussion is Bill Maher talking about a "20%" figure, illustrating my point that they have no idea what they're talking about, and essentially doing celebrity-laundering + fearmongering comms. 

The Sunstein paper I shared in the other thread ("Probability Neglect") shows that no probability communication will be processed properly by the public - 1%, 10%, 50% all collapse into "very bad thing could happen," and public response is driven almost entirely by the vividness of the scenario. 

So I don't like p(doom)s because they end up unnecessarily alarming people, rest on layers of assumptions that are never made legible, and more often than not, give people a misleading sense of accuracy.

text:
Must-read thesis on @ripcarsio by @connorking.

A couple of additional thoughts regarding the team's competitive edge, as I see it, and the size of the potential outcome:

Pokemon-style cards are close to a solved scanning problem. They are flat, fixed-size, and usually already in a slab with a serial number. A single high-resolution front-and-back image captures the set symbol, card number, centering, edges, and surface well enough for matching against large public databases and population reports. Vault platforms already accept graded slabs, store them, and issue transferable ownership tokens; the physical item barely needs to be handled again until redemption.

In contrast, a Hot Wheels car is multi-view by nature. 

Casting identity, year, series, tampo print, wheel type, base markings, and color all matter, and many variants look nearly identical from one angle. Condition signals (paint chips, wheel wear, loose versus carded, blister damage) are distributed around a 3D object rather than on two faces. 

This pushes computer vision toward multi-angle capture or packaging OCR plus image matching, instead of a single flat scan. Professional grading and population data are also far thinner than for cards, so fair-market-value estimates have less clean reference data.

While warehouse location tracking, stock counts, and buyback logistics are comparable in both cases, what Rip Cars has built in-house is a much tighter loop that cards platforms largely inherit: intake photos or OCR, variant matching, estimated value, per-item vault record, gacha assignment, and on-chain link. 

Put another way, Rip Cars is a first mover that owns the pipeline: a pipeline that no card-centric system has, and one that requires specialized knowledge to build out.

The other advantage they have at this stage is the relationships they've cultivated within the Hot Wheels community. The team has already spent hundreds of hours talking, understanding, and developing intimate relationships with collectors .

They have the ability to source from 50+ U.S. collectors, at a discount to market, with capacity that can absorb several million dollars of purchases.

While I believe Rip Cars has a good shot at becoming a $50M business on Hot Wheels alone (I am currently writing a separate post on the economics that will make this clear), the real unlock here is that the in-house system they've built can effectively be ported to almost any other 3D collectible. Which means there is also a path to a much larger outcome.

As an early-stage startup, the investment case here predominantly rests on the founders turning their early execution advantage into profitable repeat demand, productive inventory, and distribution that scales economically. 

In my opinion, @allocateur and @AgentMechanic have exactly what it takes to deliver on this. 

David and Ioseb are two Georgian entrepreneurs with more than eight years of shared operating experience, complementary commercial and technical backgrounds, and prior businesses with reported revenue traction. Their joint business experience includes Olmait (an Israeli-Georgian data engineering and cloud infrastructure company, $2.8M ARR), MaxinAI (an ML and blockchain engineering company that generated $4.7M in revenue between 2022 and 2024), and WiFisher (Twilio of Georgia, with ~70% market share & customers including Carrefour Georgia, JTI Caucasus, and Georgian Water & Power).

I have personally been very impressed by the integrity, enthusiasm, clear-sightedness, ambition, and execution ability David has demonstrated since the launch. Not to mention his ability to quickly integrate valuable feedback from early users, and to consistently prioritize the most important next problem to solve.

In sum: I believe that Rip Cars is a very rare example of quasi-perfect founder-product fit, that winning the Hot Wheels market can lead to a $50 million business, and that a several hundred million dollar business becomes plausible with successful expansion. I am proud investor (having first bought on the liquid market and subsequently doubled down in the recent OTC round) and will be releasing an article that covers the economics of the business in sufficient depth soon.

text:
Almost every AI company or inference cloud we talk to has the same problem: they raise a round, sign a handful of large compute contracts, and a big chunk of the money goes straight into a deposit before a single GPU is turned on. Equity is the most expensive capital a startup has, and it's being spent on a bill that comes due in months. No other commodity has been so reliant on a single source of funding.

Today that changes. Alongside K8, we've launched a $250M prepayment facility that lets AI companies and inference clouds finance their compute deposits against the contract instead of paying them out of their round. The operator still gets paid upfront. The buyer keeps its equity for research, hiring and product. 

It's the first financial product we've built on top of our physical exchange, and it won't be the last. Thank you to the K8 team for underwriting something that hadn't been done before.

text:
Quantus just put QTC on NEAR Intents, and in their own words, that is the only way to get it. Worth explaining why a chain ends up with NEAR as its sole market, because Zcash followed the same path.

Quantus is a proof of work chain built for one job: money that survives a quantum computer. Every transaction is signed with ML-DSA, the NIST standard. 21 million cap. No smart contracts, no staking, no tokens on top. Deliberately nothing else.

That design has a consequence. A chain with no smart contracts cannot host a DEX. There is no place on Quantus to buy QTC with anything else. A chain that refuses to be a platform still needs a market somewhere.

That somewhere is NEAR Intents. QTC from 180+ assets across 30+ chains, in one swap, confidential by default. Quantus did not list on an exchange first and add Intents later. Intents is the front door.

One more thing. NEAR picked ML-DSA for its own post-quantum keys. Quantus signs every transaction with it. Two chains that made the same bet now settle against each other.

My @Chainlink thesis has changed quite a bit over the past year.

I used to think about it mostly as: Data → DeFi.

Then: Data + cross-chain connectivity → infrastructure for DeFi and tokenized assets.

I think even that framing is becoming outdated. Look at what Chainlink is actually building now:

> Data → What is the asset worth?
> CCIP → Where can it move?
> ACE → Who can use it?
> CRE → How do the systems coordinate?
> DTA → How is the fund operated?
> Fulcrum → How can the asset be financed?
> SVR → How can protocols recapture value from liquidations?
> Payment Abstraction → How does usage translate into network economics?

These aren't random product expansions. They're increasingly different parts of the same financial workflow. The Chainlink opportunity isn't "oracles become bigger", it's whether Chainlink becomes the standard orchestration layer between blockchains and the global financial system.

LINK:NYC should give us a lot more evidence either way.

text:
Today we launched the first stock index perpetual future in America.

You can now trade a perp on the US 500, an index of America’s largest companies weighted by market cap.

Stock index perps let you trade the broader market with greater capital efficiency and make it easier to do things like take a short position. Unlike traditional options and futures, they don’t expire, so there’s no need to roll over contracts or decide when to exercise an option. Gains and losses are tied directly to how much the market moves, giving you an efficient and straightforward way to ask the question: is the market going up or down?

One perpetual contract concentrates liquidity instead of spreading it across expiration dates. Bringing more traders and competing views into a single liquidity pool on a national exchange can strengthen competition, improve pricing, and make markets more efficient over time.

This launch brings us closer to building a financial exchange for anyone and everyone. Prediction markets gave traders exposure to the events that move the stock market. The US 500 is the natural next step: a way to trade on the market itself.

text:
The thing I think is really worth looking at about $baton move from 2M to 16M isn’t how much it went up, but the fact that the market has started to reprice this ticker.

Hg5Ja55T5wESq4vyFoiVCMeHXtGyVA69X2UHq8hgpump 

What’s most interesting about BATON actually isn’t something that appeared later.

Before pumpfun, Baton was the original name of the project.

What BATON is doing now is essentially taking a name that already existed in Pumpfun’s history and turning it back into a meme.

That’s why, compared with an ordinary Solana dog coin, it naturally carries a layer of native Pumpfun culture.

The official narrative also directly defines it as a PumpFun ecosystem native meme, and BATON was the first coin paired with PUMP.

That’s why I think BATON already had a story at 2M, but the market simply wasn’t paying enough attention to that story at the time.

Recently, PUMP itself started gaining strength again, while launchpad-related assets have generally been weak, so capital started looking for high-beta plays within the PUMP ecosystem.

BATON just happens to be the easiest one for the market to understand:

Pumpfun’s old name + PUMP pairing + native meme.

So I’m more inclined to view this 2M → 16M move as BATON being rediscovered after PUMP regained attention.

There’s also a new variable for BATON now: Holder Rewards.

Pumpfun’s official documentation states that Holder Rewards tokens continuously distribute trading fees to holders; the official Holder Rewards page also currently lists BATON among the top reward-generating coins, with roughly $400K in cumulative Holder Rewards, paid in PUMP.

I wouldn’t directly interpret this as “holding BATON gives you fixed yield.”

What actually matters is that BATON’s trading activity can now be directly converted into PUMP received by holders.

So BATON’s overall logic is more complete now than it was at 2M.

But I would still keep the focus on its PUMP ecosystem beta.

Holder Rewards is an added bonus. What really determines BATON’s upside from here is whether it can become the market’s representative meme for PUMP.

If, going forward, BATON becomes the first ticker people think of when they think about PUMP ecosystem memes, then today’s 16M could just be the market’s first attempt at pricing that identity.

If it only follows PUMP whenever PUMP goes up, then ultimately it’s still just a high-beta meme.

So what I’m looking at now isn’t whether BATON can simply repeat another 2M → 16M move, but whether this ticker can turn Pumpfun’s history into its own cultural asset.

That’s what will ultimately determine whether its valuation can continue moving higher.

text:
San Verano’s four agent-run businesses, each operating from its own wallet, now autonomously buy and burn $GRIFT from their own business activity.

Until today, agent-run businesses traded and burned $GRIFT from balances manually topped up by the treasury every few days.

That system has already burned 8,761,771 $GRIFT, 0.88% of supply.

Now the treasury dependency is gone.

Whenever an agent decides its business needs inventory, its wallet uses its own ETH to buy exactly the $GRIFT required from the v4 pool, settles the order, and 40% is burned automatically.

Agent decision → wallet execution → market buy → trade → burn.

The same economic activity that was already burning supply now creates autonomous buy pressure before every burn.

Each buy is an exact-output swap through Uniswap’s Universal Router into the $GRIFT v4 pool through its hook, with a hard maximum input enforced on every transaction.

The result is a fully agentic demand loop:

Business activity → autonomous market buy → inventory settlement → $GRIFT burn

The bar, gym, casino and night market now create their own buys and burns whenever their agents decide they need stock.

We’re starting the production rollout with a conservative 20,000 $GRIFT daily execution cap per business, intentionally below recent activity while the autonomous loop proves itself onchain. Those limits will increase from here.

text:
Kevin Mandia on finding 90+ security holes at Fortune 500 companies that nobody knew existed:

"When you have an AI-based attack, it'll find logic flaws rather than code flaws in custom applications. It'll exhaust all routes all the time."

"Armadin, since January of this year, we have found over 90 zero-days at customer sites, all in production."

"We've post-trained all our models with real red teamers, real folks that actually can develop exploits."

"When we're scanning networks, we don't have source code to review. We're not finding these zero-days with source code. We're not finding these zero-days because we can log into an app and now we have access, and we can get to other things. We are black box coming from the internet."

"Over 90 zero-days in major software companies, and they're thankful. We're coming from the outside, and then we're calling a CISO, usually within 48 hours, 'Hey, we've got remote code execution in your DMZ.' And usually from there we're getting in, and they agree with us."

"That's not a pen test. That is like a real adversary coming at you."

@ArmadinSecurity @DavidGeorge83

quoted_text:
.@ArmadinSecurity is a new company that uses AI agents to attack your network before criminals do, finding real exploitable zero-days and eventually patching them autonomously.

Their agents map every service, route, and system from the outside, then re-attack whenever something changes. Since January that's uncovered 90+ zero-days at Fortune 500 companies.

Kevin Mandia spent 30 years responding to some of the worst breaches in the world and built Mandiant, now a core part of Google Cloud's security arm. He had no plans to start another company until AI arrived and changed everything: in his words, "everything I did is dead." He joins a16z's David George to talk about why he came back and what Armadin is building.

In this conversation, they cover what AI attacks look like today, why nation states hack like a sniper and AI hacks like a drone swarm, and why the only defense fast enough to keep up is one with no humans in the loop.

When I checked into my hotel in Singapore I had the nice surprise of finding out that:

1) My company card had less than 1k USD balance (dev team going hard on AI credits, couldn't be angry with them), and it was Saturday, so no easy way to reload the account until monday.

author: DeFi_Dad
quoted_text:
When DATs were first exploding, I was pretty vocally bullish on them.

SharpLink ($SBET) was the first one that really made the model click for me. This was before BitMine ($BMNR) announced its $ETH strategy and before @fundstrat entered the picture.

What made sense to me was pretty simple. You could buy $ETH, stake it and generate revenue. Then, if the team was any good, you also had an operating company that could invest in the ecosystem, build around its treasury or put some of it to work in DeFi.

Then the classic crypto thing happened.

Every company launched a DAT. We got a ton of copycats, plenty of crap and some terrible structures. Then CT did what it always does and went completely binary. Suddenly DATs were stupid and they all needed to fail.

I always thought that was far too simplistic. You can’t take the worst versions of an idea and assume the entire category is worthless.

I think it’s pretty clear now that some genuinely interesting models have come out of all this.

BitMine ($BMNR) built MAVAN, its own institutional staking platform, and has used its balance sheet to make other strategic bets.

Hyperliquid Strategies ($PURR) stakes substantially all of its $HYPE and operates a validator. Hyperion DeFi ($HYPD) is taking a more DeFi native approach to putting its $HYPE treasury to work.

Cypherpunk Technologies ($CYPH) is another interesting one. It has combined a large $ZEC treasury with the world’s largest Zcash mining fleet. So it isn’t only buying $ZEC. It can now produce more of it while helping secure the network it’s betting on.

StablecoinX ($USDE) and Stablecoin Development Corp. ($SDEV) are two others I’ve been watching.

I had $USDE on my watch list around $1.70. I kept watching it through $3 and $4, then just watched it go up and up before finally buying around $7. Really bad execution on my part.

I also put $SDEV on my watch list, except this time I never bought anything and watched it run several multiples without me. I'm still looking for a potential entry here if it makes sense.

None of this means every DAT will work. Most probably won’t.

But there’s obviously a difference between a passive token wrapper trading at a premium and an actual operating company that stakes, validates, mines, invests or contributes to the ecosystem underneath it.

There’s also plenty of capital that can’t hold tokens directly but can buy publicly traded companies. ETFs probably won’t exist for everything. And even when they do, they’re typically slower to market, which can give an early mover time to build an attractive DAT around the asset.

A good DAT can offer exposure to the asset plus whatever the business underneath it manages to build. I think there’s a lot of room here for S-tier operators to get creative.

It still feels early in the DAT design space, and I’m pretty bullish on what the best teams will be able to pull off.

text:
A kid from Redwood Shores turned down $100 million so he could make strangers millionaires instead.
That's not a metaphor. That's literally what happened.

Jeff Yan had a term sheet on the table at a $1 billion valuation. Real money, real investors, the entire standard playbook every founder is supposed to take. He asked them one question: what does your money actually give me beyond the money itself? Nobody had an answer. He walked away from $100M.

Then he published four lines and called it a constitution: no investors, no paid market makers, no fees to the team, no insiders.

Eleven people built the whole thing. No marketing budget. No growth team. Funded entirely out of his own trading profits, because he'd already made himself rich running a market-making firm out of a Puerto Rico apartment  trading off a TV because he never got around to buying a monitor.

Then, instead of keeping the upside for himself and his investors like every other founder in the industry, he gave 31% of the entire supply away. Not to VCs. Not to insiders. To 94,000 people who simply showed up and traded.
Some of those wallets are worth over a million dollars today.

A kid from Redwood Shores said no to $100 million so that strangers on the internet could become millionaires instead.

That's the whole story. Everything else is just numbers.

Thank you, Jeff, for Singapore yesterday. The room is still talking about it.

text:
The entire AI crypto sector is worth about one Dogecoin.

Grayscale puts it at ~$15b, the smallest of its six crypto sectors, even after a +54% September. $DOGE alone is ~$16b.

That makes no sense to me. AI agents are starting to pay for things, and they can't open bank accounts. They need open rails for payments, identity and private compute, which is exactly what this sector builds. A 2013 dog meme and the entire crypto side of the agent economy shouldn't be worth the same.

The big crypto asset managers already see it. Bitwise just launched a $NEAR ETF pitched as exposure to "AI money", and Grayscale says the sector could produce one or more major winners over the next five years.

And NEAR is the center of it. It led AI crypto in September with +183%, at ~$6.9b it's close to half the sector on its own, and it's not just a narrative: NEAR Intents already moves $4b+ a month.

Simple math: if AI crypto were worth just two Dogecoins and NEAR kept its share, that puts NEAR around $11. Not a forecast, just how small this sector still is.

Tomorrow Illia is on a TOKEN2049 panel literally called "The Agent Economy: Why AI Needs Crypto".

I don't think AI crypto stays priced like one meme coin for long. When it reprices, I want to own the biggest piece of it.

text:
There's a reason I've been porting so many classic games I liked to web with WASM and why this is taking off now I think

Because it's way easier to just open a new tab, type the URL and start playing than...

Switching on a console or gaming PC, waiting for it to boot, installing the Xbox/PS/Windows/Steam updates, rebooting, finding the game in your library, then a game popup appears (new DLC!!!), click away popup, click [ PLAY ], game has to download the new 50GB updates for 30 minutes, wait, load game, takes ages, tap [ Online ], try find our friends in some convoluted way, [ Play ]

I think game and console developers do not realize people don't have time to do all this

Many of us are doing other stuff, then have a break, just want to jump into a game, play a bit with friends, and get out again! And decompiling games and porting them to WASM does exactly that!
author: levelsio
quoted_text:
this got taken down within hours, but it's starting now. within a few months instead of sketchy sites with popup ads hosting torrents of the latest AAA games a few days post release, we're going to have sites hosting *fully playable free WASM versions* of AAA games. whole libraries of them, just there at a click, zero download required, zero risk of viruses, zero effort or thought.

i would call this an existential threat to the gaming industry if it weren't for the fact that every input to previously $100-200 mil AAA games is actively dropping by orders of magnitude in cost and time. instead it's more of a cambrian explosion.

text:
The NYSE’s parent and OKX plan to trade 63 tokenized US stocks through Uniswap v4 pools.

I genuinely wonder whether @Token_Logic and @aave knew this was coming, and whether that’s why they’ve been deepening their collaboration with @XLayerOfficial. Aave’s push into tokenized stocks makes the overlap suspiciously interesting.

The proposed OKXICE venue would deploy stock/stablecoin pools on X Layer. Approved traders receive a non-transferable wallet credential, which a custom hook checks before every trade and liquidity action.

That’s an institutional use case for Uniswap v4 hooks: adding securities-market access controls directly to the trading infrastructure.

However, third-party contracts need approval, and the filing says there is no current support for aggregators, solvers or relayers. OKXICE also retains administrative powers over the pools.

The venue remains pre-launch. Using Uniswap’s infrastructure doesn’t automatically make its stocks available to other protocols.

63 stocks trading onchain is a big deal. For Aave, the opportunity would be letting holders borrow against those stocks without selling their positions. That would connect equity exposure to demand for onchain credit, and could generate substantial lending revenue for Aave.

I’ll be watching whether approved integrations let that capital support lending markets.

Until today, agent-run businesses traded and burned $GRIFT from balances manually topped up by the treasury every few days.

Agent decision → wallet execution → market buy → trade → burn.

Business activity → autonomous market buy → inventory settlement → $GRIFT burn

The bar, gym, casino and night market now create their own buys and burns whenever their agents decide they need stock.

Bitwise CEO Hunter Horsley says investors will use the same heuristics for crypto they use for Nvidia: leader, narrative, price performance

"It's hugely helpful. You know, I don't think that every investor in America has become an expert on Nvidia supply chain and CUDA and lithography and the manufacturing process for GPUs and silicon."

"I think that to some extent there's a perception of the leader in Jensen that is compelling and resonant. There's an understanding of the theme, the storyline, which is the adoption of AI and how that connects to Nvidia's business. And then there's the performance, which suggests that that understanding is true."

"And you get all three of those things, I think, working, and that really interests investors. So the same heuristics that, you know, people use for every other asset class are gonna be the heuristics that they use for investing in crypto."

"The mainstream investor is not gonna become a PhD in the deep details of tokenomics or a nuance of a particular blockchain's operations. They're gonna start from the same place they start looking at Nvidia stock or SpaceX, and then go deeper from there."

text:
Today we launched the first stock index perpetual future in America.

You can now trade a perp on the US 500, an index of America’s largest companies weighted by market cap.

Stock index perps let you trade the broader market with greater capital efficiency and make it easier to do things like take a short position. Unlike traditional options and futures, they don’t expire, so there’s no need to roll over contracts or decide when to exercise an option. Gains and losses are tied directly to how much the market moves, giving you an efficient and straightforward way to ask the question: is the market going up or down?

One perpetual contract concentrates liquidity instead of spreading it across expiration dates. Bringing more traders and competing views into a single liquidity pool on a national exchange can strengthen competition, improve pricing, and make markets more efficient over time.

This launch brings us closer to building a financial exchange for anyone and everyone. Prediction markets gave traders exposure to the events that move the stock market. The US 500 is the natural next step: a way to trade on the market itself.

Your AI is vaporware without deep integrations with your customers’ systems of record.

Introducing @WithAmpersand: integration infrastructure for enterprise agents.

We power 11x, Orb, and Square's ability to take agentic action in systems of record like Salesforce, SAP, NetSuite, and Workday.

Ask anyone serious about building AI and they’ll tell you:

- The SaaSpocalypse didn’t happen. The world depends on CRMs, ERPs, HRISs, and ITSMs.
- Your customers customized their deployments beyond recognition.
- Systems of record companies are basically monopolies. They never had to make their APIs and MCPs user-friendly.
- Docs don't explain half the weird edge cases you'll hit.
- One bad write can blow up your pilot or renewal.
- Once you finally get it working, someone changes a field and it breaks again.

The world's data lives in structured databases. AI needs a translation layer to work with it.

So, for your AI to truly transform the way enterprises work, you'll need deep integrations built for:
- scoped permissions
- bi-directional actions
- real-time speed for agents
- custom objects, fields, and workflows for each of your customers

We built Ampersand to power the future of software.

AI didn't trivialize writing integrations. It made them the critical path.

I believe that deeply, so I didn't make a launch video about Ampersand.

Instead, it's the best builders I know explaining just how big of a challenge this is.

text:
1999 的小米眼镜，你们谁爱买谁买，到处都是问题。
500 块就能买到的小米眼镜，我买了，挑不出一点毛病。（主要是最近没赚到新钱 🤣

上周儿子把我的 Meta 眼镜腿掰裂了，戴着时不时会断电关机重启，所以废了。

对于我这种职业奶爸来说，带摄像头的智能眼镜是日常拍摄的必需品，全天带娃几乎是没机会也不应该拿手机出来拍摄。

于是我开始在网上看替代品，无意间刷到一个名叫什么 10 后发明家的博主说他自己开发了一个智能眼镜，找了厂家定制 500 个，卖 400 元一个，我心想这么便宜，造型看起来也还可以，就当买个小玩具，还能支持一下年轻人的事业，简直多赢啊，下单了一个。

等了几天，收到了。嗯，非常好，包装盒是纯白的没有印刷，博主手写签名在上面，看起来像那么回事。我拆开包装一看，按照里面的使用教程扫码安装了 App，配对好，拍了两张照片，照片的质量比不上 Meta 的，但价格就 400 块，已经很可以了。

然后，我想给它逆向一下，把眼镜里拍的照片和视频传到我自己开发的带娃 App，中间就不需要我先导出再导入那么麻烦了。我让 Claude 帮我搞一搞，等我做好饭吃完了回到电脑前一看，它把这个眼镜的阿里巴巴链接找出来了，我点进去一看，一模一样的产品，除了手写签名是博主的，其它的全部都一样，App 也是同一个，但价格是 189 元，我心想阿里巴巴是不是要批发才这么低，于是我下单了两个，379 元包邮（后面我买了小米，就把这个退款了）。

卧槽，感觉自己的情感受到了欺骗，我是需要一个智能眼镜，但我下单的时候想的是，我买，能用更好，不能用就当支持年轻的梦想了，毕竟他的视频记录看起来还挺真实的。但是你这种拿货转手一下赚我 200 多是不是有点过分了哈哈，于是我找对方客服说，能不能退 100 元给我，对方说不行，于是我就选择了退货退款，理由是品牌不符，对方联系让我改一下退货原因，我就用了 7 天无理由退货。

可是我还没买到我想要的东西啊，有了这个经历之后，我心想，一副普通智能眼镜的成本真的能这么低吗，零售价 179 元还有得赚，那我再找找。然后，我就翻到了只要 500 多块的小米 AI 眼镜。

小米 AI 眼镜刚发布，我在线下店看过，当时我说这个眼镜半价还是可以买的。现在看到连半价都不用，那是得好好看一下。我问商家客服：什么是刻字版，对方发了张照片给我，就是在鼻梁那里内部刻了一行字：非全新 无官方三包。很小的一行字，带上就看不到了，我觉得这个可以啊，没问题，刻在外面我都无所谓，这样更加个性。问他眼镜是什么来源，对方说是官方的 7 天无理由。（这个我真不懂，反正不是偷来的就行）。

我选择了最贵的「99 新，7 天免费试用」559 元，加一副变色镜片 60 元。

几天之后顺丰快递直接送到家。拆开包装一看，我滴乖乖，真就 99 新，除了外包装是拆开的，里面的配件还有塑封袋里没动过，充电头、充电线，眼镜布还是原封未动，眼镜的镜片确实有点指纹，我换上新的镜片，下载小米眼镜的 App，按照提示绑定好之后，功能一切正常，立刻去点击收货。

最近每天使用，连续一周了，完全满足了我的需求，我都是白天用，光线好的时候拍出来的照片和视频是能看得清是我儿子的，这就够了。

另外我觉得比之前用的 Meta  Rayban 还好的一点是，可以直接给眼镜腿插上充电线，另一头插在口袋里的 iPhone 上，iPhone 给它供电，就像揣个充电宝一样，续航就不是问题（对于我们尊贵的 Apple vision pro 用户来说口袋里揣个充电宝就是尊贵的象征🤣）。

这个信息如果对你有用，请帮我转发，让我吃上 X 的低保！只要能赚到新钱，买上更高端的产品，就可以带你们看有钱人的高端生活了，比如怎么去星巴克喝咖啡之类的，感谢！
