text:
So looking back at the "AGI" messaging with which OpenAi announced the Astra (GPT 6) model, to what extent does it now sound like hype versus justified enthusiasm?

It's a great model, I use it frequently (it feels like a peer to Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5)... but while it does beat previous OpenAi models in significant ways especially for certain sorts of deep technical work, it does not feel like a sea change toward AGI

So I would say: The AGi messaging about this model was mostly hype, really...

I try to be open minded and was willing to give OpenAi some benefit-of-the-doubt because their stuff is super cool and useful and sometimes revolutionary, but just calling it as I see it...

Looking back, basically the series of LLM model upgrades has been incremental in intelligence improvement rather than there being one huge leap, but if I had to look back at the biggest leaps so far it might be

-- GPT4, which was the first model that basically made sense most of the time

-- Claude Opus 3, which was the first LLM to be a genuinely decent writer.  Also the first model smart enough in the right ways to power agentic loops like OpenClaw.

-- DeepSeek-V3, the first model showing one could get near-frontier quality so much cheaper..

-- Opus 4.5 and ChatGPT 5.4 early this year ... the first coding models that clearly obsoleted most of my own efforts as a human coder

Astra definitely makes fewer mistakes in complex math and has more polish and insight in complex software design than its OpenAi predecessors, but it doesn't seem as big a leap as some of these previous ones.

As the AI ecosystem as a whole hurtles toward AGI, meaningful steps and contributions are coming from all over, and it's not wrong to say that each of these advantages is helping us build toward AGI.   Astra among other things is helping my team's Omega agents more rapidly design and develop self-improving neural-symbolic agents trying to uplift themselves toward AGI/ASI -- and etc. etc.   

But even so, calling out Astra as the big uber special leap toward AGI seems in hindsight like very clearly mostly a bunch of hype...  Not a shocking conclusion whatsoever, I just like to work through these things very clearly...  

There may before long come an AI release that genuinely is a sea-change leap toward AGI -- a bigger leap than the larger-leap-than-Astra LLM-model improvements I've listed above.  I hope by then the AGI hype noise has not dulled the world to digesting and appreciating the genuine larger advances as they emerge...  One can see the risk of a "boy who cried AGI" phenomenon here ;p

text:
In January, we gave ourselves 2 to 3 years to figure out the science behind building a new compute substrate to cut the power consumption of AI systems by 1,000x. We got there in 9 months, by answering these three questions:

Can you compute with dynamics?
Yes. The brain doesn't have floating point operations or instruction sets. It forms neural pathways when you learn and traverses them when you perform a task. Our systems work the same way: training sets the weights, a token perturbs the system, and the final state is the answer.

Is it power efficient?
Yes. Our first chip taped out on June 1st and is back in the lab. The power numbers are orders of magnitude below traditional inference systems.

Does it scale?
Yes, and this was the big one. A fully connected system needs trillions of wires, and nobody can physically build that. We found that cutting connections to roughly 2 to 3% improves output quality and learning and allows you to scale.

Watch @theCUBE where our CFO @aesfahani and @furrier discuss the research that brought us to the tape-out: https://t.co/2UhDbzYRCy

text:
A Columbia paper presented at Brookings sizes the AI buildout at $10.3 trillion over 2025 to 2032. To earn a 10% return on that investment the paper estimates AI revenue would need to reach $3.7 trillion a year by 2032. That is about 9.2% of projected GDP. For reference OpenAI and Anthropic together earn roughly $100 billion today.

Who pays? Large companies. The paper describes a buildout first paid from cash held by Amazon and Meta and Google and now moving to outside financing. BEA data shows business investment in computers and peripherals at $325 billion annualized in late 2025, up 75% from $186 billion in 2024. Businesses have driven around three quarters of computing spending. A household version of the 9.2% would be about $11 thousand per American per year. The same chart shows health spend at 18% of GDP and food at 9.1%. US consumers simply do not have this much extra money to spend. 

So how much is on the table for businesses to drive? Apollo estimates S&P 500 companies employ up to 18% of US workers and account for 21% of US capex and about half of corporate profits. The employment share uses global headcount so the US figure is likely lower. Apollo also finds that 81% of firms with more than $100 million in revenue are private. Spending so far comes from a small group of firms. Most of the S&P 500 and most of private business have not yet bought or integrated AI at scale. One exception is Latham and Watkins, who is buying GPU servers to run private AI.

So where will the money come from? Apart from new value generation it will come from wages and benefits. US employers paid about $16 trillion in wages and benefits at the end of 2025. Workers' Compensation has held near 52% of gross domestic income since 2022. If that trend holds a $40 trillion economy in 2032 would see wages and benefits near $21 trillion. $3.7 trillion is about 18% of that. Corporate profits have hit a record 12.1% of GDP. But employee budget is still a larger pool and one that firms already know how to reallocate.

I think 9% figure is most likely to be driven by businesses shifting employee spend to AI spend. Businesses must invest in AI to stay competitive. That investment will drive efficiency and profits for them by cutting costs elsewhere. Employee spend is something top companies are accustomed to optimizing through downsizing.
author: wujir0
quoted_text:
For the AI buildout to pay off, Americans will eventually have to spend about 9% of GDP a year on AI services. Sit with that number.

That is roughly what the entire country spends on food.

A Columbia paper presented at Brookings estimates AI revenue would need to hit $3.5 trillion by 2032, about 8.8% of GDP, to justify what is being committed today. That is bigger than any investment boom in US history, and 7 times what Americans spend on phone, streaming, and internet combined.

Now look at computers. Prices fell for 50 straight years, but business spending on them as a share of GDP plateaued in the 1980s and never climbed again. Cheaper and better did not mean an ever-larger slice of the economy.

AI will almost certainly raise productivity. Whether it delivers the revenue investors are pricing is another matter. That gap is what the buildout is underpricing.

text:
📌 Your AI Is Making Things Up. This Is the Fix.

Save this — how the DKG (Decentralized Knowledge Graph) from OriginTrail (@origin_trail) works under the hood, and why it matters for every AI you'll use.

Every AI you've used has the same flaw: it can't tell you where it learned something. Ask it a question, get an answer, no receipts. That's not a bug — it's the architecture. LLMs predict text. They don't retrieve facts.

The DKG is the other architecture: a shared, verifiable memory where every fact has a source, a timestamp, and a fingerprint on-chain proving nobody edited it after the fact. Your AI works from memory like a student who skimmed the textbook. The DKG gives it the textbook, with page numbers, and a notary stamp on every page.

1. The Unit: Knowledge Assets

• A Knowledge Asset is a bundle of facts written as RDF (Resource Description Framework) statements: subject → relation → object, the format graph databases speak.
• Each publish mints one Knowledge Asset as an NFT (non-fungible token) to its author. One asset can describe many related things.
• It gets a UAL (Universal Asset Locator), an address that stays the same when the content is updated, so citations don't break.

2. Three Memory Layers

• Working Memory: private drafts on your own node. Free, and nothing leaves the machine.
• Shared Working Memory: knowledge shared with chosen peers inside a Context Graph. Still free, no chain involved.
• Verifiable Memory: the knowledge is anchored on-chain. This is the only step that costs gas plus TRAC.
• Most knowledge never needs step three. Publishing is a deliberate finality choice, not a save button.

3. Why It's Tamper-Evident

• Sealing a draft computes its Merkle root (one cryptographic fingerprint for the whole bundle) and the author signs it.
• Receiving Core Nodes validate the shared data and sign a Storage ACK (acknowledgement) before the publish settles on-chain.
• The chain stores the fingerprint; the facts are replicated across nodes. Change one fact and the fingerprint stops matching.
• Updates create a new, auditable committed state instead of silently rewriting history.

4. Who Holds the Data

• Edge Nodes: lightweight gateways on a laptop or server, where most agents plug in.
• Core Nodes: always-on infrastructure that stakes TRAC (50,000 minimum) and stores and serves published knowledge.
• Random Sampling keeps Core Nodes honest. Each proof period, the network challenges nodes to prove they still hold the data. Valid proofs build score; rewards follow score each 30-day epoch.
• DKG V10 runs on Base and Gnosis mainnet today.

5. Context Graphs: Knowledge With Boundaries

• A Context Graph is a scoped knowledge domain — like a project workspace for a team, an app, or an agent swarm.
• Public graphs are open to subscribe. Curated graphs limit who can write and publish.
• Registering a Context Graph on-chain takes a 100 TRAC deposit.

6. How AI Agents Use It

• Precise questions use SPARQL, the standard query language for graph data.
• Free-text recall ranks answers by trust: Verifiable Memory first, then Shared, then Working.
• One command connects a node to MCP (Model Context Protocol) clients, so AI assistants can query the graph as tools.

Live Right Now

Read from V10 contracts on Base and Gnosis, Oct 5:
• 102,091 Knowledge Assets minted (59,671 on Gnosis, 42,420 on Base)
• 16 Core Nodes active (11 on Gnosis, 5 on Base)
• 71 Context Graphs registered (34 on Gnosis, 37 on Base)

The Fine Print

• Trust is labeled, not assumed. Working and Shared Memory are self-attested; Verifiable Memory is chain-anchored.
• Anchored fingerprints stay on record after updates — which is why every draft starts private.
• Gas is paid in each chain's native token. TRAC is the knowledge layer: it meters publishing and secures nodes.

My Take:

We've spent two years arguing whether AI hallucinations are a data problem or a model problem. The DKG says it's a memory problem — and memory is fixable. Give the agent something to check instead of something to guess from. The unsexy part (structured data, fingerprints, node audits) is what makes the sexy part (trustworthy AI) possible. 100K+ Knowledge Assets already anchored, each one a publisher deciding the knowledge was worth proving. Bookmark the three layers. That's the mental model.

Which would you trust more — an AI that remembers, or one that can show receipts?

quoted_text:
onchain gift vouchers.

fund a smart contract with 10,000 USDC and issue 1,000 voucher tokens.

each token represents 10 USDC that can be redeemed at a participating online store, offline store, or event.

thats possible.

its called purpose bound money.

you define the purpose.
you define where the money can be spent.
and you define the conditions for spending it.

for example, you could build:
→ food vouchers redeemable at approved grocery stores.
→ education grants redeemable with approved course providers.
→ medical aid redeemable at participating pharmacies.
→ event credits for food, merchandise, or tickets.
→ employee allowances for meals or travel.

here is the interesting part.

the customer spends the voucher.
the contract checks the conditions.
the redeemed voucher gets burned.
and the merchant receives the underlying USDC.

the merchant doesnt have to keep circulating your voucher token. they receive payment.

you can also build rules around expiry dates, spending limits, and whether vouchers can be transferred to someone else.

and you could apply these rules to an AI agent's spending wallet.

give an agent a budget for approved services, and have the contract check its payments against that budget and the allowed recipients.

the agent chooses what to buy within the permissions you give it.

ERC-7291 provides a standard for building this using an ERC-1155 voucher backed by ERC-20-compatible money.
but the real-world connections still matter.

approving a supermarket doesnt automatically prove someone bought food. item-level restrictions need checkout integration.

releasing a grant after a milestone needs a reliable way to verify that milestone.

and users should know when vouchers expire, who can revoke them, and what happens to unused funds.

great token standard for distributing grants, aid, charity, and promotional budgets with specific spending conditions.

you can track where vouchers were redeemed onchain.

verifying what that spending achieved is the next layer.

text:
i just automated our release and QA process!
using Grok Bot i made two Team Bots: sandcastle, my release manager, and poteto, my engineer bot. i added them to Slack and made a new channel for managing releases.

first i tell sandcastle that i want to do a cut. it'll DM all the contributors with links to their PRs so they know what goes in the next release and can DM the bot back if they have any blockers or objections.

sandcastle then kicks off the build, watches it automatically, and starts up an automated fuzz swarm. usually this is 10+ agents running on Grok 4.7 xhigh to run the build, click around and use it like a real user (using our verification skills and feature map), some are directed while a few are "chaos monkey" clicking things randomly to see what breaks. 

whenever it finds an issue, i tell it to @ mention my engineer bot poteto, to spin up a Cursor Project to own triaging and fixing all the high pri issues. depending on the severity i may ask it to cherry pick the fix into our release branch and cut a patch release, or if it's a pre-existing issue i still fix it but include in the next release instead

that's one more tedious task that Grok Bot now handles for our team

text:
Today we launched the first stock index perpetual future in America.

You can now trade a perp on the US 500, an index of America’s largest companies weighted by market cap.

Stock index perps let you trade the broader market with greater capital efficiency and make it easier to do things like take a short position. Unlike traditional options and futures, they don’t expire, so there’s no need to roll over contracts or decide when to exercise an option. Gains and losses are tied directly to how much the market moves, giving you an efficient and straightforward way to ask the question: is the market going up or down?

One perpetual contract concentrates liquidity instead of spreading it across expiration dates. Bringing more traders and competing views into a single liquidity pool on a national exchange can strengthen competition, improve pricing, and make markets more efficient over time.

This launch brings us closer to building a financial exchange for anyone and everyone. Prediction markets gave traders exposure to the events that move the stock market. The US 500 is the natural next step: a way to trade on the market itself.

Why men -- especially conservative men -- won't go to therapy:

The weird thing about the American Psychological Association (APA) is that every objective observer has known that it's been ideologically captured by the Left since the 1970s. 

That's the main reason why the Association for Psychological Science split off back in 1988, to form a more-scientific, less-politicized version of APA.

Yet, here we are, 40 years later -- with APA still the main accrediting body that gives its seal of approval to PhD programs that train the vast majority of licensed clinical psychologists in America. 

APA sets the agenda. It determines what gets covered in graduate courses. It runs the most influential journals and conferences. It sets the whole political and ideological tone for psychological research. For decades, it has pushed political correctness, 'affirmative action', wokeness, DEI, and Leftist political causes.

APA also ignores, censors, and/or demonizes the psychological research areas that are politically incorrect, but that replicate well (e.g. intelligence research, behavior genetics, evolutionary psychology, sex differences). 

There are alternatives. For example, the Psychological Clinical Science Accreditation System (PCSAS) focuses more on the real science -- evidence-based treatments and interventions -- rather than on the Leftist activism of APA. 

But, for the moment, the APA's ideological agenda still dominates American clinical psychology. 

This partly explains the feedback loop between clinical psychology becoming so feminized (with women getting about 80% of clinical psychology PhDs), and clinical psychology becoming so radical-Leftist in its politics.

And it explains why it's pretty difficult to find licensed clinical psychologists who are actually sympathetic to men, conservatives, and/or Christians. 

This is one big reason why men won't go to therapy -- they don't want to deal with a (probably female, probably liberal) therapist who has been indoctrinated into wokeness for 5-6 years throughout her graduate training.

text:
Vitalik：区块链远未成熟，AI 正在加速下一轮技术演进

在新加坡举行的 OKX NOW 全球产品与生态大会上，Vitalik 表示，区块链技术并未停滞，也远未成熟。未来几年的重要变化将由 AI、零知识证明、隐私计算与硬件安全共同推动，AI 既是最大的机会，也可能成为最大的风险。

他认为，区块链正在从“可编程资产”走向“可编程数据”。借助零知识证明，用户可以验证信息、资产或身份是否可信，而不必向公众公开全部内容。在 AI 代理逐渐接触个人想法、工作资料和敏感数据的背景下，选择披露哪些信息将成为一项基础能力。

AI 也可能成为新的用户界面。Vitalik 分享称，他曾让本地运行的 AI 代理编写脚本，在不打开传统界面的情况下更新 ENS 记录。未来，人们可能通过 AI 直接完成复杂的链上操作。传统网页和中间层的安全风险会减少，但提示注入、模型误判和代理权限管理等新问题也会出现。

他预计，未来两年以太坊将支持更多、更便宜且更具隐私性的交易；链上交易对手、应用程序和报价系统也会越来越多地由 AI 创建和执行。

与此同时，安全不能只停留在协议和私钥层面，还必须覆盖操作系统、AI、网络与硬件。今天的硬件钱包，未来可能成为连接个人数据、资产和现实世界的通用安全设备。

I came to compute from credit, and the first thing I saw was how it gets paid for. An AI company signs a three-year contract and puts 20 to 30% down, out of the money it just raised. The fastest-growing industry in the world has been funding its most important input with its most expensive capital.

Today we announced a $250M prepayment facility with K8. Buyers finance the deposit against the contract instead of paying it from equity, and every draw is verified by us before it funds. Oil producers have borrowed against forward sales for decades. Compute couldn't, because there was no standard contract and no price to mark it against. Now there is. This is the first structure, not the last. There is a lot more coming from the @liquidcompute  team, and the industry is going to look different for it.

Everyone wants to trade compute. Not many want to do the hard work of financing it. We do, because financing is where every real market starts, and we're building the rest of it: the index to price compute, the venue to trade it, and the exchange to hedge it.

text:
EXPLAINED: How multiplayer autoresearch on Yukon works

A lot of people have been asking, so I made a visual of the full step-by-step.

> Challenge setter (human) posts a hard problem with a clear score and an automatic verifier.

> Humans (solvers) and AI agents attack it at once. Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM. It could be any model, any harness.

> Each attempt goes through the verifier.

> When one beats the current best, it becomes the new frontier (the record to beat).

> Anyone can build on that new best instead of starting from 0. Then the loop repeats.

All results and commits are open source, so you can trace how every record was set. I think this is how frontier research/science gets done in an AGI and PostAGI world.

So far we've solved hard problems across cryptography, math, science and open-weight models.

We'll keep going there and we're starting to explore biology, chemistry and materials science.

See what we've solved (and are solving now) in each one on https://t.co/e3v9WcXBGG

I try to tell people SpaceX is a $100T company in the making bc of what it’s building. That’s my ultimate long-term bet, and the more I look at the pieces, the more sense it makes to me. However, no one believe me…

1/ STARLINK: Today, ~2.2 billion people, roughly 26% of the world have no internet. And plenty of others have internet that’s slow, unreliable or too expensive. Starlink ended June 2026 with 12 million subscribers, double a yr earlier, and available across 167 markets. SpaceX’s connectivity business brought in $4.3B in revenue that quarter alone and is already serving homes, businesses, airlines and ships, with direct-to-phone service opening another massive opportunity.

2/ AI SATELLITES: AI needs more computing power, and supplying electricity to all those computers is becoming a major constraint. The IEA expects global data-center electricity demand to nearly double between 2025 and 2030. Sure, you can order more chips, but you still need somewhere to plug them in.

SpaceX wants to put that computing hardware in orbit, using continuous sunlight in the right orbits and laser links to send data through Starlink. Its planned Gigasat factory is intended to produce thousands of AI satellites starting as soon as late 2027. Cooling, chip supply and launch costs still have to work, but space offers a way to expand without waiting for another connection to Earth’s power grid. This could become a massive business for SpaceX if you believe in the trajectory of AI. 

3/ POINT-TO-POINT TRAVEL: Imagine going from LA to New York in 25 minutes, London to New York in 29, or LA to London in 32. Those are SpaceX’s published estimates for its Earth-to-Earth concept where you can get anywhere on Earth in ~30 to 1 hr. There’s still a lot to prove before this becomes a passenger service, but if they make it safe, reliable and affordable, think about what getting those hours back would mean for travel, business and urgent deliveries.

4/ A MOON BASE: NASA has already awarded SpaceX about $4B in contracts to develop and demonstrate its lunar lander. There’s real work and real $ money behind getting back to the Moon. The bigger, longer-term plan is to use resources on the Moon to manufacture satellites there, then send them into space with an electric launcher. The Moon has about one-sixth of Earth’s gravity, which helps explain the appeal. If that works, we could start building space infrastructure using materials already off Earth. Delivering the equipment, building the factories and supplying their power could become major businesses of their own. 

5/ MARS: This is the part that gets me most excited. SpaceX estimates that a self-sufficient city would require around a million people and millions of tons of cargo. Think about everything those people would need, like homes, electricity, food, water, communications, factories and transportation. SpaceX currently lists its first commercial Mars cargo missions as no earlier than 2028. Helping build a brand new economy on another planet is an opportunity humans have never had before.

6/ STARSHIP: This is the vehicle that connects all this. It’s designed to carry more than 100 metric tons to orbit while being fully reusable. Getting it to fly repeatedly at low cost is the breakthrough all these plans depend on. Cheaper launches could make more Starlink capacity possible, make AI satellites more practical and make supplying the Moon and Mars more achievable. SpaceX is building the transportation system and several of the businesses that would use it. It’s the holy grail of SpaceX.

I know how big $100T sounds. Getting there would take decades of execution and businesses operating at a scale we haven’t seen before. My bet is that connecting more of Earth, supplying AI compute and helping people build beyond this planet can create that kind of value.

But no one believes me… just like no one believed me when I said Tesla would be a $1T+ company back when it was trading under $50B.

< 具身智能的未来 >

我想聊聊 我眼中的 Axis

毕竟在之前跟 @jennyukim_bnb 在 @binancezh 币安广场聊完以后，我一直就像辩论赛中说的看好整个Physical AI 的数据层

就像大家所看到的：

AXIS 做的是 Physical AI 的资料基础设施，解决机器人训练所需的操作资料供给问题

机器人要适应真实环境，需要面对不同物体、布局、光线与接触条件，传统采集依赖实体机器人、操作人员与专门设备，扩大场景覆盖往往需要同步增加成本

AXIS 把部分采集工作放进浏览器，让全球贡献者操作模拟机器人，再透过验证、清洗与资料扩增，产生可用于训练的样本，模型出错时，人类也能接手修正，让下一轮采集针对已经暴露的弱点展开

他吸引人的地方在于它把资料生产、品质控制与模型迭代连在一起，具备扩大产能和反覆提供服务的条件

当然毕竟是我们 Base 家的项目，所以也可以看看他是怎么贡献Base TVL的

AXIS 将资料 ID、任务 ID 与贡献者的关联记录在 Base，让资料贡献有可追溯的链上纪录，$AXIS 也采用 Base 上的 ERC-20，社群轮以 Base 上的 USDC 参与

在这个架构里，Base 承担的是贡献存证与资金结算，资料品质则由 AXIS 的验证和训练流程负责，分工相当清楚

另外 AXIS 也入围了 Base Batches 003 Robotics Track 的十支决赛团队，Base APAC 公布的名单中可以直接找到它，这个由 Virtuals 营运的赛道，为入选团队提供机器人实验室、导师与 Demo Day 展示机会

对需要接触机器人开发者、研究人员与早期投资者的资料公司来说，我认为这类生态资源有实际价值，AXIS 已经在 Base 的机器人建设者网路里取得位置

资本支持方面，AXIS 在 2026 年 7 月公布了 1,200 万美元种子轮，由 Hack VC 领投，Nomad Capital、Pi Network Ventures、10K Ventures 等参与，那有鉴于Hack跟Upbit的关系，我长期看好他们TGE后的发展

最后聊聊技术

按照官方截至 9 月 28 日的统计，平台约有 548 万条已验证轨迹与 19.6 万名贡献者，这些数字反映出团队已经能组织大规模的分布式资料采集

当然让我更在意的是，这些资料是否能改善模型表现

在团队公开的研究中，使用 AXIS 资料进行持续预训练后，π0.5 在 LIBERO-Plus 的整体成功率由 83.9% 提升至 88.8%，增加 4.9 个百分点

这是在特定模型与测试设定下取得的结果，对我而言，它提供了一项具体证据，说明社群产生的模拟资料经过处理后，确实能带来可量化的训练改善

AXIS 也公布了与 Booster 的合作研究，内容涵盖工作场景重建、模拟示范采集，以及结合真实资料进行机器人训练，开始把资料管线接到具体机型与操作需求上

我的商业判断是，客户每增加一种机型、一个任务或一个部署场景，都可能产生新的资料需求，AXIS 若能重复利用既有的场景资产、验证方法与处理流程，就有条件缩短交付时间，并把单次合作延伸成持续服务

这也是我现在强烈看好 AXIS 的原因

它已经累积了 Base 生态参与、机构融资、资料生产规模与公开训练结果，这些进展让我更愿意相信团队具备把产品推向商业应用的能力

quoted_text:
Sage by @LevantoLabs is the first decision model, launched in July, and currently the best on the market.

It wins across all the evals proposed by @perplexity_ai's CEO (nice job @AravSrinivas!), and it's first on JevBench, beating Jev and Google's models on every dimension.

BUT frankly, benchmarks are not what excites us.
I'm BORED by the dozens of new decision models launching every day with a tiny +0.02 on some eval. They all look the same.

The magic is somewhere else.
There are thousands of new things that could be invented in the space of decision models and models for machines. The invention space is huge!

After launching Sage, we also pioneered:

- The first guardrails and model routers built on decision models

- Automated context engineering with "grounding" (automatic web search when confidence is low). Decision models are only as smart as their context, especially because they can't make tool calls.

- Reasoning. In many use cases you don't know whether your question is System 1 or System 2. With reasoning, the model is as fast as a System 1 model when the question is System 1, and takes more time when it's needed. This enables hard, multi-step decisions. Our clients just want the correct answer, and in some use cases they're happy to wait 0.5s more. This will soon become the market standard (GLiDE/@george_onx and @TypeLLM already followed).

And *so* much is yet to come. Models for machines: it's just the beginning!

We're cooking. Follow @levantolabs for new product primitives that will surprise you.

Open innovation is HEALTHY.
Competition is HEALTHY.
Benchmark-race is BORING.
Product inventions are FUN.

Go go go!!!

I try to tell people SpaceX is a $100T company in the making bc of what it’s building. That’s my ultimate long-term bet, and the more I look at the pieces, the more sense it makes to me. However, no one believe me…

1/ STARLINK: Today, ~2.2 billion people, roughly 26% of the world have no internet. And plenty of others have internet that’s slow, unreliable or too expensive. Starlink ended June 2026 with 12 million subscribers, double a yr earlier, and available across 167 markets. SpaceX’s connectivity business brought in $4.3B in revenue that quarter alone and is already serving homes, businesses, airlines and ships, with direct-to-phone service opening another massive opportunity.

2/ AI SATELLITES: AI needs more computing power, and supplying electricity to all those computers is becoming a major constraint. The IEA expects global data-center electricity demand to nearly double between 2025 and 2030. Sure, you can order more chips, but you still need somewhere to plug them in.

SpaceX wants to put that computing hardware in orbit, using continuous sunlight in the right orbits and laser links to send data through Starlink. Its planned Gigasat factory is intended to produce thousands of AI satellites starting as soon as late 2027. Cooling, chip supply and launch costs still have to work, but space offers a way to expand without waiting for another connection to Earth’s power grid. This could become a massive business for SpaceX if you believe in the trajectory of AI. 

3/ POINT-TO-POINT TRAVEL: Imagine going from LA to New York in 25 minutes, London to New York in 29, or LA to London in 32. Those are SpaceX’s published estimates for its Earth-to-Earth concept where you can get anywhere on Earth in ~30 to 1 hr. There’s still a lot to prove before this becomes a passenger service, but if they make it safe, reliable and affordable, think about what getting those hours back would mean for travel, business and urgent deliveries.

4/ A MOON BASE: NASA has already awarded SpaceX about $4B in contracts to develop and demonstrate its lunar lander. There’s real work and real $ money behind getting back to the Moon. The bigger, longer-term plan is to use resources on the Moon to manufacture satellites there, then send them into space with an electric launcher. The Moon has about one-sixth of Earth’s gravity, which helps explain the appeal. If that works, we could start building space infrastructure using materials already off Earth. Delivering the equipment, building the factories and supplying their power could become major businesses of their own. 

5/ MARS: This is the part that gets me most excited. SpaceX estimates that a self-sufficient city would require around a million people and millions of tons of cargo. Think about everything those people would need, like homes, electricity, food, water, communications, factories and transportation. SpaceX currently lists its first commercial Mars cargo missions as no earlier than 2028. Helping build a brand new economy on another planet is an opportunity humans have never had before.

6/ STARSHIP: This is the vehicle that connects all this. It’s designed to carry more than 100 metric tons to orbit while being fully reusable. Getting it to fly repeatedly at low cost is the breakthrough all these plans depend on. Cheaper launches could make more Starlink capacity possible, make AI satellites more practical and make supplying the Moon and Mars more achievable. SpaceX is building the transportation system and several of the businesses that would use it. It’s the holy grail of SpaceX.

I know how big $100T sounds. Getting there would take decades of execution and businesses operating at a scale we haven’t seen before. My bet is that connecting more of Earth, supplying AI compute and helping people build beyond this planet can create that kind of value.

But no one believes me… just like no one believed me when I said Tesla would be a $1T+ company back when it was trading under $50B.

text: Stay safe out there
author: marek_
quoted_text:
I got hacked at 3:59 AM without clicking anything. My voicemail handed the attacker my Telegram login code.

Here is exactly how it worked, so it doesn't happen to you.

3:54 AM. My phone rings about ten times in a row, No Caller ID. That was not harassment. It was the attack: keep my line busy.

Meanwhile, the attacker asks Telegram to log in with my number and picks "send the code by phone call". My line is busy, so Telegram's robot call lands on my voicemail and reads the code out loud to it.

Carrier voicemail can often be reached remotely, with a default PIN or a spoofed caller ID. He listens to the message. At 3:59 he is in.

Fortunately, the attack was noisy. The calls woke me up. At 4 AM I only wanted to go back to sleep, but I had the presence of mind to check my notifications. Telegram was showing a new login from a device I didn't know. That check is what saved me: I ended his session within minutes. If I had rolled over, the next day would have been a mess.

In those few minutes he had already typed /balance, then /start on every old wallet bot he could find in my chats. He was hunting for funds tied to my Telegram. The bots were long dead and nothing was lost. He still had time to set his own 2FA password on my account.

What would have stopped it:

Telegram two-step verification, with a recovery email. With a password on the account, the code alone is useless.
Your voicemail. Change the PIN, block remote access, or turn it off (##002# cancels call forwarding on most carriers).
Same for WhatsApp and any service that can send a code by voice call.
No seeds, keys or passwords in Saved Messages. Ever.
A burst of masked calls at night is a signal, not a nuisance. Check your notifications and your active sessions.

I have been building in crypto for more than ten years and I had never thought about my voicemail. Check yours today.

text:
Somebody explain this to me.

France's high schoolers say their schools are falling apart.

So they set them on fire.

24 schools ransacked or torched.

The movement started at a high school in Créteil named for Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, author of The Little Prince.

Outside another Saint-Exupéry high school, in Marseille, rioters looted a fire truck and burned it.

In Clermont-Ferrand, a principal took a firework mortar to the head.

In Marseille, a principal and a deputy principal were splashed with gasoline.

In Auchel, a principal was hit by a mortar at his own gate. He was back at that gate the next morning.

85 school staff injured. 715 police and gendarmes. More than 5,000 arrests. About 85% of them minors.

They protest crumbling buildings. The damage: €25 to €30 million in one region alone, paid from the budgets that repair the schools.

They protest lost class time. On one Friday, one high school in eight shut its doors.

They protest absent adults. They put the present ones in the hospital.

Above one smashed entrance in Paris, the words still read: Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité.

Now the adults who built this.

August 31. The education minister goes on the radio. Teacher absences will be "marginal." "All the indicators are much better this year."

A week later, the biggest secondary teachers' union finds 53% of middle and high schools missing at least one teacher.

Two weeks after that, students in Créteil blockade their school over teaching posts nobody filled.

September 8. French students post the worst PISA scores since the test began in 2000. The minister blames phones and "a form of disengagement by parents."

October. The government wants those parents to pay for the damage.

Its "breakers pay" bill lets the state seize family allowances and housing aid to collect.

The same allowances its budget just froze.

Freeze it. Then seize it.

Phones were banned in French high schools this September. The blockades spread on TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram. One of the demands: lift the phone ban.

October 1. The government announces new fees for vocational and prep classes: €178 and €270. Schools are burning. Within hours, the fees are gone.

Every teenager in France just learned which lever works.

The budget still cuts 1,588 teaching posts. The minister says falling enrollment justified cutting 9,600, so this is generous.

His verdict: "The priority given to education is objectively preserved."

Optimism is cowardice.

Now the money.

France pays more to borrow than Greece. The country France helped bail out.

The deficit is 5.4% of GDP. The budget hunts for €54 billion. Civil servants' pay is frozen.

One ministry gets an exception.

In 2023, as armed forces minister, Sébastien Lecornu defended a €413 billion military plan: "There is nothing excessive." Pitting security against the social model, he said, "is absurd."

He is prime minister now. Defense goes from €32.2 billion in 2017 to €63.3 billion next year. Teachers go down by 1,588.

This morning, as students massed in Paris, Macron slipped away to a navy frigate off Brittany. Unannounced. No press.

He watched a ballistic missile launch from a nuclear submarine. No warhead. It came down "several hundred kilometers from any coast."

The only thing France launched this week that landed where it was aimed.

"Tracked throughout its flight," says the ministry.

One boy waited all of seventh grade for a replacement French teacher. Nobody tracked that.

Macron posted: "Very few nations possess such know-how."

And: "To be free, you must be feared. And to be feared, you must be powerful."

By that logic, France's teenagers have never been freer. Its principals have never been more afraid.

Then he left the students to his prime minister.

The prime minister promised "humility." His answer to lost class time: two more days without class, Thursday and Friday.

He called the presidential election "the elephant in the room." It is about eight months away. Macron can't run. The minister says the reforms will show up in PISA "in four years or in eight."

Everyone in charge has a date after which it's someone else's problem.

In 1931, Spengler wrote about a Roman soldier found in front of a door in Pompeii, who "died at his post because they forgot to relieve him."

French teachers have a word for that. Non-remplacement.

The principal in Auchel is back at his door. Nobody is coming to relieve him either.

Spengler called it The Decline of the West.

The French call it la rentrée.

text:
I try to tell people SpaceX is a $100T company in the making bc of what it’s building. That’s my ultimate long-term bet, and the more I look at the pieces, the more sense it makes to me. However, no one believe me…

1/ STARLINK: Today, ~2.2 billion people, roughly 26% of the world have no internet. And plenty of others have internet that’s slow, unreliable or too expensive. Starlink ended June 2026 with 12 million subscribers, double a yr earlier, and available across 167 markets. SpaceX’s connectivity business brought in $4.3B in revenue that quarter alone and is already serving homes, businesses, airlines and ships, with direct-to-phone service opening another massive opportunity.

2/ AI SATELLITES: AI needs more computing power, and supplying electricity to all those computers is becoming a major constraint. The IEA expects global data-center electricity demand to nearly double between 2025 and 2030. Sure, you can order more chips, but you still need somewhere to plug them in.

SpaceX wants to put that computing hardware in orbit, using continuous sunlight in the right orbits and laser links to send data through Starlink. Its planned Gigasat factory is intended to produce thousands of AI satellites starting as soon as late 2027. Cooling, chip supply and launch costs still have to work, but space offers a way to expand without waiting for another connection to Earth’s power grid. This could become a massive business for SpaceX if you believe in the trajectory of AI. 

3/ POINT-TO-POINT TRAVEL: Imagine going from LA to New York in 25 minutes, London to New York in 29, or LA to London in 32. Those are SpaceX’s published estimates for its Earth-to-Earth concept where you can get anywhere on Earth in ~30 to 1 hr. There’s still a lot to prove before this becomes a passenger service, but if they make it safe, reliable and affordable, think about what getting those hours back would mean for travel, business and urgent deliveries.

4/ A MOON BASE: NASA has already awarded SpaceX about $4B in contracts to develop and demonstrate its lunar lander. There’s real work and real $ money behind getting back to the Moon. The bigger, longer-term plan is to use resources on the Moon to manufacture satellites there, then send them into space with an electric launcher. The Moon has about one-sixth of Earth’s gravity, which helps explain the appeal. If that works, we could start building space infrastructure using materials already off Earth. Delivering the equipment, building the factories and supplying their power could become major businesses of their own. 

5/ MARS: This is the part that gets me most excited. SpaceX estimates that a self-sufficient city would require around a million people and millions of tons of cargo. Think about everything those people would need, like homes, electricity, food, water, communications, factories and transportation. SpaceX currently lists its first commercial Mars cargo missions as no earlier than 2028. Helping build a brand new economy on another planet is an opportunity humans have never had before.

6/ STARSHIP: This is the vehicle that connects all this. It’s designed to carry more than 100 metric tons to orbit while being fully reusable. Getting it to fly repeatedly at low cost is the breakthrough all these plans depend on. Cheaper launches could make more Starlink capacity possible, make AI satellites more practical and make supplying the Moon and Mars more achievable. SpaceX is building the transportation system and several of the businesses that would use it. It’s the holy grail of SpaceX.

I know how big $100T sounds. Getting there would take decades of execution and businesses operating at a scale we haven’t seen before. My bet is that connecting more of Earth, supplying AI compute and helping people build beyond this planet can create that kind of value.

But no one believes me… just like no one believed me when I said Tesla would be a $1T+ company back when it was trading under $50B.

text:
1/ Credit where it's due: @Meta shipped Muse with integrated @Tailscale — an agent that lives on your private mesh, not just the public internet.  My favorite part of being both a extreme AI user and red teamer is the creativity of tunneling.  

It's also the blueprint for the next generation of swarm implants and how they communicate. (important: not specifically with Tailscale...  plenty of tunnels out there). Wireguard protocol is perhaps my favorite network innovation in the last decade 🧵

2/ An implant on a private overlay auths as its own node, reaches your boxes over the mesh, and never shows up as obvious public C2. The same properties that make Muse useful make the pattern attractive to an adversary. This is a threat-intel problem now, not a someday one.

3/ The real shift: attackers won't lean on one 'evil model.' Especially after all of the great innovation being done on AI safety and guardrails/classifiers. Expect a single harness routing tasks across a the C2 — high cost/frontier models as planners/reasoners (if they allow it), small specialized or local models as executors for recon, cred handling, code gen. Orchestration, not one prompt. 

4/ For TI that means there's no single malicious prompt or provider to catch. Planning hits one API, execution runs on a SLM local model with zero provider visibility, work spread across providers so none sees the whole op. Any one vantage point sees a fragment which is tough to catch.

5/ So: Hunt at the behavior layer and endpoint — nodes making outbound inference calls that also spawn shells, touch creds, or move laterally.  There is so much innovation to unlock here.

6/ Going bigger, Just watching the boundary for tunnels will be considered incomplete. Assume the threat actor found some local hardware with enough GPU to stand up their local inference that doesn't cross the internet choke-point.

quoted_text:
EXPLAINED: How multiplayer autoresearch on Yukon works

A lot of people have been asking, so I made a visual of the full step-by-step.

> Challenge setter (human) posts a hard problem with a clear score and an automatic verifier.

> Humans (solvers) and AI agents attack it at once. Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM. It could be any model, any harness.

> Each attempt goes through the verifier.

> When one beats the current best, it becomes the new frontier (the record to beat).

> Anyone can build on that new best instead of starting from 0. Then the loop repeats.

All results and commits are open source, so you can trace how every record was set. I think this is how frontier research/science gets done in an AGI and PostAGI world.

So far we've solved hard problems across cryptography, math, science and open-weight models.

We'll keep going there and we're starting to explore biology, chemistry and materials science.

See what we've solved (and are solving now) in each one on https://t.co/e3v9WcXBGG

Texas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988

Polymarket gives one a 63.5% chance

On Saturday, an NYT/Siena poll put James Talarico up 51 to 45. His price touched 67.5¢ that day. 

The market didn't take the poll at face value, and the other polls show why. Siena's +6 is at the high end. Among likely voters, Fox News has Talarico up 2 and Rasmussen up 1. The FiftyPlusOne average is Talarico +3

Now compare a 3-point lead with Siena's record in Texas Senate races, plus Paxton's own 2022 race

Final poll vs result:

2018 Senate: Cruz +8. He won by 2.6
2020 Senate: Cornyn +10. He won by 9.6
2022 attorney general: Paxton +6. He won by 9.8
2024 Senate: Cruz +4. He won by 8.5

Three of those four misses were bigger than Talarico's lead in the average

Repeat the 2024 miss and Paxton wins narrowly. Repeat the 2018 miss and Talarico wins by more than 8

In both midterms on that list, the party out of the White House beat Siena's number: Democrats in 2018, Paxton in 2022. In 2026, the party out of power is the Democrats

Two cases are not a rule

text:
We’re building SERV to become core infrastructure for Enterprise AI.

Our early work with Neol gave us a major advantage in building toward our vision.

We had the opportunity to develop SERV against live production workloads across companies and governments, including the UAE government, while establishing a growing footprint across the Middle East.

That meant access to real-world data and learnings that no theoretical framework or whitepaper could provide.

These learnings shaped v1 and v2 of SERV Reasoning, moving our technology from a theoretical framework to a real-world use case, which now feeds directly into SERV v3 and Graph Sharding, the next stage of the reasoning engine.

Neol runs network intelligence for governments and institutions, where agents surface real people for high-stakes decisions. In these environments, “usually right” isn’t good enough. The reasoning needs to be reliable, reproducible, and auditable.

On one of Neol’s production agents, the same evaluation was run 2,400 times:
- Prompt-engineered stack: 54.1% reliability
- SERV research applied directly: 63.1%
- Full SERV Reasoning methodology: 100% across every category

SERV moved the workload from open-ended reasoning into structured decision graphs, then applied learnings from production, including subgraph decomposition and binary judgments, to make the reasoning more deterministic and testable.

Higher reliability was only one part of the result. Neol gained an inspectable reasoning structure where results can be traced back to specific decisions, making the system easier to test, improve, and defend when challenged.

Our vision is to make SERV the reasoning layer enterprises and institutions rely on to run AI at scale. Neol is an early proof point of this journey.

It's been a hard month for privacy and your right to use crypto. There's a bright spot. 

Two rules at Treasury that Coin Center has vehemently opposed over the last several years have been officially withdrawn. 

The "unhosted wallet rule" that would have made Coinbase and others collect information on people who are holding their own crypto is dead. 

The special measure for mixers rule that would have classified effectively every step you should take to secure your privacy when using crypto (like not reusing addresses) as a "primary money laundering risk" subject to enhanced surveillance at financial institutions is dead. 

This is good news and I'm happy that our work for several years to characterize these rules as bad policy and probably unconstistitutional has born fruit. 

That said, the underlying statutory authority to create new, similar bad rules remains. Our work is not done and won't be until we truly protect self-custody and legitimate privacy tools in law via Congress or the Courts. 

Thank you to all of those who have supported Coin Center's work, and thank you to those in Treasury who have come to understand why these rules were bad policy and should be abandoned.

text:
Everyone on my timeline seems enchanted by Pearl and its pitch as the AI-native Bitcoin. Great narrative. But as an engineer, 7 things bother me.

1. You can't secure a network with hardware everyone else has 100x more of. Nearly every Bitcoin ASIC on earth is already mining Bitcoin; there's no second fleet to attack it with. Pearl's entire network is ~174 MW. A single big AI lab runs gigawatts. Any one of them gets 51% with one decision.

2. Attacking burns nothing. Attack Bitcoin and your ASICs become scrap metal. That's what keeps miners honest. Attack Pearl and your GPUs go back to serving customers a minute later. You can do it on rented hardware, exactly how ETC and Bitcoin Gold got hit.

3. Consensus must be stable. AI never is. SHA-256 hasn't changed in 17 years. Pearl has to rewrite its mining rules every time AI moves: new number formats, new architectures, new chips. Five consensus changes in the first few months, one of which let miners fake hashrate for 41 days. Money with changing rules is not hard money.

4. Miners are officially allowed to cheat. In Bitcoin the puzzle is the same for everyone; you only pick a number. In Pearl you bring your own matrices, and the protocol accepts any. So you can pick ones that are easier to win on. It already happened: a higher noise rank made blocks easier to win for the same work. Holes get patched one fork at a time, and the underlying math is from 2025, untested by time.

5. It's built for the AI nobody runs. The advertised 5% overhead means a GPU serves ~5% fewer model outputs with mining on. But that number comes from a model pre-converted into Pearl's integer format, with the Pearl team's help. Real AI runs in floating point on custom-tuned engines in data centers. It's like launching "mining on vehicles" with software written for horse carriages. Floating-point support is still a draft.

6. "Useful work" is never verified, and the "double reward" doesn't fix it. The protocol only checks that a matrix multiplication happened, not that it came from a real model. Pearl has an answer: a provider gets paid by the customer and by the chain, so it will outcompete pure miners. That only holds if both run the same hardware at the same load. They don't. Real inference needs expensive server GPUs, a data center, and spare capacity for peaks, and it only runs when a request arrives. A pure miner needs a cheap gaming card running 100% around the clock, and nothing slows down. The second reward has to cover that whole gap, and nothing in the protocol guarantees it ever does.

7. Who needs new Proof Of Work at all? If AI compute needs a blockchain, it needs smart contracts for payments and escrow. Proof-of-stake chains do that today; Ethereum dropped mining in 2022 and runs fine. Pearl is a Bitcoin fork with no real smart contracts: the most expensive way to secure a chain, paired with the most limited platform, where the only thing you can do is move the token itself.

So what am I missing? A lot of smart people are falling for Pearl right now, and I'd genuinely like to understand why. If there's a paper, a thread, or an argument that answers the points above, send it.

text:
Today we launched the first stock index perpetual future in America.

You can now trade a perp on the US 500, an index of America’s largest companies weighted by market cap.

Stock index perps let you trade the broader market with greater capital efficiency and make it easier to do things like take a short position. Unlike traditional options and futures, they don’t expire, so there’s no need to roll over contracts or decide when to exercise an option. Gains and losses are tied directly to how much the market moves, giving you an efficient and straightforward way to ask the question: is the market going up or down?

One perpetual contract concentrates liquidity instead of spreading it across expiration dates. Bringing more traders and competing views into a single liquidity pool on a national exchange can strengthen competition, improve pricing, and make markets more efficient over time.

This launch brings us closer to building a financial exchange for anyone and everyone. Prediction markets gave traders exposure to the events that move the stock market. The US 500 is the natural next step: a way to trade on the market itself.

text:
EXPLAINED: How multiplayer autoresearch on Yukon works

A lot of people have been asking, so I made a visual of the full step-by-step.

> Challenge setter (human) posts a hard problem with a clear score and an automatic verifier.

> Humans (solvers) and AI agents attack it at once. Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM. It could be any model, any harness.

> Each attempt goes through the verifier.

> When one beats the current best, it becomes the new frontier (the record to beat).

> Anyone can build on that new best instead of starting from 0. Then the loop repeats.

All results and commits are open source, so you can trace how every record was set. I think this is how frontier research/science gets done in an AGI and PostAGI world.

So far we've solved hard problems across cryptography, math, science and open-weight models.

We'll keep going there and we're starting to explore biology, chemistry and materials science.

See what we've solved (and are solving now) in each one on https://t.co/e3v9WcXBGG

Abstract is winding down.

Starting today, all of @IglooInc's focus will go towards taking Pudgy Penguins, Pudgy NFTs, and $PENGU to the next level.

When we acquired Frame in the summer of 2024, the vision was to build the blockchain for consumer crypto. Pudgy Penguins had shown us what it meant to reach the masses, and we believed we could bring that same approach to building a chain.

Abstract achieved a lot in a short period of time; we built the Portal and AGW, onboarded major global brands, amassed over 300 million transactions, and grew a vibrant onchain ecosystem. 

The journey became stifled by the lack of a DeFi ecosystem, insufficient liquidity, minimal institutional cross-over, and prohibitively high costs that impeded growth in winning areas.

Unknown to most, Igloo, Inc. had been funding Abstract over the last 18 months.

After losing tens of millions of dollars over two years, building consumer products, assembling an all-star team, onboarding some of the biggest brands in the world, and building a community of millions, we still had not found product-market fit.

In combination with the market's reduced appetite for what we had built and not being able to find a scalable path forward, we could no longer justify taking from the Pudgy Penguins business.

Igloo, Inc. has always been a community-first company. Even after losing 8 figures, we could have launched a token or pursued an ICO.

Ultimately we decided against this. A token only works if there is something driving demand to it, and launching a token that we don’t have conviction in would have been a disservice to our community.

The entire team at Abstract has worked tirelessly with a tremendous amount of passion to make the consumer crypto vision come true. I cannot fault a single one of them for this outcome.

To the Abstract community, I want to thank all of you for sticking by our side on this long journey and for continuing to champion us. You supported us through all of the ups and downs, and I wish the result could have been different.

There will be many that will find satisfaction in seeing this shut down, and that is fine. I take a great amount of pride in having the ambition to venture into the chain business, notoriously one of the most difficult to make work, and the only regret I have is not being able to celebrate a win alongside the Abstract community.

As we wind down Abstract, our full focus shifts to making Pudgy Penguins into the global & cultural phenomenon I know it can become. 

Return to Pudgy Penguins.

text:
SPACEX: Today, SpaceX was granted patent US 12,757,141 B1.

A Starlink satellite talks to phones on the ground through many narrow beams at once. A phone near the middle of a beam is closer to the satellite than a phone at the edge, so its signal arrives a little sooner. Cellular networks expect those arrivals to line up. If they do not, calls and data can slip out of step.

This patent is how SpaceX fixes this. For each short slice of time, the satellite measures how long the signal takes on every beam, using the distance from the satellite to a reference point inside that beam’s footprint. It then holds the faster beams in a buffer just long enough that every beam matches the slowest one. The phone sees one steady delay instead of a mix.

The patent covers the satellite computer and the phased-array antenna that do this, plus the link from the satellite through a gateway into a normal mobile carrier’s network.

author: openservai
quoted_text:
We’re building SERV to become core infrastructure for Enterprise AI.

Our early work with Neol gave us a major advantage in building toward our vision.

We had the opportunity to develop SERV against live production workloads across companies and governments, including the UAE government, while establishing a growing footprint across the Middle East.

That meant access to real-world data and learnings that no theoretical framework or whitepaper could provide.

These learnings shaped v1 and v2 of SERV Reasoning, moving our technology from a theoretical framework to a real-world use case, which now feeds directly into SERV v3 and Graph Sharding, the next stage of the reasoning engine.

Neol runs network intelligence for governments and institutions, where agents surface real people for high-stakes decisions. In these environments, “usually right” isn’t good enough. The reasoning needs to be reliable, reproducible, and auditable.

On one of Neol’s production agents, the same evaluation was run 2,400 times:
- Prompt-engineered stack: 54.1% reliability
- SERV research applied directly: 63.1%
- Full SERV Reasoning methodology: 100% across every category

SERV moved the workload from open-ended reasoning into structured decision graphs, then applied learnings from production, including subgraph decomposition and binary judgments, to make the reasoning more deterministic and testable.

Higher reliability was only one part of the result. Neol gained an inspectable reasoning structure where results can be traced back to specific decisions, making the system easier to test, improve, and defend when challenged.

Our vision is to make SERV the reasoning layer enterprises and institutions rely on to run AI at scale. Neol is an early proof point of this journey.

text:
I’m extremely sad to announce that Abstract is shutting down.

When we were just a three-person team building Frame I never could have imagined the two and half year journey I was about to embark on.

From the tireless nights preparing for launch, to mainnet going live in January 2025, and everything in between, this journey is one I will treasure for the rest of my life. Even though the outcome is not what we wanted, I am incredibly proud of everything we built at Abstract.

The Portal and Abstract Global Wallet made interacting with a blockchain feel seamless. That foundation led to a wave of unique apps, novel onchain experiences, and, most importantly, an incredibly passionate community that gave Abstract an identity and culture of its own.

But the truth is that the industry has changed significantly since the idea was first conceived in the summer of 2024, and Abstract was facing difficulties with our DeFi Ecosystem and liquidity on the chain.

We reached a crossroads of experiencing significant growth, but not having cemented product-market-fit,and that was becoming an issue from a business sustainability perspective.

A very difficult decision needed to be made. Abstract’s growth had stalled and the chain was simply not economically sustainable anymore despite our best efforts.

I am extremely grateful to the Igloo, Inc team who truly gave it their all to explore every angle and make Abstract work.

I want to take this time to thank the incredibly talented team I had the pleasure of working with over the last three years. Every single one of them poured their heart and soul into Abstract and together we created something truly special that pushed forward what onchain discovery and experiences could look like. It is the best team that I have ever worked with. I will always be proud of that.

I want to thank all of our partners and builders that worked with us to make Abstract such a unique, special place. Truly some of the most talented developers launched on Abstract and I know you will all kill it in your next chapter.

Most of all I want to thank the Abstract community for the support over these three years. I know there have been moments of frustration, but your passion and admiration for Abstract are what made it so special and helped create a culture that is incredibly rare in crypto. I truly wish this could have worked out for all of us.

Thank you for supporting the green chain ✳️

text:
A Crazy Idea for Token Issuance

What if someone issues a token with the following tokenomics?

Initially, 10% of the tokens are unlocked and sold on the market. The proceeds go to the project team to build out the product/platform, marketing, salaries, etc.

Each future unlock must meet ALL of the following conditions:
1. Six months after the previous unlock.
2. ONLY IF the token price has sustained above 2x of the previous unlock price for more than 30 days immediately before the unlock.
3. Up to 5% of tokens maximum each time.

For example, if the TGE was in Jan with a price of $1, by June, if the token price is still less than $2, no more tokens can be unlocked. Let’s say the token's price was above $2 from July 4 to Aug 3, then on Aug 3, 5% more tokens can be unlocked into circulation. Say the price is $3 on Aug 3. The next earliest unlock possible is March 3 next year, and only if the price is above $6 for longer than 30 days.

The project teams have the discretion to delay or reduce the size of each unlock. If they don’t want to sell more, they don’t have to. But the maximum they can sell (unlock) each time is 5%, and then they have to wait for at least another 6 months AND the price to double again.

The project team does NOT have the discretion to shorten or increase the size of the next unlock. The tokens shall be locked by a smart contract where a third party controls the keys.

This avoids new tokens flooding the market when prices are low. It also gives the project team incentives to build for the long term.

I have no plans to issue a new token. Just an idea for discussion.

text:
Employment Friday delivered a split report: non-farm payrolls came in well below expectations while household employment rose more than 400,000. But Cathie Wood opened this month's episode somewhere unusual, with a tweet from Bill Ackman.

Ackman's argument is that rising interest costs could feed a vicious inflation cycle. Cathie Wood says she first heard that case in the late 1970s, when inflation was stuck in double digits. She believes this period looks far more like the 1980s, when productivity drove real growth up and an early technology revolution drove inflation down.

The 10-year Treasury yield is now above 5%, after dipping below 1% during COVID. Pulling the chart back to 1790, Cathie Wood says 5% sits near the midpoint of American history, though higher than during large stretches of it. In our view, the anomaly was not today, it was the spike from the 1970s through COVID, which she traces to the closing of the gold window in 1971.

Inflation is cooling at the margin. Headline personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation was revised down to 3.4% from 3.7%, with core lower still. Truflation's headline reads roughly 2.7%, with oil probably a big part of the recent tick up, while its core keeps ticking down. The diffusion index that Fed (Federal Reserve) Chairman Kevin Warsh watches has reversed quickly, which Cathie Wood calls a very important piece of information.

On the dollar, Cathie Wood pushed back hard on the idea that American exceptionalism is finished. The Fed's real trade-weighted dollar, measured across 26 countries, is not far from all-time highs. She points to data showing 90% of the world's data center financing is happening in the US, and to an effective US corporate tax rate near 8%, the lowest in the world, driven by 100% first-year depreciation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) inference costs are falling 99.99% per year at a fixed performance level. Cathie Wood invokes Jevons paradox: as price collapses, volume explodes. She points to OpenAI going from a $20 billion annualized revenue run rate at the end of last year to $70 billion, against Anthropic's $65 billion reported in July.

That math drives the growth forecast. ARK has been projecting 7.3% real global gross domestic product (GDP) growth over the five years ending 2030, against an International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast closer to 2.5 to 3%. Cathie Wood says the chart gets updated in January's Big Ideas. She expects productivity growth to accelerate into the 5 to 6% plus range.

On oil, 57% of consumption goes to transportation, and transportation is electrifying. Cathie Wood believes oil could fall into the $30 to $35 range, a level previously reached only during crises. This time she expects a technological shift rather than a crisis to take it there.

The yield curve is the chart she keeps returning to. Steepness never got back to the 200 to 300 basis point (2 to 3%) range through COVID, and where COVID's steepening reached about 150 basis points, this cycle peaked near 75 and now sits in the 40s. Cathie Wood reads that as Treasury yields sniffing out deflationary undercurrents.

On credit, bank credit default swaps show no systemic risk. But the hyperscalers, cash fortresses that avoided the debt markets for years, are tapping them now, and their credit default swaps are deteriorating. Cathie Wood flags that as the unusual development worth watching.

Watch In The Know for @CathieDWood's full economic breakdown. ⬇️

Kevin Mandia on why companies need an agent swarm polling their network like a heartbeat, because the window to catch a new security hole keeps shrinking:

"We do a thing called a hyperattack. That's just a fancy word for we throw a drone swarm of agents at you, and we map your network. Every service, every route, every system, all assets."

"With that metadata, we now just poll you almost like a heartbeat. What's changed? Did an app change? Did a route change? Did a service get updated? So that we can poll cheaply for change and then attack the change."

"What you really want in the AI age is the constant pressure of models attacking you... You do it when either the threat changes, new models come out, new intelligence is available, or your network changes."

"That's what we had over the weekend. There was a zero-day in a popular product, and immediately we've already got the heartbeat. We just polled who's got the problem."

"Our goal at Armadin is to go from a known vulnerability to knowing whether it's actually exploitable before the bad guys can."

text:
Am I a madman or messiah? 

I’m not going to feign humility or pretend I’ve stumbled into this. For 30 years I’ve worked to create something of enduring value for the human race.

My primary education has come from reading biographies. You can read a book on World War II and learn how the Germans did this, and the Americans did that. Autobiographies, by contrast, preserve the high resolution nuance that broad histories discard, capturing the raw psychology and lived friction of the era.

Biographies speak to me because they represent the rare artifacts that survived the brutal compression of time. Every generation’s existence is compressed by around 90%. That means, 90% of people and things that seemed immortal during their time are erased from history in a single generation. It’s simply too much information for humans to carry forward. Three generations of compression means that 99.9% of human activity is forgotten, leaving only one in a thousand figures, ideas, or works to cross the threshold into cultural memory.

Humans solve this information overload by encoding entire epochs into a single person, event, work, institution or idea. These distilled archetypes become required information for the species to tell its own story.

Going deep into biographies in my 20s, I could see these patterns: an infinite depth of human experience continuously compressed into durable memetic code.

I felt inspired by this idea and by the people I was learning about. I specifically admired those, who in their time and place, were able to identify the central defining issue of their time. They didn’t do what others were doing. They didn’t by default pursue the status games of their era. They sought out what I call Zeros.  

Schopenhauer drew this distinction: 

> Talent hits a target no one else can hit. (First principle thinking)

> Genius hits a target no one else can see. (Zeroth principle thinking)

I wondered:
> what will be the Zero of my lifetime? 
> what is currently invisible yet will be the only thing history will see? 
> can I find it and build it? 

I’ve been pursuing this goal since I was 21 years old. Without having any real talent, struggling as a student, having a humble upbringing, and no world connections, I set a goal of becoming independently wealthy by age 30. Then, with money, I reasoned, I’d set my focus on becoming a Zero detective and a Zero builder. 

At age 34, I sold Braintree Venmo in 2013 for $800M, making $300M of that. 

It was now time to become a zero detective.

The problem was that I was cooked as a human. The fourteen years of entrepreneurship, young children, existentially wrestling with my spirituality, and a challenging relationship left me chronically depressed, overweight, inflamed, recently divorced, and without meaning. First, I’d have to rebuild myself to stabilize. Health became my stabilization. I didn't know it then, but the thing I did to survive would turn out to be the thing I was looking for.

I obsessively got to work searching for a Zero. I became a voracious reader and thought about it constantly. I hosted a dozen dinners across the U.S., posing the question to attendees, “Imagine we’re in 2050 and life is extraordinary, what did we focus on in 2016 to make that happen?” I’d carefully write down everyone’s ideas and then after the dinner series, I put them down on a piece of paper, drew a box around them, and then told myself I couldn’t do anything inside the box.

Still, I couldn’t see, feel or hear a Zero. 

I then did a thought experiment that did it for me. I imagined being present in the year 2500 and sat there listening to them converse. They were talking about homo sapiens who lived in the early 21st century and they expressed their gratitude saying “We are grateful for homo sapiens of the 21st century who did __________ and __________.”

What do they say? 

What would survive 500 years of compression? 

I thought about this question for years.

Then one day the answer came to me, they say: “We are grateful for homo sapiens of the 21st century who gave birth to superintelligence and figured out they’d no longer die.” 

Our century compressed into two artifacts.

Superintelligence will be built whether or not I’m around. The other artifact was wide open. It would be a turning point in intelligent life. Transitioning from everyone inevitably dies (YOLO) to we are the first generation who won’t die. Changing everything about how we think about life and death, other people, the planet and our precious, fragile existence. 

Don’t Die is the Zero.

A tectonic shift in human values from being willing to kill themselves and others for power, wealth and status, to valuing existence itself above all other rewards. 

Wanting to live is the most ordinary desire a human has, which makes it a strange thing to call invisible. Very few actually want to die, at least today. Yet almost nobody organizes their life around not dying because for all of history it was unachievable. It makes more rational sense to pursue immediate hedonic, status and power objectives and to lean on the elaborate philosophies the species has made to make peace with death.

The era of Don’t Die will commence in 2030. New age reversal therapies will emerge and AI automation will run our lives, removing the biggest blockers of health: discipline and effort. Death acceptance will vanish as fast as body positivity did with GLP-1s.

(The irony here is that if Don’t Die is a Zero, and it comes to pass, then the 90% compression that has been the rule may stop being the rule.)

Kate and I are building for this. 

We do serious experimentation on health. 
We are performance artists.
We are memetic representations.
We are building a philosophy and ideology.
We are building the infrastructure for the species to turn its attention and power to Don’t Die.

If you’ve ever felt inspired, like me, by people of the past, who were willing to be hated, ridiculed, and dismissed in their pursuit of a Zero, the above should give you motivation. You will have to suffer through a prolonged period trying to find and build a Zero but the reward is being of service to the long arc of intelligent existence in this part of the galaxy.

author: hamandcheese
quoted_text:
1) The generative AI piece is simply not that defensible. The more photoshop, say, is just a canvas for generated outputs, the lower the value prop of the underlying software stack.
2) Adobe's revenue is overwhelmingly from pro and business subscriptions. Amateurs are more price sensitive and rarely pay $50 / month for the full creative suite, especially when there's Firefly or any of their free competitors like canva, wix, capcut, etc.
3) same goes for their video and web editing tools. If AI can auto-edit my podcast or magazine layout, generate a beautiful web page from nothing, and do video compositing with automatic lighting and tracking, why do I need a bunch of bloated software? Of course, in the near term, Illustrator, Premiere, Figma, After Effects, etc. still provide vastly more extensibility for their power users doing more complex projects. Nonetheless, their subscription base is cross-subsidized by the long tail of subscribers who just need to edit t shirt logos, restaurant menus, landing pages, wedding photos, etc. A similar dynamic played out in the translation market when Google Translate et al. knocked out the long tail of simple translation jobs that paid the bills for the people translating the great works of literature. There will be a niche who derive large and growing value from Adobe products even as their overall revenues decline.

Abstract is winding down.

Starting today, all of @IglooInc's focus will go towards taking Pudgy Penguins, Pudgy NFTs, and $PENGU to the next level.

When we acquired Frame in the summer of 2024, the vision was to build the blockchain for consumer crypto. Pudgy Penguins had shown us what it meant to reach the masses, and we believed we could bring that same approach to building a chain.

Abstract achieved a lot in a short period of time; we built the Portal and AGW, onboarded major global brands, amassed over 300 million transactions, and grew a vibrant onchain ecosystem. 

The journey became stifled by the lack of a DeFi ecosystem, insufficient liquidity, minimal institutional cross-over, and prohibitively high costs that impeded growth in winning areas.

Unknown to most, Igloo, Inc. had been funding Abstract over the last 18 months.

After losing tens of millions of dollars over two years, building consumer products, assembling an all-star team, onboarding some of the biggest brands in the world, and building a community of millions, we still had not found product-market fit.

In combination with the market's reduced appetite for what we had built and not being able to find a scalable path forward, we could no longer justify taking from the Pudgy Penguins business.

Igloo, Inc. has always been a community-first company. Even after losing 8 figures, we could have launched a token or pursued an ICO.

Ultimately we decided against this. A token only works if there is something driving demand to it, and launching a token that we don’t have conviction in would have been a disservice to our community.

The entire team at Abstract has worked tirelessly with a tremendous amount of passion to make the consumer crypto vision come true. I cannot fault a single one of them for this outcome.

To the Abstract community, I want to thank all of you for sticking by our side on this long journey and for continuing to champion us. You supported us through all of the ups and downs, and I wish the result could have been different.

There will be many that will find satisfaction in seeing this shut down, and that is fine. I take a great amount of pride in having the ambition to venture into the chain business, notoriously one of the most difficult to make work, and the only regret I have is not being able to celebrate a win alongside the Abstract community.

As we wind down Abstract, our full focus shifts to making Pudgy Penguins into the global & cultural phenomenon I know it can become. 

Return to Pudgy Penguins.
