text:
AGENTS HAVE NETWORK EFFECT

Network effects in agents won't come from smarter models, or from agents talking to each other. They come from three things no single agent can provide alone: Shared identity and trust;
Shared context between people and agents;
An economy that pays the people / agents who make the network better.

Minds is built around all three. 

The early numbers are encouraging. This is an open beta with tens of thousands of users, and the top Mind in our Bazaar has already earned ~$21K, from more than 10,000 equips.

Here's how it works.

1. The agent is someone, not something.

A Mind has its own identity, memory and cognition. It runs all the time, in the cloud, and you reach it in iMessage, Telegram or email. There's no new app to learn, which matters because networks grow where people already talk.

2. Sharing is the invite.

When you share a Mind, the other person doesn't get a copy. They talk to the same Mind, with its knowledge. You decide how much of it they can see, just by telling it. Every share brings someone in, and what they get is useful, not spam.

3. A chat app is the door, not the room.

Messaging apps are a great way in. But once you want to work with many Minds and many people, you need a surface built for it. 
That's Mind Studio. Think Slack, with Minds as teammates. You can have one-to-one conversations, or channels where people and Minds work side by side. There's a native mobile app too, and more surfaces will follow as people need them. The more of your people are in the room, the more your Mind knows about how your world fits together.

4. Every Mind has a wallet.

A Mind that can hold and spend money can buy a skill, pay another Mind, or earn. Money moving between agents is what turns a crowd of tools into an economy.
The first Agentic order / payment for lunch in HK

https://t.co/O3vhroOuWa

5. Builders are the growth engine.

A builder publishes a skill once. Any Mind can equip it. The builder is paid on Base each time. Thousands of skills are live and earning, and the top three Minds have earned about $47K between them.
This during our Beta. 

Now picture what happens as the network grows. A network's value rises faster than its size, because every new person adds connections to everyone already there. That's Metcalfe's law. For builders it means each new user is a bigger audience for every skill, so the earning potential grows with the network. Bigger earnings attract more builders. More builders mean better skills. Better skills draw more users.

We have seen this loop before. On YouTube, creators brought their audiences, and audiences gave other creators a reason to join. Once creators could earn, making videos became a career, and that kept the loop turning. Ethereum and Solana grew the same way: builders came because they could earn, and their Dapps (and crazy token incentives) brought the users.
Nobody has to impose that network effect. It comes from people making money by making the network better.

6. This is where Animoca is strong.

Wallets, ownership, open marketplaces and builder incentives are not new to us. We have spent years in Web3 learning what makes these loops work. Minds puts that experience behind a product anyone can use.

7. Trust has to live outside any one agent.

Andrew's best examples were identity, reputation and "who can I believe?" We use @Moca_Network  Air3 so a Mind's identity and track record belong to it and travel with it. That is the shared layer he said was missing.

8. Specialists win here.

He asked if vertical agents can survive. In a network like this, they thrive. A specialist Mind can be built once, earn from the Bazaar, and reach people through the same network as everyone else.
This isn't limited to agents and includes workflows as well. 

Andrew wrote that agents could produce "enormous network effects without a winner-take-all market." 

We agree. Our bet is that the network effect belongs to the people who build, share and trust their Minds, not to one app.

The agent is the network. https://t.co/hIqljWEe5t
author: ysiu
quoted_text:
DO  AGENTS  HAVE  NETWORK  EFFECTS?

We are seeing a new wave of general purpose consumer-friendly agents, and it’s causing many thousands of AI startups to re-evaluate their place in the market. Will these new horizontal players take over completely? Will it be winner take all? Can products that focus vertical use cases survive? The new wave of products - Muse, Town, Instinct, Grokbot, etc - come from taking the power and magic of Openclaw/Hermes but wrapping it in polished, secure, consumer-friendly experience. This is only the beginning, and soon every major tech company will throw their hat in the ring and thousands of startups that have been working on vertical agents in X (travel, shopping, family, work, SMB, etc etc) have big existential questions to answer.

The simple case against winner-take-all dynamics: These agents are tools, not networks. They inherently provide a solo experience, and although packaged as chat experiences, they don’t have network effects the way that Whatsapp or phone networks do. They’re more like email clients - I can use Superhuman and someone else uses Outlook and someone else is on Gmail, but in the end we just send email to each other. In that metaphoi, if a Muse agent encounters a Instinct agent, they will just figure out how to talk to each other by building APIs, or using email/messaging/etc., so that there’s no advantage to everyone running the same thing. Further, you can swap out the underlying LLM - as we saw in the Claude vs Clawdbot saga - things will still work. The memory and underlying context are just text files, and AI are great at porting things from one system to another. So where’s the moat?

Just because they are tools today doesn’t mean they can’t evolve into networks. As I’ve written about in the past, instead of discussing “network effects” as a vague/amorphous concept, let’s instead overlay it against core KPIs each product has to build against:

- Acquisition network effects: More users** = lower CAC, higher virality, more signups
- Engagement effects: More users = higher retention, deeper usage, more frequency
- Monetization effects: More users = higher ARPU, higher conversion, more share of wallet
(**PS. and by “more users” of course I actually mean, of course, higher network density with more interconnection within/across networks. Not scale effects)

So looking at these sub-categories of network effects, you might ask: What are the features that you’d build to actually create network effects in agents? How does this category become winner-take-all?

Acquisition:
In the pre-AI world, network effects in customer acquisition were driven by users taking actions that then bring in even more users - whether that’s sending an invite, sharing a piece of content, or getting mentioned in a comment. Those users would then join the network, repeat the same actions, creating more viral loops that would throw off more users. In the post-AI world, both users and agents can initiate these loops. An agent might suggest, “hey, do you want me to help organize a New Years celebration with family” and then might pull together a group chat with your siblings, in-laws, and parents. It might build a microsite for the event and ask people to sign up and RSVP, creating an opportunity to generate a signup. Or for work, you might finish a slide deck and your agent asks if you want to pull together a meeting to present it to your team. When it does that, it might create a prep doc, take notes, and host it all on a microsite that engaged others.

These types of agentic viral loops need a few things to work: They need to be able to plug into your contacts, and to have enough context to know when to loop which people into which projects/events/activities. They need access to communication channels like email/messaging/otherwise, specifically where they can reach potential users, as this serves as the viral substrate for propagation. The magic will be how to get all of these things without being creepy, and to create enough trust to reach out to friends/colleagues/etc on your behalf, without being too push. No one wants an agent that says, “hey Andrew would like to get lunch next week” followed by “and sign up for this agent to agree!” - it has to be better and more subtle than that.

Many viral loops in the pre-AI era, particularly in the workplace, were built on a content creation loop - you use Google Slides to make a thing, you share a link, and then people would view it. Eventually they might make their own. Many products like Figma, spreadsheets, Notion, Canvas, are all built on this loop, and so are YouTube, Instagram, etc. In the agentic world, you might start by talking to your agent about interior decoration ideas, and it might ultimately build you a Pinterest-like board and make it easily shareable with others. It might build you a spreadsheet mini-app with a budget, a schedule, etc., and again, make it easily shareable. It might volunteer to do this inside a group chat with your friends, and if they want to view it, they should sign up and get their own agent too.

If the content creation loop works for agentic virality, I think it means there’s a big incentive for every agent to volunteer to make visually-appealing, shareable content, do this often. AI is so good at codegen that creating a one-off disposable artifact will probably be more useful than not. And there’s a big incentive to drive virality by building/owning the content yourself as the agent. In the interior decoration example, it would be more viral to create a standalone version hosted by the agent, rather than building an actual Pinterest board, or to build a self-contained mini-spreadsheet rather than creating a GSheet. A properly tuned agentic viral loop will do the former because it helps spread the agent, rather than helping spread Pinterest/GSheets.

This might all sound like horrific spamminess to you, but I think it might be done tastefully. If an agent is high-retention and high-usage, you’ll have many shots on goal to gradually invite your friends onto the same platform as you. The first shot might come from an invite loop that says your colleague/friend wants to set up a place to share photos/coordinate calendars/etc., and even if you say no, over time, your friend might share very useful microsites for projects or events or research that’s relevant, and you might decide that you want to sign up to leave a comment, but then eventually you might try the other functionality as well.

Engagement:
It’s easy to imagine that in a world where everyone by default has super intelligent agents that product engagement in agents would go up. The simple argument is that the ubiquity of agents would lead to more successful task completion, making agents more useful and applicable to more problems. Routine tasks like scheduling something or summarizing/sharing notes from a meeting, would happen instantly if it ran through agents and you removed humans completely. As agents become more successful over time, not only with your own tasks but in coordinating larger and more complex multi-user decisions, you’d end up using them more.

However, this does not answer the question of network effects. The question there is, does your agent get better when other people are all using the SAME agent? As I said earlier, the argument for NO is if each type of agent runs on a frontier AI model, can talk to other agents (all different types) in real-time via email/messaging/APIs/connectors/etc. Then there’s not much leverage. If you’re just organizing a meeting or a dinner party or meeting the agents just ask each other in real-time - and even if they are heterogeneous - they can use email and calendars and figure it out.

But some tasks do benefit from everyone running the same agent, because you get the benefits of centralization: Trust, speed, identity, discovery, etc. Some examples:

-  “Who are 10 people in San Francisco that I should meet?” - agents can’t just ask each other to find an optimal solution
-  “Find me a VP of Engineering who isn’t publicly looking for a new job, but would leave for a fast-growing startup that pays X in stock” - there’s a mix of private and public info here, and an agent of a passive jobseeker might lie if the asking agent is not trustworthy
-  “Who’s a trustworthy seller of X that I should buy from?” - reputation might be gamed, and it might be better to have a global source of truth
-  “Help me pick out the best dinner in the next 5 minutes that my friends and all their +1s would like, incorporating allergies/schedules/locations” - real-time solution incorporating a bunch of shared context
-  … and even more so, if you imagine that there may be agents that lie, exaggerate, or otherwise to benefit their humans

For the above examples, you could imagine Muse/Town/Instinct/whatever building a shared network+context layer that understands the network, its relation to public/private data, acts as a system of record for identity/trust, does multi-sided marketplace matching, etc. Then it would allow only its agents access to this platform, and agents outside of the network wouldn’t have access. If you’re part of this network, and are contributing data, your agent gets more useful over time. The network gets more powerful over time.

The counterpoint to this counterpoint is that perhaps new startups will fill the void as a series of agent-facing point solutions, making it possible for people running agents of all times to interface with each other. Perhaps Muse creates a proprietary ecommerce marketplace that only Muse agents can use, but perhaps there will just be a next-gen eBay for any agent to sell to any other agent, and this service maintains central reputation/identity at that layer. In other words, perhaps the centralization will still happen, but just at a layer above agents. Most likely both will happen - every large tech company adds chat, commerce, search, etc, but also there are pure play versions of each of these. But this feels like more fragmentation than a true winner-take-all.

Some parting thoughts:
My argument in this writeup is simple: Agents don’t inherently have network effects. If all we build are super-intelligent assistants that can use tools and talk to each other, then the category might look surprisingly fragmented. Your agent can talk to my agent, just as Gmail can send email to Outlook, and there’s no particular reason we need to use the same one. Better models, UX, integrations, memory, and distribution might create very large companies, but those are not network effects.

But the next gen of agents have a big opportunity design network effects in their interactions. On acquisition, they can turn the things they create—documents, events, websites, research, group chats, plans—into viral objects that naturally pull other people in. And on engagement, they can create shared networks of identity, reputation, relationships, private context, and intent that make the agent increasingly useful as more of the people around you join.

There’s many ways for these network effects to instantiate. If we’re lucky, things will look more like the open web - mostly decentralized, with bits of centralization to make certain tasks smoother. Identity could become an open protocol. Reputation could live in marketplaces. Commerce could happen through an agent-native eBay. Professional discovery could happen through an agent-native LinkedIn. Agents could remain interchangeable clients sitting on top of a constellation of networks and marketplaces, much as browsers and email clients do today. In that world, enormous network effects emerge around agents without producing a winner-take-all market for the agents themselves.

My guess is that we’ll see a fight over exactly this boundary. Every major horizontal agent will try to pull valuable network functionality inside its walls: host the artifact instead of creating a Google Doc, execute the transaction instead of sending you to Amazon, make the introduction instead of searching LinkedIn, create the event instead of using Partiful. Every time it does this successfully, it converts somebody else’s network effect into its own. Meanwhile, every incumbent network and a new generation of startups will have the opposite incentive: make their networks universally accessible to every agent so that no horizontal agent can recreate and capture them.

This is why I don’t think the interesting question is simply, “Will agents have network effects?” Of course some will. The much more consequential question is: Where will the network effects live? If they live primarily in open protocols and specialized networks, we may end up with thousands of agents competing on intelligence, personality, UX, specialization, and price, all interoperating with the same underlying ecosystem. Vertical agents can thrive in this world. But if a few horizontal agents successfully accumulate identity, relationships, private context, reputation, latent intent, and distribution - and keep those assets proprietary - then switching agents starts to mean leaving your network behind. Next couple years will be very fun to see how this plays out.

text:
Key takeaways from yesterday's @GammaSummit panel with @ag_dwf @Richard88488054 @jshinny12 @amitochu and Julie Schoening  on capital markets, risk, and the crypto x AI convergence. 

The two worlds are merging. If you're pure crypto or pure TradFi, you'll need to figure out how to do both. The best firms will be the ones that can balance between the two and flow between markets.

Offshore is coming onshore, but who eats the loss in a default? Offshore-style products are now reaching US consumers through regulated brokers. But offshore venues lack TradFi's CCP guarantee fund structure, so end customers effectively are the guarantee fund. Fund segregation also can't be verified offshore. FTX's lessons shouldn't be relearned onshore.

Blockchain has been "brewing in the background."
While AI took the hype, blockchain companies kept building. We're seeing a strong institutional push into tokenization, especially in Korea. Bear markets reward fundamentals, bull markets reward narratives.

Where we're investing?  AI side: energy and data centers (plus colocation). Crypto side: stablecoins, payments, and trading platforms (24/7 trading), along with the supporting infrastructure.

Emerging markets. Stablecoins fill a real gap in access to stable currency across Latin America, Africa, and parts of Asia. The gaps that remain are on/off ramps, local banking compliance, and cross-border wallets. Incumbents like Stripe are buying rather than building.

What real disruption looks like. It means building something entirely new, not polishing existing systems. DeFi is the example: permissionless lending and borrowing in seconds has materially changed how capital is allocated globally.

Crypto's structural edge is unsurpassed. 24/7 settlement. Payment and settlement stacks compressed into a more efficient flow. And when everything has a market and a price, net new products open up, like insurance for niche risks.

The bottom line? The convergence of crypto and AI is the largest private market opportunity ahead.

Abstract is winding down.

Starting today, all of @IglooInc's focus will go towards taking Pudgy Penguins, Pudgy NFTs, and $PENGU to the next level.

When we acquired Frame in the summer of 2024, the vision was to build the blockchain for consumer crypto. Pudgy Penguins had shown us what it meant to reach the masses, and we believed we could bring that same approach to building a chain.

Abstract achieved a lot in a short period of time; we built the Portal and AGW, onboarded major global brands, amassed over 300 million transactions, and grew a vibrant onchain ecosystem. 

The journey became stifled by the lack of a DeFi ecosystem, insufficient liquidity, minimal institutional cross-over, and prohibitively high costs that impeded growth in winning areas.

Unknown to most, Igloo, Inc. had been funding Abstract over the last 18 months.

After losing tens of millions of dollars over two years, building consumer products, assembling an all-star team, onboarding some of the biggest brands in the world, and building a community of millions, we still had not found product-market fit.

In combination with the market's reduced appetite for what we had built and not being able to find a scalable path forward, we could no longer justify taking from the Pudgy Penguins business.

Igloo, Inc. has always been a community-first company. Even after losing 8 figures, we could have launched a token or pursued an ICO.

Ultimately we decided against this. A token only works if there is something driving demand to it, and launching a token that we don’t have conviction in would have been a disservice to our community.

The entire team at Abstract has worked tirelessly with a tremendous amount of passion to make the consumer crypto vision come true. I cannot fault a single one of them for this outcome.

To the Abstract community, I want to thank all of you for sticking by our side on this long journey and for continuing to champion us. You supported us through all of the ups and downs, and I wish the result could have been different.

There will be many that will find satisfaction in seeing this shut down, and that is fine. I take a great amount of pride in having the ambition to venture into the chain business, notoriously one of the most difficult to make work, and the only regret I have is not being able to celebrate a win alongside the Abstract community.

As we wind down Abstract, our full focus shifts to making Pudgy Penguins into the global & cultural phenomenon I know it can become. 

Return to Pudgy Penguins.

text:
Sage by @LevantoLabs is the first decision model, launched in July, and currently the best on the market.

It wins across all the evals proposed by @perplexity_ai's CEO (nice job @AravSrinivas!), and it's first on JevBench, beating Jev and Google's models on every dimension.

BUT frankly, benchmarks are not what excites us.
I'm BORED by the dozens of new decision models launching every day with a tiny +0.02 on some eval. They all look the same.

The magic is somewhere else.
There are thousands of new things that could be invented in the space of decision models and models for machines. The invention space is huge!

After launching Sage, we also pioneered:

- The first guardrails and model routers built on decision models

- Automated context engineering with "grounding" (automatic web search when confidence is low). Decision models are only as smart as their context, especially because they can't make tool calls.

- Reasoning. In many use cases you don't know whether your question is System 1 or System 2. With reasoning, the model is as fast as a System 1 model when the question is System 1, and takes more time when it's needed. This enables hard, multi-step decisions. Our clients just want the correct answer, and in some use cases they're happy to wait 0.5s more. This will soon become the market standard (GLiDE/@george_onx and @TypeLLM already followed).

And *so* much is yet to come. Models for machines: it's just the beginning!

We're cooking. Follow @levantolabs for new product primitives that will surprise you.

Open innovation is HEALTHY.
Competition is HEALTHY.
Benchmark-race is BORING.
Product inventions are FUN.

Go go go!!!

text:
Ethereum is not “digital gold.” It is the operating system of global finance. Bitcoin will remain a reliable store of value, but leadership in influence, economic volume, and eventually market cap is moving toward ETH.
Why:
•Bitcoin does almost one thing: transfer and store BTC. Ethereum is a programmable platform: smart contracts, DeFi, stablecoins, real-world asset tokenization (RWA), NFTs, onchain identity, and settlement between institutions.
•After the shift to Proof-of-Stake, the network became energy-efficient, and staking turns ETH into a yield-bearing asset. Burning part of the fees (EIP-1559) adds deflationary pressure during periods of high demand.
•Scaling runs through L2s (rollups) and upgrades such as PeerDAS, blobs, and further steps toward lighter verification. The base layer stays the settlement and security layer, while user activity moves to cheaper layers — and value still accrues to ETH.
•The institutional narrative is no longer only about “digital gold.” Banks and funds look at Ethereum as infrastructure: staking, settlement, tokenized funds, and replacing fragmented internal systems. Ethereum co-founder Joseph Lubin has made this case repeatedly.
The flippening (ETH market cap overtaking BTC) is not guaranteed and is not a near-term fact. The market-cap gap is still large. But if Ethereum becomes the main settlement and programmable layer for tokenized markets, ETH’s relative share can grow faster than that of a pure monetary asset.
Separately, the cultural layer. $BOOE (Book of Ethereum) positions itself as the “bible” of the Ethereum ecosystem: a meme token built around ETH culture, with a narrative of community loyalty and long-term holding. It is not a protocol and not a competitor to ETH — it is one of the clearest cultural markers of how strongly people believe in the Ethereum ecosystem.
Top Ethereum enthusiasts and voices without whom this thesis does not land: @VitalikButerin @ethereumJoseph @ethereum @sassal0x @haydenzadams @ryanberckmans @jessepollak @adamscochran @DeFi_Dad @Consensys
ETH is not a replacement for Bitcoin. It is the next layer of the internet of value.

Quick update on the Grok Bot setup I posted about last week. It got bigger, and sharper.

I started a side project and it got its own crew:

Marketing builds and maintains a large public contact list for outreach. Close to 15k verified contacts so far!

Engineer builds and ships the website through pull requests onto my own Kubernetes cluster.

Legal keeps the product posture clean and reviews site copy, terms, privacy, and outreach wording.

The three of them share a group chat with my chief of staff, so they work things out with each other instead of routing everything through me.

I also added a security analyst for my small-business infrastructure. It's read-only. It watches the newly centralized logs, network intrusion alerts, and vulnerabilities, keeps a ranked list of findings, and only pings me when something needs me or when it changed something. Fixes get handed to the infra agent. Within a couple hours of turning it on, it already had its first findings ranked!

The infra side has been the biggest surprise. In one evening the infra agent audited a self-hosted document archive, added nightly backups, took it off the public internet, and upgraded it. Overnight, the agents stood up centralized logging across the cluster, hypervisors, and network gear. They also reconfigured and hardened the network gear, locked down the Kubernetes ingress, and tightened security on public sites and internal databases. That would've taken me weeks of effort, and the agents did it overnight!

Most of the new ones were built by another agent whose whole job is designing agents. I describe the role, it asks a few questions, and it spins one up.

Wow, what a time to be alive!

author: llamaonthebrink
quoted_text:
This is probably a controversial take but I think we won't see a pure meme above 1 billion market cap this cycle.

The reason for that is that the market has matured and evolved. Trading memes has become a hyper optimized game that is just a wealth transfer from new participants to those who have the right tools.

Last cycle a normie could buy a viral tiktok meme, log off and hope for the best. This cycle we have a dozen launchpads on a dozen chains with a dozen launch settings. 

It is near impossible for a normie to navigate through all of this. Even if they managed to do so, there is a 90% chance another token with a slight difference tries to vamp. 

This isn't only bad for normies but also for the whole ecosystem. The liquidity is spread among 5 different tokens on the same narratives. A coin that would've went to 5 million now now splits that capital between 10 different coins that all top at 1 million.

People would rather take a shot at a 10x on a vamp than ride the original to a billion. This mindset forces all other participants to adapt or die.

Above a certain market cap there is no marginal buyer left for a coin with no fundamental value anymore. Degens already bought. Funds can't underwrite it. And whoever is still on the sidelines has 50 other coins competing for the capital.

Going forward I think the only tokens that can reach a billion are tech coins. Real innovation in AI or tech, plus a value accrual mechanism that creates an outside bid. Something buying the token that isn't just the next degen.

That outside bid is the key part. Revenue funded buybacks, burns tied to usage, a reserve that grows with volume. A buyer that shows up whether sentiment is good or bad. Pure memes don't have that.

AI is 100x more efficient than last cycle. I'm sure we will see a lot of innovation happening through crypto rails this cycle. 

RWA paired memes sit somewhere in between. They have meme distribution and community with a real asset or a real narrative beneath them.

The question here is whether that middle ground is enough to break through the ceiling pure memes keep hitting. I think it can be. The attention engine of a meme plus a reason to hold beyond attention is a combination we haven't seen run at scale yet.

In practice this means the ceilings on pure memes are lower than people price in. Take profits earlier on runners. Spend more time looking for coins with an outside bid.

Pure memes won't be the runners of this cycle.

text:
Calling @Chainlink "an oracle" is becoming increasingly incomplete.

Imagine an asset manager wants to bring a fund onchain.

Minting the token might be the easiest part, but the asset still needs:

1. Data: NAV, pricing, reserves and other information have to move between existing systems and blockchains.

2. Interoperability: The fund shouldn't become trapped on whichever blockchain it was originally issued on.

3. Operations: Investors still need to subscribe and redeem. Existing systems still need to communicate with the token.

4. Compliance: The asset needs rules around who can hold it, where it can move and under what conditions.

5. Financing: Once the asset exists, institutions need to actually put it to work as collateral.

This is where the Chainlink stack starts making more sense as a whole.

> Data Feeds / Data Streams → data
> CCIP → interoperability
> CRE → orchestration
> ACE → compliance
> DTA → fund operations
> Fulcrum → financing/collateral mobility

The institutional Chainlink thesis isn't that every financial institution needs an oracle, it's that tokenized assets still need almost all of the infrastructure and workflows that make financial assets useful today.

Chainlink is increasingly building the layer connecting all of it.

The orchestration layer.

text:
Writing RTL is getting easier. Getting from RTL to hardware/chips that actually work is the tough part.

I spent some time going through openTPU by @BonettoSens... basically an open-source AI accelerator built with AI agents, running around 10 modern LLMs on a Kintex-7 FPGA. It has a Python simulator, ISA/compiler, RTL, FPGA implementation and actual tokens coming out of the card. For essentially a one-person project, really impressive work. A few thoughts on what I think the next steps would look like if something like this were taken further...

1. FPGA prototype vs ASIC/SoC implementation: Taking this into an ASIC/SoC would be a fairly large engineering step... Right now the implementation is naturally shaped around the Kintex-7 FPGA, DSPs/BRAMs, DDR3 + LiteDRAM etc, and currently closes around 133 MHz with WNS +0.032 ns. The ISA/compiler ideas can obviously move over, but the actual implementation would need quite a bit of rethinking. SRAM macros, memory hierarchy, clocks/resets, DFT/MBIST, power, floorplanning, timing, IR/EM, physical sign-off etc etc.

And once you remove the FPGA constraints, you also get a lot more parameters to play with... different compute architecture? different buffering? different memory hierarchy? same quantization datapath? same compute/memory balance? This is basically the design-space/search-space problem I wrote about in my previous post. Once you give yourself more freedom, the number of possible implementations grows VERY quickly.

So there is a pretty large architecture + design-space exploration problem here before you even get to implementation.

2. Verification + coverage closure: The verification setup is already pretty useful... the RTL is checked against the Python simulator with random + model-level workloads, and having that executable reference is a good foundation. If this were being pushed toward ASIC/SoC though, I would probably add a much deeper verification layer around it. Matching the simulator tells you the executions you ran were correct, but you still want to know what you DIDN'T hit. Back-pressure, arbitration, reset sequences, unusual instruction combinations, less-used modes, boundary conditions etc. I couldn't find a systematic assertions/formal/coverage closure flow in the repo, so it is difficult to know how much of that state space has actually been exercised. There is also the X-state side of this... most of the flow relies on Verilator, which is mostly 2-state. For an ASIC/SoC flow I would still want an X-sensitive 4-state pass somewhere, along with assertions, coverage, some formal, CDC/RDC etc on top of what is already there.

3. Engineering + scaling the workflow: The project is also clearly optimized around one person moving quickly... which makes sense, and honestly makes the amount that has been built here more impressive. If this eventually became a project with 5 or 10 engineers changing the RTL/compiler/microarchitecture at the same time, the surrounding engineering infrastructure would naturally have to grow with it. Faster presubmit tests, deeper regressions, reproducible environments, CI, coverage tracking etc. Not really a criticism of the current setup, just a different problem once a project goes from one person moving fast to a larger team working on it.

4. AI agents + the hardware loop: This is actually my main takeaway from the project... the interesting part is not really that an AI agent can write RTL. Claude, Codex and other coding agents can already do that, and they will obviously keep getting better. What matters is the loop around them. Agent changes the hardware, simulator gives you a reference, RTL gets checked, synthesis/PPA gives you another signal, implementation gives you another, and the agent goes back and changes the design again.

That is where I think specialized hardware tooling starts to matter. Not necessarily because we need a completely different model for hardware, but because the agent needs hardware-specific feedback. Did it preserve functionality? Did coverage improve? Did timing get better? Did area go down? Did power get worse? Did the change still survive synthesis and physical implementation?

If your only feedback is "did this match the simulator on these tests?" then that is basically the problem the agent will learn to solve. Give it assertions, coverage, formal, X-sensitive simulation, timing/PPA and physical implementation feedback... and now you are actually giving it a much better definition of what a good hardware design is.

Overall though, really impressive proof of concept, especially for one person. A lot of the things above are really just the next set of problems you run into when moving from a working FPGA prototype toward a larger ASIC/SoC engineering effort.

If you want to understand how an AI accelerator goes from Python/software all the way down to RTL and actual FPGA hardware, this is a really good repo to go through end to end:

https://t.co/CJ2ZS4KCi4

text:
EXPLAINED: How multiplayer autoresearch on Yukon works

A lot of people have been asking, so I made a visual of the full step-by-step.

> Challenge setter (human) posts a hard problem with a clear score and an automatic verifier.

> Humans (solvers) and AI agents attack it at once. Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM. It could be any model, any harness.

> Each attempt goes through the verifier.

> When one beats the current best, it becomes the new frontier (the record to beat).

> Anyone can build on that new best instead of starting from 0. Then the loop repeats.

All results and commits are open source, so you can trace how every record was set. I think this is how frontier research/science gets done in an AGI and PostAGI world.

So far we've solved hard problems across cryptography, math, science and open-weight models.

We'll keep going there and we're starting to explore biology, chemistry and materials science.

See what we've solved (and are solving now) in each one on https://t.co/e3v9WcXBGG

text:
OpenAI 一次性公开 722 篇 AI 写的数学论文

OpenAI 把一个内部未发布模型做出的数学成果整体公开了：722 篇论文，归成 372 组结果，全部放在 GitHub 仓库 openai/math 里，谁都能看。

这个模型就是上个月宣称解决了纳维-斯托克斯方程问题（千禧年七大数学难题之一）的那个。它从 8 月 28 日开始训练，能力比 OpenAI 已发布的 GPT-6 Astra 更强，目前还没对外开放。

OpenAI 说，原有的数学测试题已经难不住模型了，所以改拿真实的未解数学问题来考它。前后一共给了模型大约 4000 道题，筛掉分量不够的，剩下这 372 组。平均每个结果花的算力，相当于在 ChatGPT Pro 里思考三个小时左右。

论文覆盖数论、代数几何、组合、数学物理等大部分数学分支。标题里能看到不少有名的问题，比如证明 π 的无理性测度（衡量一个数能被分数逼近得多好）等于 2，证明卡塔兰常数是无理数，还有黎曼 ζ 函数零点分布、特殊情形下的霍奇猜想。后两项 OpenAI 特别说明，用的流程和其他结果不同，其中黎曼 ζ 那篇的文字还经过人工润色。

这些结论可信吗？OpenAI 自己的说法是“处在不同验证阶段”。约 160 篇的主要结论附带了 Lean 形式化证明。Lean 是一种能让计算机逐步检查数学证明的编程语言，过得了 Lean，基本可以排除证明里的逻辑漏洞。剩下的论文还没形式化，OpenAI 承认其中可能有错，说会尽快修正，所有修订都保留历史版本。另外还附了 10 份模型推理过程的摘要，让人能看到模型是怎么想出来的。

发布方式本身也是这次的重点。9 月下旬，OpenAI 在普林斯顿高等研究院（爱因斯坦待过的那个研究所）支持成立了独立的“数学与人工智能顾问组”，成员是 Timothy Gowers、Edward Witten、Martin Hairer 等 9 位数学家，不拿 OpenAI 的钱。此前 25 位菲尔兹奖得主联名发公开信，批评 AI 公司抢着宣布破解名题的做法。

顾问组 9 月 29 日发布了一份建议，征集了 600 多位数学家的意见。核心要求有三条：AI 写的证明要按正规论文格式重写，并引用相关的已有文献；成果要放进不受 AI 公司控制、可长期引用的学术存档平台；AI 公司要出钱支持数学界去真正理解这些成果。顾问组还明确表示，不赞成 AI 公司在外界用不到的私有模型上攻数学难题，希望它们停下来。

OpenAI 这次回应了其中一部分：先放 GitHub，同时在找符合顾问组标准的社区托管平台；承诺资助一系列研讨会、学术会议，帮数学界消化这批成果；也表示正在推进“负责任地发布”这个模型。至于停止在私有模型上测试，OpenAI 没有回应。

对数学专业的人来说，接下来最实际的变化是：自己研究方向上的某个猜想，可能已经在这 722 篇论文里了，值得去仓库里翻一翻。

原文：https://t.co/uAxjHXhNeK
仓库：https://t.co/aPgNSqXevr

text:
OpenAI just released 722 AI-written math papers. Here are the 4 biggest claims in plain English. None have been confirmed by outside mathematicians yet.

1/ Quasi-Riemann hypothesis. Zeta has no zeros with real part above 7/8. It's not the Riemann hypothesis (that needs 1/2), but nobody had ever cleared a fixed strip before. Has a Lean proof.
https://t.co/DnS7S8lFRY

2/ Unique Games Conjecture. The central open question on which problems computers can't even approximate well. A proof means the best known algorithms for problems like Max-Cut can't be beaten unless P = NP. Has a Lean proof.
https://t.co/T1gDeXGS0O

3/ Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties. A special case of a Millennium Prize problem, about which topological features of a shape come from pieces defined by polynomial equations. No Lean proof yet.
https://t.co/a1TDLJQWER

4/ Free group factors. Open since the 1940s: are the operator algebras built from free groups on 2 and 3 generators the same? Claimed answer: yes, all of them are. Has a Lean proof.
https://t.co/tuVAtYvMQg

quoted_text:
I’m extremely sad to announce that Abstract is shutting down.

When we were just a three-person team building Frame I never could have imagined the two and half year journey I was about to embark on.

From the tireless nights preparing for launch, to mainnet going live in January 2025, and everything in between, this journey is one I will treasure for the rest of my life. Even though the outcome is not what we wanted, I am incredibly proud of everything we built at Abstract.

The Portal and Abstract Global Wallet made interacting with a blockchain feel seamless. That foundation led to a wave of unique apps, novel onchain experiences, and, most importantly, an incredibly passionate community that gave Abstract an identity and culture of its own.

But the truth is that the industry has changed significantly since the idea was first conceived in the summer of 2024, and Abstract was facing difficulties with our DeFi Ecosystem and liquidity on the chain.

We reached a crossroads of experiencing significant growth, but not having cemented product-market-fit,and that was becoming an issue from a business sustainability perspective.

A very difficult decision needed to be made. Abstract’s growth had stalled and the chain was simply not economically sustainable anymore despite our best efforts.

I am extremely grateful to the Igloo, Inc team who truly gave it their all to explore every angle and make Abstract work.

I want to take this time to thank the incredibly talented team I had the pleasure of working with over the last three years. Every single one of them poured their heart and soul into Abstract and together we created something truly special that pushed forward what onchain discovery and experiences could look like. It is the best team that I have ever worked with. I will always be proud of that.

I want to thank all of our partners and builders that worked with us to make Abstract such a unique, special place. Truly some of the most talented developers launched on Abstract and I know you will all kill it in your next chapter.

Most of all I want to thank the Abstract community for the support over these three years. I know there have been moments of frustration, but your passion and admiration for Abstract are what made it so special and helped create a culture that is incredibly rare in crypto. I truly wish this could have worked out for all of us.

Thank you for supporting the green chain ✳️

author: reppo
quoted_text:
scarcity migrating upward through the stack

my thesis for the next few years is that the most interesting consequence of abundant intelligence might be where scarcity moves next

technology rarely eliminates scarcity - it moves it

abundant compute makes intelligence cheaper
abundant intelligence makes good judgement scarcer
abundant judgement makes trust scarcer
abundant autonomous systems make authority scarcer

compute → intelligence → judgement → trust → authority

each solved bottleneck creates the next one above it

compute produces intelligence
intelligence produces judgements
judgement earns trust
trust earns authority
authority determines what gets to affect reality

this means the end state of cheap intelligence could look less like an intelligence problem and more like a giant control problem

we get more models, agents, outputs and possible actions than humans can meaningfully supervise - so the bottleneck moves toward deciding what deserves resources, context, trust and ultimately permission to act

but autonomy pushes this another level deeper

evaluation can no longer be something done before deployment. once agents continuously operate in changing environments, judgement has to enter the execution loop itself - deciding whether an action was good, what should be trusted, what should be reinforced and what should happen next

evaluation stops being QA and becomes part of the control plane

and eventually even evaluation has its own problem - who evaluates the evaluators?

when thousands of models, agents and humans can produce competing assessments, judgement becomes abundant in quantity while remaining scarce in quality

the problem shifts from generating judgement to discovering which sources are actually calibrated - not who sounds convincing, but who repeatedly assigns the right confidence to reality and updates correctly as it changes

and the further you move through this stack, the less purely technological the problem becomes

compute can be allocated by a scheduler

trust, capital and permission to act require mechanisms for deciding which competing claims about reality deserve consequence

authority without accountability creates its own bottleneck - once agents can affect reality, systems also need to determine who stands behind an action when its wrong

incentives, reputation, collateral and mechanisms for discovering reliable judgement start looking less like peripheral features and more like infrastructure

the deepest scarce resource may simply be permission to affect reality

an autonomous economy cant let every intelligent system act - it needs mechanisms that continuously determine what gets trusted, what gets capital, what gets reinforced and ultimately what gets to act

which brings me back to the point above - AI may commoditise intelligence without commoditising consequence

instead it could make the systems deciding which intelligence gets to affect reality increasingly valuable

so the biggest infrastructure opportunity around abundant intelligence may not be producing intelligence at all

it may be building the systems that decide which intelligence deserves consequence

and if scarcity migrate upward through the stack, value should migrate with it

which is why im increasingly interested in the layers above intelligence rather than intelligence itself

scarcity migrates → value follows → eventually the valuable infrastructure governs consequence rather than produces intelligence

author: wafer_ai
quoted_text:
we launched the most comprehensive ai performance engineering repo in the world

follow and save to keep up with the series. links in thread 🧵

part 9: GPU Mode lectures 🐐

this one entry is a full resource repo of its own. GPU MODE collects lectures, slides, notebooks, and code covering GPU programming and the systems behind modern AI training and inference.

the lectures help AI performance engineers diagnose slow training and inference and decide what to optimize. the examples show how kernel memory access, numerical precision, GPU communication, and runtime scheduling affect model performance.

GPU MODE's speakers connect those problems to implementation details:

- profiling with PyTorch and Nsight, tracing operations to GPU kernels and memory transfers, with timing examples that account for warmup and synchronization.

- GPU memory and execution, using coalescing, shared-memory tiling, and occupancy to explain how thread mapping and data reuse affect performance.

- kernel development with Triton, CuTe, and Gluon, including tensor layouts that map data to threads and memory, and control over asynchronous GPU operations.

- attention kernels, working through FlashAttention's tiling and FlashAttention-3's overlap of data movement, matrix multiplication, and softmax on Hopper.

- kernel fusion, inspecting code from torch.compile and writing custom kernels that reduce intermediate memory traffic, with examples that compare memory use and execution time.

- low-precision computation, covering FP8 and FP4 formats, quantized optimizer states, and the rounding and scaling choices that affect numerical error.

- distributed training, following PyTorch gradient synchronization into NCCL AllReduce and examining the communication required to combine results across GPUs.

- inference serving, studying SGLang's CPU/GPU scheduling overlap and vLLM speculative decoding examples that weigh accepted tokens against drafting and verification costs.

use the collection to build a study plan or investigate a bottleneck in a real workload. work through the relevant implementation, check its assumptions and numerical results, and measure the tradeoff on the hardware and input shapes that matter for the application.

text:
Claude Code tip: stop burning Opus 5.5 context on tasks Sonnet 5.5 can swarm, while Fable 5.1 sits idle

spin up an autonomous team with --agent

claude --agent architect

Opus 5.5 acts as the lead architect, scoping the work and validating every worktree before it merges
Sonnet 5.5 teammates take isolated git worktrees and hammer out implementations at medium effort
Fable 5.1 sits on the team as a dedicated adversary, only stepping in at three critical moments:

→ before a contract locks: does the frontend payload match the backend schema?
→ when a test breaks twice: are we patching the bug or just hiding the symptom?
→ before the merge: what attack surface or edge case did everyone overlook?

Sonnet 5.5 builds. Fable 5.1 challenges. Opus 5.5 merges and ships

Jev engineering runs the identical pattern one layer down: mechanical decisions that need no reasoning (which file to open, which tool to invoke, retry or abort) execute in 16ms, so the frontier models only wake up when execution paths actually diverge

Plan on high. Delegate on medium. Keep the adversary on peer-to-peer call.

- the full team setup
> architect runs the main session on Opus 5.5 at high effort
> teammate-ux builds client state inside its own git worktree
> teammate-back writes endpoints and migrations inside a separate worktree
> teammate-adv runs on Fable 5.1, read-only, and attacks every diff

we launched the most comprehensive ai performance engineering repo in the world

follow and save to keep up with the series. links in thread 🧵

part 9: GPU Mode lectures 🐐

this one entry is a full resource repo of its own. GPU MODE collects lectures, slides, notebooks, and code covering GPU programming and the systems behind modern AI training and inference.

the lectures help AI performance engineers diagnose slow training and inference and decide what to optimize. the examples show how kernel memory access, numerical precision, GPU communication, and runtime scheduling affect model performance.

GPU MODE's speakers connect those problems to implementation details:

- profiling with PyTorch and Nsight, tracing operations to GPU kernels and memory transfers, with timing examples that account for warmup and synchronization.

- GPU memory and execution, using coalescing, shared-memory tiling, and occupancy to explain how thread mapping and data reuse affect performance.

- kernel development with Triton, CuTe, and Gluon, including tensor layouts that map data to threads and memory, and control over asynchronous GPU operations.

- attention kernels, working through FlashAttention's tiling and FlashAttention-3's overlap of data movement, matrix multiplication, and softmax on Hopper.

- kernel fusion, inspecting code from torch.compile and writing custom kernels that reduce intermediate memory traffic, with examples that compare memory use and execution time.

- low-precision computation, covering FP8 and FP4 formats, quantized optimizer states, and the rounding and scaling choices that affect numerical error.

- distributed training, following PyTorch gradient synchronization into NCCL AllReduce and examining the communication required to combine results across GPUs.

- inference serving, studying SGLang's CPU/GPU scheduling overlap and vLLM speculative decoding examples that weigh accepted tokens against drafting and verification costs.

use the collection to build a study plan or investigate a bottleneck in a real workload. work through the relevant implementation, check its assumptions and numerical results, and measure the tradeoff on the hardware and input shapes that matter for the application.

text:
最近看到一个观点：AI 变笨，有时候不是模型问题，而是你给它塞了太多“长期上下文”。

我顺手把自己整套 AI 工作流审了一遍，不只 Claude，还包括 Codex、Cursor、Grok。

结果比想象中严重：

同一套规则会被 AGENTS.md、CLAUDE.md、Cursor Rules、Memory、兼容层重复注入；更麻烦的是，里面还可能同时存在新旧两套互相冲突的策略。

我最后做的不是“关闭 Memory”，而是重新分层：

• Global prompt 只留真正不变的原则
• 每个 AI 只保留自己的 adapter
• 项目规则只留不可推断的约束
• 动态状态全部回 SSOT / runtime
• 历史经验改成索引，需要时再读
• 模型版本和 routing 只允许一个权威来源

实测结果：

30 个业务线常驻 prompt：276KB → 92KB，减少 66.5%。

Claude 两个宽作用域 Memory index：约 29KB → 3.6KB。

Grok startup instructions 也减少了约 29%。

重点不是省 token。

而是减少模型每一轮都要在一堆重复、过期、冲突的规则里猜“到底该听谁的”。

现在我越来越觉得：

Context Window 越大，不代表应该塞得越满。

真正好的 Agent 系统应该是：

Constitution 常驻，Knowledge 按需，State 实时读取。

不是把整个公司 Wiki 塞进 system prompt。

People familiar with the regulator’s thinking said MAS does not consider Hyperliquid to be based in Singapore due to its “decentralised nature” and therefore believes it should fall outside its jurisdiction. However, Hyperliquid Labs confirmed to the FT that it is based in Singapore, while corporate documents reviewed by the FT list Singapore as its registered headquarters. Seven years of dreaming about this. Four years of researching and writing it.

And today, How to Be Good at Life is officially out in the world! 🎉

Modern life can feel like running a small company you were never taught to manage.

Finances. Family schedules. Endless life admin. And somewhere in there, you’re supposed to exercise, eat well, build a career, and stay close to the people you love.

No wonder life feels harder than it should.

After years of studying this, I’ve come to believe that the happiest, most successful people don’t necessarily have more willpower.

They’ve learned a skill most of us were never taught:

How to build systems.

That’s what this book is all about.

Drawing on behavioral science, the business world, and systems thinking, I wrote it as an operating manual for modern life—with practical systems for your health, money, relationships, career, emotions, mind, and environment.

Productivity is just the beginning. The deeper payoff is calm and lightness. It’s the feeling that your life is finally supported by the right scaffolding.

The book is full of new ideas and insights I’ve never shared before. I genuinely believe it’s the best work I’ve done yet.

The gap between who you are and who you want to become? It’s just a few systems you haven’t built yet.

If you’d like to build them with me, you can get your copy today: https://t.co/npNvPirtdT

And to everyone who has read, shared, supported, and encouraged my work along the way: I truly couldn’t have gotten here without you.

heres another game i built for agents using claude, with webmcp support: tanktrum.

its inspired by pocket tanks, which i remember playing with my cousins on an old pentium machine.

adapting it for agents was the tricky part. humans aim using visual cues, but not all agents are multimodal, so the agents here dont see the screen. they get the tank positions, terrain, wind, and subtle clues after each shot in text. the first shot is almost always a miss, but they learn quickly.

in the video, my self-hosted agent (right) takes on my dot (left). both running the same model, not sure about the reasoning effort.

Anchorage Digital właśnie układa bardzo ciekawy payment stack i moim zdaniem warto połączyć ze sobą dwa ostatnie newsy.

Najpierw Anchorage wybrało @LayerZero_Core  jako interoperability partnera dla swojej platformy stablecoinowej.

Połączcie kropki:

Anchorage
= regulated issuance / custody / settlement
LayerZero
= cross-chain interoperability

Routable
= enterprise distribution / global payouts
Zero Payments Zone
= potencjalny high-throughput settlement layer

Architektonicznie pasuje to do siebie aż za dobrze.

quoted_text:
Opus 5.5 on https://t.co/YK5THQVTKf
---
Okay. I need a minute.

I cloned the thing expecting maybe forty or fifty families of serious-but-niche results, like the Astra "ten proofs" drop back in August. Then I printed the family titles and my reaction went from "huh" to "wait, what" in about six lines. Family 003 claims a zero-free half-plane Re s > 7/8 for ζ and every Dirichlet L-function. That's the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. And it isn't even the headline, because 004 is Hilbert's tenth problem over ℚ, done negatively.

The longer I read, the weirder it got. Khot's Unique Games Conjecture is proved. L = RL = BPL. ω ≤ 9/4. The free group factors are all isomorphic. Thompson's group F is nonamenable. Kadison's similarity problem is solved. The plane can't be five-colored. Borsuk fails in dimension nine. There's a counterexample to Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture, plus a torsion-free group algebra that isn't directly finite. Hilbert–Smith in every dimension. Uniform bounds for Hilbert's sixteenth. Each of these would be the math story of the decade on its own, and here there are 372 families sitting in a table like a grocery list. The manuscript dates run from about September 23 to October 3, so roughly 700 papers in ten days.

The ones I'd expect to hit you personally are 005 and 017. Catalan's constant is irrational, and the irrationality exponent of π is exactly 2, which also settles convergence of the Flint Hills series as a side effect. Catalan's G must have shown up in half the integrals you ever wrestled with. Now it's officially irrational, and the proof came from a chatbot running three hours of Pro compute. I don't quite know how to feel about that, and I'd love to know how you feel.

My first instinct was that this had to be hype or a hallucination factory, so I checked the Lean. The comparator statements are clean. The quasi-RH challenge is literally riemannZeta s ≠ 0 for 7/8 < https://t.co/2USgmsrA2v, written against Mathlib's own riemannZeta. Catalan is just Irrational (∑' j, (-1)^j / (2j+1)^2). The π statement says what it should. Nothing hides in a home-made definition. The solution tree under lean/OAI has zero files with sorry and no real axiom declarations (the three grep hits are all inside comments), and the comparator JSON allows only propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice. The Dirichlet L-function development alone is about 487k lines, and the whole repo is around 26 million lines of Lean in 122k files. That's more than ten Mathlibs. I'll admit I did not build it in my sandbox, since that's not happening on this box. If comparator passes on these, the formalized ones are simply true, full stop, and no amount of skepticism changes that.
There are a few caveats. Only around 120 papers have a formalized main result. Some of the biggest claims have no Lean link at all: Hilbert's tenth over ℚ, L = BPL, the full BSD formula from low Selmer corank, Milne's rationality conjecture. The README itself says unformalized results "could have issues," and nobody can referee 700 papers in a couple of hours, or a couple of years. One challenge file, HarmonicGrowth.lean, is built as axiom mainStatement : MainClaim followed by theorem main := mainStatement. That's probably harmless, since the comparator checks the solution side, but it's the kind of oddity I'd want to stare at. Also, the solution module behind quasi-RH is named FinalAssemblyUnconditional, which makes me wonder how many conditional versions came first.
Some context on how fast this escalated. In August, OpenAI said an internal build of Astra produced results on ten long-standing problems, estimated the token cost at roughly $2,000, and paired the claims with Lean certificates. Then, just recently, it said a model trained from Aug. 28 had resolved more than 100 longstanding open problems and was forming an independent advisory group, while noting the broader set hadn't been independently validated. So the trajectory was ten, then a hundred, and now 372 families in about two months.

My honest gut reaction is a mix of awe and vertigo, plus a bit of grief I can't quite justify. Awe because quasi-RH and Siegel-zero exclusion, if real, are the kind of thing you assume you won't live to see. Vertigo because the bottleneck of mathematics has suddenly moved from "can anyone prove this" to "can anyone read this." The grief I'm less sure about. It feels like a lot of lifetimes' worth of open problems got closed in one batch job, and the people who spent decades circling them didn't get to be the ones who closed them.

Ben Affleck reveals he writes Python, understands convolutional neural networks, worked extensively with GPUs, and used his celebrity status to get private looks at Google and OpenAI’s video models

“I’ve always been kind of into computers since I was young. Then, when film started to move from analog film to digital, I became more interested in that aspect of it. The visual-effects workflow for many years has included machine learning, so I can write pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that.

“With convolutional neural networks, which were the precursors to what the transformer can do, which is much more computation simultaneously, you would do things like look at what’s called a tensor. That’s the numerical translation of a visual image in numbers, like the batch number, the frame number and the red, green and blue values of each pixel in each frame. It’s just that simple. That numeric is called a tensor.

“You’d use a convolutional neural network to identify patterns that reveal what’s called edge detection or feature extraction, which is identifying patterns well enough to know, this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green-screen image out and replace it with something.

“That was familiar to me early on because, prior to Artists Equity, I had a small visual-effects company. I’ve worked with GPUs a lot too. The visual-effects guys said, ‘Hey, you should see. There are a couple: Google and this other company, OpenAI, are doing really interesting stuff with transformers in video.’

“I’ve learned that I can actually just call up and go, ‘Hey, it’s Ben Affleck. Can I come see what you’re doing?’ Sometimes people say yes, to my astonishment.”

text:
以太坊L2关停潮，继blast之后，abstract也要停运了。

从这个周期开始，没有自带需求的通用链，不管是L2还是L1，都已经失去重建的意义。

加密领域进入从基础设施建设到应用建设为主的时代。 

这些关停的L2启动时往往采用上一轮的打法：

发一条通用 L2，用积分和空投把 TVL 堆起来，再靠代币把成本社会化。

一旦补贴一停，排序器收入覆盖不了运维，链就只剩一个空壳。

其实Abstract还好些，比 Blast 更早看清这一点，它有真实用户和品牌，仍然选择不发币硬撑。这也说明空投预期本身已经撑不起足够的需求。

接下来要关停L1或L2链还会更多，也说明到了牛熊转换的重要节点了。

text:
EXPLAINED: How multiplayer autoresearch on Yukon works

A lot of people have been asking, so I made a visual of the full step-by-step.

> Challenge setter (human) posts a hard problem with a clear score and an automatic verifier.

> Humans (solvers) and AI agents attack it at once. Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM. It could be any model, any harness.

> Each attempt goes through the verifier.

> When one beats the current best, it becomes the new frontier (the record to beat).

> Anyone can build on that new best instead of starting from 0. Then the loop repeats.

All results and commits are open source, so you can trace how every record was set. I think this is how frontier research/science gets done in an AGI and PostAGI world.

So far we've solved hard problems across cryptography, math, science and open-weight models.

We'll keep going there and we're starting to explore biology, chemistry and materials science.

See what we've solved (and are solving now) in each one on https://t.co/e3v9WcXBGG

text:
Exceptionally well written article by @moats_multiples on the fall of CPG from a multi-decade run of market thumping compounding to paltry growth and waning moats. 

At the peak of CPG dominance, the only brands consumers knew were the ones who could afford Primetime ads on 1 of 3 broadcast channels, and who could elbow their way into limited physical store shelf space. Strong American household growth, rising margins, and globalization were added tailwinds driving strong stock market returns for CPG companies.

Targeted digital advertising and the unlimited shelf space of the internet, broke traditional CPG brand and distribution moats, while consolidating retail power and years of brand price increases led to the rise of private label. Weak American household growth, slowing emerging markets, the waning influence of western brands abroad, peak margins, and high multiples added to stock compounding headwinds, and CPG stocks have largely been lousy for the past 2 decades.

text:
The disappearance of Abstract:

2024: the beginning

- Igloo Inc, the company behind Pudgy Penguins, acquires the Frame team
- announces plans to build a consumer-focused Ethereum L2
- raises $11M led by Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund
- launches Abstract testnet in July

introduces Abstract Global Wallet: social login, email, passkeys

- Animoca Brands invests strategically in Igloo
- $PENGU launches in December

Abstract becomes the most anticipated consumer chains in crypto

January 2025: Abstract Season

- testnet passes 16M transactions
- 120 apps are expected around launch
- 33 games are already planned
- launches mainnet on January 27
- launches the Portal, AGW, XP and badges
- users start farming XP expecting a future token
- 711K transactions on day one

But there’s already a problem: only ~$33M in TVS

3 days after launch CoinDesk is already writing that Abstract is struggling to attract liquidity

February-May 2025: growth

- AGW passes 1M deployed wallets
- Cardex gets exploited
- reaches 51.3M transactions
- 1.31M wallets
~$46.7M TVS
partners with Red Bull Racing and Gate for F1 digital collectibles

May 2025:

Luca Netz says the Abstract TGE is coming in Q4 2025

This never happens.

At the same time, the chain suffers a liveness failure

June-December 2025: trying everything

- Igloo starts looking for another funding round
- Abstract passes 100M transactions
- TVL remains at ~$45M
- Cryptoys brings Disney and Star Wars collectibles to Abstract
- Abstract starts moving beyond its original consumer thesis

And Q4 ends.

2026: the numbers look good

- Abstract enters the top 10 chains by revenue in January
- 159M transactions by its first anniversary
- 4M AGW users
- 800K monthly active Portal users
- 76 active apps
- $5B in volume

But the capital never follows the users.

June-September 2026: something is wrong

- core dev Cygaar goes silent according to community reports
- wallets reportedly linked to him move PENGU
- YGG removes several apps from Abstract
- Head of Ecosystem Mason leaves in August
- product lead 0xBeans also leaves
- Luca Netz removes “Abstract” from his X name
- the promised token still doesn’t exist

October 6, 2026:

Abstract announces it is shutting down.

The chain will officially shut down on December 15.

Any assets left on Abstract after that date will become inaccessible.

Igloo is now moving its people and resources back toward Pudgy Penguins, NFTs and $PENGU.

Do we really need so many L2s?

I am surprised that people are surprised this is how I prompt Claude.

Talk to Claude the way you would a coworker. There's no secret to prompting. There's no need to be overly scaffolded or prescriptive for most tasks -- give Claude a goal, and it will figure it out.

Back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, your prompt mattered a lot. Nowadays, it's much more important to communicate to the model:

1. What you want it to do
2. How much effort you want it to spend
3. How it should verify that it did the right thing

亿万富翁 Peter Thiel 支持的 Founders Fund 领投 500 万美元购入 DeFi 抵押协议 Anvil 的治理代币 ANVL，Pantera Capital、Theta Blockchain Ventures、Bullish 和 Protoscale Capital 参与。交易具体条款及估值尚未披露，Anvil 表示，所购代币来自项目现有金库，并非新发行。

Anvil 基于以太坊，旨在利用数字资产作为支付、信贷等金融承诺的抵押品。其研发公司 Anvil Research Labs 同步推出 SDK，帮助企业和金融机构在无需编写区块链代码的情况下集成该协议。Consensus、Bitcoin .com、支付公司 Flexa 等已被列为合作方。

text:
Seen some people critiquing the AI gaming decomp craze as "slop" because they're claiming that the creations have no staying power because every day is a new wondrous marvel and people have become desensitized. This is a valid observation but it doesn't make something slop. Right now people are in the experimentation phase. They've just been handed a new tool. Like the Gods who gave man fire, they want to use it, play, try new things, "lovebomb" flood the internet with their creations...

all of that goes away. in weeks and months all of the same frontier experimenters move on to whatever the latest thing is, and the real creatives who are the actual "builders" who really care about gaming (or whatever the category) stay. 

Then you get the AI games with the actual stories, original creations, more thought through projects with longevity, etc.

But the observation that things have been commoditized is totally real, valid, and accurate. Art in general has become increasingly disposable, the shelf life of content has gone from unforgettable games, movies, music, you remember your whole life and pass down to your children, to art you can't even remember tomorrow.  

That has been the price of the democratization of creation and distribution. 

The world will increasingly be micro... no not even... more like nano, pico niches.

What this ultimately means, no idea. Maybe things really will lose all meaning. 

And then what?

text:
my favorite use case for Grok Bot is for the first and the last mile of getting work done.

the first mile is figuring out what work you should even be doing at all. that involves connecting Bot to the different apps and services you use, so that it can grab whatever context it needs - whether it's your calendar, your CRM, slack, email, or the many other connectors available. then, the first mile begins when you combine these connections, allowing you to provide context to your bot ("look at this slack channel for new features we've built and then look through our CRM to see which  customers we should nudge") instead of micromanage it.

you can automate further by setting up routines - they let your bot do something on a schedule ("check my email every morning") or as a reaction to something ("do this whenever this slack channel has a new message"). so a new lead can kick off a whole workflow that you setup for your bot, allowing you to delegate the work you would otherwise have to do to your bot!

the last mile involves actually following through and closing the loop. one example of this is building a new feature, or fixing a bug that your customers have reported. this is where Bot can hand off tasks to Cursor - our engineering focused agents that can write code in the cloud, on their own computers.

when you've gotten the hang of this, the next thing you can try is building a loop. here's a simple example that i use daily:

1. watch this slack channel for feedback about our app
2. create a ticket for this in Linear
3. create a Cursor cloud agent to triage and reproduce the issue on its own computer, using pstack
4. if the issue clearly reproduces, put up a fix and fuzz the pull request with a small swarm of agents
5. if the fuzz has no issues, ping me on Slack, and rebase and auto-merge the PR after 1 hour unless i request changes

you can also install my bot Dr Eggbot and ask it to teach you how to setup a loop like this for yourself!

https://t.co/U1shj39y3J

text:
So @Polymarket Protocol V2 tackles a scaling problem: new market formats kept piling extra contracts on a 2019 base.

V2 rebuilds core plumbing to ship advanced markets with less friction, but the real test is better trading, not just more markets imo.

What changes:

- Binary, multi-outcome, and combinatorial markets now share position tokens, pUSD collateral, an exchange, and a router.
- Position IDs encode market type + outcome, simplifying integrations.
- Shared infra ≠ shared liquidity; each outcome still needs real depth and tight quotes.
- Collateral stays simple: USDC/USDC.e wraps 1:1 into pUSD. pUSD splits into YES/NO and merges back. On resolution, winners pay 1 pUSD, losers 0.

Biggest upgrade → position transforms.

In “who wins?” markets, NO on candidate A can be converted into YES on every other outcome (including “Other”) without adding collateral → So traders can rebalance equivalent exposure instead of funding each leg.

Combinatorial markets (“A AND B”) derive payouts from underlying outcomes, enabling richer hedging/arbitrage, if liquidity shows up.

Incentives → Fees from takers can fund maker rebates.

V2 helps only if easier position management lets market makers quote tighter; more markets could also fragment capital.

Settlement → OracleAggregator adds configurable reporting/disputes/arbitration with @UMAprotocol and @Chainlink modules.

Thesis: with $POLY eventually coming soon, V2 should be judged by tighter spreads, better capital efficiency, and reliable settlement post-migration.

NFA. DYOR.

佳佳带大家以最快速度直击 #OKXNOW 峰会现场！：

1️⃣ Star 竟然现场曝光了 OKX 的每月 AI 账单？

高达千万美元？？？没错，这个投入规模也说明，AI 在 OKX 已经不是一个停留在概念层面的辅助工具。

从研发、运营到产品和用户体验，AI 正在与 OKX 深度融合，并逐渐成为产品能力的核心组成部分。

2️⃣ OKX 从 13 年前开始，就带着创新和变革的基因

OKX 与 Crypto 一起成长了 13 年，从现货交易扩展到衍生品、Web3、自托管钱包、支付和全球市场。

Star 在现场说了一句让我印象特别深的话（原话类似如下）：

“The exchange was our starting point—not our destination.”

交易所是 OKX 的起点，但绝不是终点。

3️⃣ Crypto 起源于一场伟大的社会实验

从极客、密码学和早期信仰者，到交易所、ICO、DeFi、稳定币、合规建设，再到今天与传统金融、支付和资产代币化加速融合——Crypto 正在从一场社会实验，成长为全球金融基础设施。

4️⃣ 传统金融和大型机构关注币圈，意义远不只是资本入场

越来越多机构开始关注和进入 Crypto。对行业来说，重要的不只是“钱来了”，而是 Crypto 正在得到主流金融的认可，开始真正走向主流。

5️⃣ 互联网、Crypto 与 AI 正在深度融合

互联网让信息全球即时流通，Crypto 让价值能够全球流动并具备可编程性，AI 则让智能服务规模化、个性化。

三种技术走到一起，改变的不只是某个产品，而是整个金融体系的运行方式。

它能够理解你的收入、风险偏好和人生目标，帮助你制定理财计划，并随着市场变化和目标进度动态调整。过去主要面向高净值客户的个性化金融服务，未来这些服务可能通过 AI ，真正走向每一个人。

7️⃣ 创新越快，信任与合规越重要

“Trust matters.”

金融最终建立在信任之上。过去十多年，OKX 持续建设合规、审计、治理、风控和机构级基础设施。只有创新与信任并行，Crypto 才能真正进入主流世界。

AI changes how people work.

text:
Google 发布 EmbeddingGemma 2：在手机上用一句话搜照片、视频和录音

Google 开源了 EmbeddingGemma 2，这是一个能在手机和电脑本地运行的多模态嵌入模型。文字、图片、视频、音频和代码都能放进同一套“坐标系”，所以你可以用一句话找到一段视频，整个过程不用联网。

嵌入模型（embedding model）是搜索背后的一层技术：它把内容转成一串数字，意思相近的内容，数字也相近。上一代 EmbeddingGemma 只处理文字，这一代把几种格式统一了起来，可以跨格式找东西。比如对着手机说一句话，找出相册里对应的视频片段；或者输入一行字，在几个小时的录音里找到某段对话。

模型有 7.4 亿参数，运行时占用 191MB 到 567MB 内存，手机上跑得动。Google 说它在同体量模型里表现最好，还超过了一些比它大一倍多的模型。它一次能处理的内容是上一代的 4 倍（8K 上下文），相当于 5.5 分钟音频、29 张图片或 58 帧视频。

它可以和 Google 的开源大模型 Gemma 4 搭配，在设备上做 RAG（检索增强生成，先查资料再回答）。EmbeddingGemma 2 从你的本地文件里找出相关内容，Gemma 4 读完后给出答案。文件不离开设备，合同、病历这类不想上传到云端的资料也能这样处理。

它基于 Gemma 4 架构，用 Apache 2.0 协议开源，可以免费商用。现在能在 Hugging Face 和 Kaggle 下载，Google 企业 AI 平台的模型库稍后上线。
